(1) *CHAR-1 (Wilful sinning)* — as the prior act that is not acknowledged: Jer 2:35 — the person has sinned (CHAR-1), and the conscience suppression is the refusal to acknowledge the sin; Ecc 8:12 — "does evil a hundred times" (CHAR-1 repeated) while conscience is absent (CHAR-4). (2) *CHAR-6 (Habitual defection)* — as the pattern that sustains conscience suppression: Ecc 8:12 — habitual sinning without conscience-registration is simultaneously habitual defection and conscience suppression. (3) *CHAR-3 (Confession)* — as the absent opposite: Jer 2:35 — "I have not sinned" is the explicit inversion of the confessional "I have sinned." The corpus defines CHAR-4 in large part by the absence of CHAR-3.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Three adjacent characteristics appear consistently. (1) *CHAR-1 (Wilful sinning)* — as the ongoing sinning that the refusal to repent sustains: Heb 10:26 — "go on sinning deliberately" — the deliberate ongoing sinning is both CHAR-1 (the sinning act) and CHAR-5 (the refusal to stop). (2) *CHAR-6 (Habitual defection)* — as the pattern the refusal to repent produces: the Kings corpus's "walked in them" (2Ki 13:6) and "all his days" (2Ki 15:18) describe the habitual defection that sustained refusal establishes. (3) *CHAR-7 (Contagious sin)* — as the communal transmission the refusal enables: "which he made Israel to sin" — the leader's refusal to repent is the mechanism through which the sinful course spreads to the community.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Three adjacent characteristics appear alongside habitual defection in the corpus. (1) *CHAR-5 (Refusal to repent)* — as the volitional sustainer of habitual defection: 1Sa 2:25 — "they would not listen" and Exo 9:34 — "sinned yet again and hardened his heart" both evidence the volitional refusal-to-turn that sustains the habitual pattern. (2) *CHAR-4 (Conscience suppression)* — as the conscience-numbing that enables the pattern: Exo 9:34's progressive hardening operates through the conscience being progressively suppressed (each hardening reduces the conscience's signal strength); 1Sa 2:25's non-listening evidences the same numbing. (3) *CHAR-1 (Wilful sinning)* — as the repeated act that constitutes the habitual pattern: habitual defection is constituted by the accumulation of wilful sinning acts (Ecc 7:20 — "does good and never sins" — the universal sinning confirms all have the underlying acts; Hos 10:9 — "you have sinned... there they have continued").

**[CHAR-7]** E — Three adjacent characteristics appear consistently alongside CHAR-7 in the corpus. (2) *CHAR-6 (Habitual defection)* — as what the community's moral orientation becomes through sustained contagious sin reception: 1Ki 15:34 — "walking in the sin of Jeroboam which he made Israel to sin" — the community walks in the transmitted sin (habitual defection) as the result of the contagious sin reception. (3) *CHAR-5 (Refusal to repent)* — as the Kings formula's "did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam" which accompanies the contagious sin accusation in adjacent verses throughout the Kings corpus.

**[CHAR-8]** E — Two adjacent characteristics appear alongside political revolt in the corpus. (1) *CHAR-19 (Transgression as deliberate boundary-crossing)*: the same root pa.sha (H6586) operates both in CHAR-8 (political-revolt register) and CHAR-19 (personal-moral transgression register). The two share a root but are distinguished by register. (2) *CHAR-20 (Faithlessness as covenant-breaking sin)*: 2Ch 21:10 — "because he had forsaken the Lord, the God of his fathers" — Jehoram's forsaking of the Lord is a faithlessness act (ba.gad-adjacent — betraying covenantal loyalty), which is the inner generating condition that produces the political revolts. CHAR-20 (faithlessness) appears as the inner condition that enables CHAR-8 (political revolt) as its consequence.

**[CHAR-9]** E — Three adjacent characteristics appear alongside sinful speech in the corpus. (1) *M06 (Hate/Contempt)* — flagged in the characteristic definition and VCG headers; VCG-01's slander is cross-registered with M06: Act 6:11's false witness, Eph 4:31's bitterness/anger-driven slander, and Col 3:8's malice-driven slander all carry contempt-toward-persons content that overlaps with M06. (2) *CHAR-1 (Wilful sinning)*: the speech-act of sinful speech is a wilful sinning event (the deliberate utterance of harmful speech — Mat 26:65's "He has uttered blasphemy" names the deliberate act). (3) *CHAR-4 (Conscience suppression)*: the corpus's evidence of conscience-bypassing in sinful speech (1Ti 1:13 — ignorant unbelief; VCG-03 — constitutive defiance) maps onto the conscience-suppression pattern of CHAR-4.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The verse evidence reveals four primary co-occurring characteristics. (1) Righteousness (M26 counterpart): the righteous/wicked contrast is the dominant structural feature of the corpus, present in virtually every VCG — Gen 18:23-25 (VCG-04), Psa 1:1-6 (VCG-04), Psa 37:10-21 (VCG-05/06), Pro 10-21 throughout (VCG-09), Mal 3:18 (VCG-02). (2) Pride (a constituent element — Pro 21:4; Psa 10:2; Isa 13:11 — VCG-03): pride co-occurs as the inner engine driving wickedness. (3) Justice/injustice (M28 or equivalent): the perversion of justice is a repeated co-occurrence — Isa 5:23 (VCG-05), Hab 1:4 (VCG-03), Pro 17:23 (VCG-09), Pro 17:15 (VCG-09). (4) Iniquity (M10b-E in the broader cluster context): ra.sha frequently co-occurs with terminology of iniquity — Psa 10:15 (VCG-05 — "wickedness"), Isa 13:11 (VCG-03 — "wicked for their iniquity"), Eze 3:18 (VCG-07 — "wicked way / wicked iniquity").

**[CHAR-2]** E — Four primary co-occurring characteristics emerge from the 90-verse corpus. (1) The cosmic-evil / evil-one dimension (M27 cross-register — VCG-01, 13V): the cosmic adversarial context co-occurs extensively with the personal constitutional evil, showing they are not independent phenomena but structurally related — the whole world under the evil one's power (1Jo 5:19 — VCG-01) frames the context in which human constitutional evil operates. (2) Unrighteousness (adikia — 8V across VCGs 05/06): co-occurs with kakia and ponēria in the vice-saturation clusters (Rom 1:29 — VCG-05), showing the three terms habitually clustering as expressions of the same constitutional condition. (3) Pride (Jam 4:16 — VCG-06; Mat 20:15 — VCG-06): arrogance/envy as the affective expressions of constitutional inner evil. (4) Faithlessness (Heb 3:12 — VCG-06; 2Th 3:2 — VCG-06): the evil heart fused with the unbelieving heart — faithlessness as the characterising inner posture of constitutional evil.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Four co-occurring characteristics emerge. (1) Wickedness (CHAR-1 — ra.sha): Pro 15:9 (vc=1688 — VCG-01): "the way of the wicked is an abomination"; Pro 15:8 (vc=1678 — VCG-03): "the sacrifice of the wicked"; Pro 17:15 (vc=1690 — VCG-01): "he who justifies the wicked" — the wicked person/way is the most frequent co-occurring subject of abomination. (2) Pride (inner-being adjacent — Pro 16:5 — vc=1689 — VCG-02: arrogant heart; Luk 16:15 — vc=21 — VCG-02: self-justifying pride). (3) Dishonesty/deception (Pro 12:22 — vc=65955 — VCG-02: lying lips; Pro 11:1 — vc=65954 — VCG-01: false balance; Deu 25:16 — vc=65936 — VCG-01: dishonest practice) — deception as inner-character condition co-occurs frequently. (4) Conscience (VCG-04: the conscience in its silenced/awakened states is the most extensively co-occurring inner faculty, present in 11 of 40 verses).

**[CHAR-4]** E — Four primary co-occurring characteristics emerge. (1) Iniquity/evil practice (M10b-E or M10 equivalent): Eze 7:3 (vc=65971 — VCG-05): "judge you according to your ways, and I will punish you for all your abominations"; Eze 18:12-13 (vc=65992-65993 — VCG-05): abomination listed among iniquity, robbery, oppression — iniquity co-occurs throughout. (2) Sexual immorality (M10c/adjacent): Eze 16:36 (vc=65986 — VCG-05): "lust poured out in your whorings with your lovers, with all your abominable idols" — whorings and abominations consistently co-occur in Ezekiel 16 and 23; Jer 13:27 (vc=65905 — VCG-04): "your abominations, your adulteries and neighings." (3) Violence (M02-adjacent): Eze 8:17 (vc=65980 — VCG-05): "fill the land with violence and provoke me still further" — abomination and violence consistently co-occur. (4) Unfaithfulness/harlotry (M10-adjacent): the Ezekiel whoring metaphor throughout VCG-05 — "whoring heart" (Eze 6:9), "whorings" (Eze 16:36; 16:43) — spiritual unfaithfulness as the co-occurring metaphorical characterisation.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Four primary co-occurring characteristics emerge. (1) Deceit/lying: Psa 7:14 (vc=38245 — VCG-02): iniquity "gives birth to lies"; Psa 36:3 (vc=38234 — VCG-04): "words of his mouth are trouble and deceit"; Psa 28:3 (vc=38232 — VCG-03): speak peace while evil in heart — deceptive speech consistently co-occurs with active iniquity-scheming. (2) Violence/bloodshed: Isa 59:7 (vc=38203 — VCG-02): "swift to shed innocent blood"; Hab 1:3 (vc=38194 — VCG-01): "destruction and violence are before me"; Hos 6:8 (vc=38196 — VCG-03): "Gilead is a city of evildoers, tracked with blood" — violence as the physical terminus of inner scheming. (3) Oppression of the weak: Psa 14:4 (vc=38229 — VCG-03): "eat up my people"; Isa 10:1 (vc=38191 — VCG-02): iniquitous decrees targeting the weak. (4) Pride/boasting: Psa 94:4 (vc=38250 — VCG-03): "all the evildoers boast" — arrogant speech co-occurs with the evildoer character.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Three adjacent characteristics appear. (1) Defiance of authority / rejection of divine order — Jude 8 (vc=14354 — VCG-01): "reject authority and blaspheme the glorious ones" — authority-rejection co-occurs directly with blasphemy as its paired expression; (2) Sensory self-indulgence — Jude 8 (vc=14354 — VCG-01): "relying on their dreams, they defile the flesh" — sensory indulgence and authority-rejection co-occur as the inner conditions that produce blasphemous speech; (3) Refusal of repentance — Rev 16:9 (vc=14352 — VCG-01): "they did not repent and give him glory"; Rev 16:11 (vc=14350 — VCG-01): "they did not repent of their deeds" — the absence of repentance is the most consistent co-occurring inner state throughout VCG-01; blasphemy and repentance-refusal are the paired positive and negative expressions of the hardened will.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's co-occurrence pattern reveals two dominant adjacent characteristic clusters appearing across multiple M10b characteristics. First and most universal: the righteous/wicked structural pair (M26 Righteousness). This co-occurrence appears across all six M10b characteristics — Char 1 most explicitly (the dominant structural feature of its corpus: Gen 18:23-25; Psa 1:1-6; Mal 3:18; Pro 10-21 throughout), Chars 3 and 4 (the devious/upright contrast — Pro 3:32; the abomination/delight antithetical structure), Chars 5 and 6 (evildoers contrasted with those who call on God — Psa 14:4; the slandered righteous in VCG-03 — 1Pe 2:12). Second: pride as a co-occurring upstream characteristic. Pride appears as a generator or companion to Chars 1 (Pro 21:4; Psa 10:2-4 — pride driving the God-exclusion constitutive of wickedness), 3 (Pro 16:5 — "everyone who is arrogant in heart is an abomination to the Lord"), and 6 (Jude 8 — sensory self-indulgence and authority-rejection as the enabling inner conditions for blasphemy). Third: unrighteousness/injustice (M28 or equivalent) co-occurring with Chars 1 (Isa 5:23; Hab 1:4), 2 (adikia throughout VCG-05/06), and 5 (Isa 10:1 — iniquitous decrees against the weak).

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-1]** E — Three characteristics appear most frequently adjacent to Characteristic 1 in the 133-verse corpus's cross-register flags and internal evidence: (1) M12 (Purity) — the universal structural opposite, present in every VCG and sub-group of this characteristic; (2) M11 (Cleansing/Restoration) — the remedial counterpart that every defilement-state generates as its necessary response; the cleansing vocabulary (washing, water of impurity, examination-and-clearance) runs throughout M10c-A-VCG-07 (Num 19 corpus) and is signalled in M10c-B-VCG-03 (Lev 22:4 — "until he is clean") and M10c-A-VCG-08 (2Ch 29:5 — "carry out the filth from the Holy Place... consecrate yourselves"); (3) M07 (Shame) — the stigma and social-exclusion register, especially in M10c-B-VCG-03: the public self-declaration (Lev 13:45 "Unclean, unclean"), the enforced isolation (Lev 13:46), and the corporate expulsion of Lam 4:15 carry M07 cross-register content alongside Characteristic 1's condition.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The INTEGRATION_NOTE carry-forward observation specified five cross-register relationships to map at T6. Re-reading §3 fresh, the co-occurring characteristics evidenced are: (1) M10 (Sin-act producing defilement-state): Rom 1:24 (VCG-02) — impurity follows the sin-acts of rejecting God (Rom 1:21-23 context); Gal 5:19 (VCG-02) — "works of the flesh" lists impurity alongside acts of sin; Col 3:5 (VCG-02) — "put to death... sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness" — impurity in a list of sin-items. (2) M11 (Cleansing/Repentance): 2Cor 7:1 (VCG-03) — the call to cleanse from defilement; 2Cor 6:17 (VCG-03) — separation as the condition for divine welcome; Isa 52:11 (VCG-03) — "purify yourselves." (3) M29 (Desire): Rom 1:24 (VCG-02) — "lusts of their hearts"; Col 3:5 — "passion, evil desire, and covetousness." (4) M08 (Pride/Contempt): 2Pe 2:10 (VCG-03) — "despise authority, bold and willful." (5) M09 (Consecration): Rev 14:4 (VCG-05) — the undefiled state defined by following the Lamb; Isa 52:11 (VCG-03) — "purify yourselves, you who bear the vessels of the Lord."

**[CHAR-3]** E — Re-reading §3 fresh. Four adjacent characteristics co-occur most frequently. (1) M10 (Sin-act): The sin-acts that produce corporate/covenantal defilement are pervasive throughout the corpus — idolatry (Eze 20/22/23), sexual violation (Num 5/Lev 18/Eze 22), bloodshed (Eze 22:3-4). The defilement-state is consistently produced by identified sin-acts. (2) M10b (Wickedness/Abomination — INTEGRATION_NOTE carry-forward): The Ezekiel idolatry corpus (VCG-02 — Eze 14:11, 20:7/18/30/31/43, 22:3-4, 23:7/13/17/30/38, and VCG-03 — Eze 5:11, 23:38, 43:7/8) carries an M10b cross-register flag — the same acts are simultaneously "abominations" (M10b) and produce "defilement" (M10c Characteristic 3). (3) M12 (Purity — structural opposite): present as the implied structural opposite throughout all five VCGs. (4) M11 (Cleansing/Restoration): the VCG-05 cleansing-promise corpus (Eze 37:23, Zec 13:1) shows M11 as the necessary response to the corporate/covenantal defilement-state.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Re-reading §3 fresh. Two adjacent characteristics are most prominent. (1) M12 (Purity/wholeness — structural opposite): present in every VCG as the implied structural positive. Luk 6:18 (VCG-02): "cured" — wholeness is the positive M12 state restored. Luk 9:42: "healed" — healing as the M12 state. (2) M27 (Cosmic-evil agents — INTEGRATION_NOTE carry-forward): the unclean spirits operating throughout the 21 verses are the cosmic-evil agents M27 analyses; the same events are simultaneously M10c (the defilement-state produced in the person) and M27 (the agent's nature and action). Mar 3:11 (VCG-03): "You are the Son of God" — the spirits' self-aware adversarial identity is M27 content co-present with M10c's defilement-state content. M11 (Cleansing/healing) is also present: Luk 6:18 — cured; Act 5:16 — healed.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's co-occurrence profiles confirm the four INTEGRATION_NOTEs and surface a consistent cluster-level pattern. Across all four characteristics, two adjacencies are universal: M12 (Purity/Wholeness — structural opposite) and M11 (Cleansing/Restoration — necessary downstream response). These two are the cluster's invariant adjacencies — every register of defilement positions M12 as its structural opposite and M11 as its designed response. Beyond these, each characteristic has its distinctive additional adjacencies. Characteristic 1: M07 (Shame/Stigma — the public declaration and enforced isolation of the disease register). questions.section: T6 — Structural Relationships with Other Characteristics
questions.question_text: What does the co-occurrence pattern show about this characteristic's place in the inner-being landscape?
questions.review_note: Genuinely Stage 2, T0.2.1-class — 'what the co-occurrence pattern shows' is behaviour-synthesis, not a Stage-1 field.

findings.session_b_note:
The co-occurrence pattern reveals several structural positions simultaneously:

**Guilt as structural counterpart (54 shared verses):** The dominant signal — guilt and forgiveness are structurally inseparable. OBS-064-011: "Guilt is the condition forgiveness addresses; the two are structurally counterpart." Forgiveness occupies the position of the primary resolution-characteristic for guilt. No other characteristic has a co-occurrence signal close to this strength (54 vs. 19 at second place).

**Strength as the most unexpected signal (19 shared verses):** DIM-064-SD019 flags this as the "strongest unexpected cooccurrence signal in this registry." Forgiveness and strength co-occur far more than expected — the connection between divine power and the capacity to forgive at scale is embedded in the corpus (Acts 5:31; Num 14:19). Forgiveness operates in the field of divine power, not merely relational gentleness.

**Mercy, repentance, love as relational cluster (16, 12, 10):** The three characteristics that most naturally accompany forgiveness in its relational operation — mercy as the disposition that generates it, repentance as the access-posture that receives it, love as the downstream state it produces. These form a coherent inner-being cluster around forgiveness.

**Faith and authority (9, 10):** The access-instrument (faith) and the claim to exercise the act (authority) both appear in the top tier. Forgiveness is contested in terms of who has authority to exercise it (Mar 2:7) and conditioned by faith as the receiving instrument (Act 10:43).

**The overall position:** Forgiveness occupies a **hub position** in the inner-being landscape — structurally connected to guilt (what it resolves), mercy (what generates it), repentance (what receives it), love (what it produces), faith (how it is received), and strength/authority (the power-field in which it operates). It is not a peripheral characteristic but a central relational node.

findings.session_b_note:
Three structural observations emerge from the co-occurrence pattern:

**Compassion sits at the centre of the love-mercy-kindness cluster (C17).** The three highest co-occurrences — love (196), mercy (76), kindness (20) — are all within-cluster adjacencies. This confirms that compassion is not a peripheral member of C17 but its structural centre of gravity. The dominance of the love co-occurrence (196 verses) raises the question whether compassion and love are truly separable in the programme's data, or whether the vocabulary is naming different aspects of a single phenomenon — a Session D question (SD-001, SD-005, SD-017).

**Compassion is structurally connected to the human relational and volitional response cluster.** Peace (37), faith (37), will (25), surrender (21), seeking (15) — these are all characteristics naming the human person's inner response to or orientation toward God. Their co-occurrence with compassion reveals a pattern: divine compassion generates a cluster of corresponding inner-being responses in the human person. The co-occurrence pattern maps the structural consequence of divine compassion in human inner life.

**Compassion is connected to distress and need as its constitutive context.** Despair (28), distress (16), guilt (17), evil (16) — these are the conditions of human inner life that compassion most consistently addresses. Their co-occurrence confirms what the vocabulary already implies: compassion operates most characteristically in the presence of human need, suffering, and moral failure. The co-occurrence landscape positions compassion as the characteristic most directly responsive to the full range of human inner-being distress.

findings.session_b_note:
The co-occurrence pattern reveals several structurally significant things:

1. **The strength-contrition relationship**: 7 shared verses with R187 (strength) is the single highest co-occurrence. This is analytically unexpected. The most plausible explanation: many of the contrition-vocabulary verses appear in lament and petition contexts where the psalmist appeals to God's strength as the counterpart to their own weakness/crushing. The verse evidence frequently pairs the crushed/contrite condition with an appeal to divine strength. This is a contextual co-occurrence (divine strength appears in the same verse as the contrite person's appeal) rather than a conceptual pairing of strength and contrition as inner-being states.

2. **The despair adjacency**: R044 (despair, 4 shared verses) is the closest expected conceptual companion in the cluster. The crushing vocabulary of contrition and the vocabulary of despair naturally co-occur in anguish and lament contexts. This co-occurrence confirms the boundary question at T1.3: contrition and despair are adjacent but distinct — they share verse contexts but are assigned to different registries.

3. **The guilt co-occurrence**: R073 (guilt, 3 shared verses) is structurally expected — penitential contrition arises from awareness of guilt. The co-occurrence confirms the moral-self-knowledge dimension of contrition. However, the 3-verse shared count is lower than might be expected if contrition were primarily a guilt-response. This suggests the vocabulary of contrition and guilt only partially overlaps in the verse evidence.

4. **The unexpected absence**: **Repentance (R135)** and **brokenness (R018)** — the two registries named in the registry description as directly related — are not in the top 25 co-occurrence list. This is a significant gap: the characteristic described as the precondition for repentance and the interior form of brokenness has minimal direct verse-level co-occurrence with either. This may reflect the fact that the registries draw on different vocabulary families even when describing related inner-being phenomena.

*New finding: the absence of repentance (R135) and brokenness (R018) from the top co-occurrence list, despite being named in the registry description as directly related, is analytically significant. It suggests the vocabulary-level evidence for the connection between contrition and repentance is weaker than the conceptual-level claim. This is a gap that should be captured as an SD pointer.*

findings.session_b_note:
The three-way tie at the top (strength R187, desire R043, evil R057) is analytically significant and unexpected.

**Expected high signals:** Unity (R167, 4 shared verses) and love (R103, 3 shared verses) co-occurring with fellowship are expected — they are structurally adjacent characteristics.

**Unexpected high signals:**
- **Desire (R043, 5 shared verses, highest):** The pairing of fellowship and desire as the most frequent co-occurrence is not anticipated from the surface definition of fellowship. Desire is the motivating inner-faculty that drives seeking. The highest co-occurrence may indicate that fellowship is constitutively desire-linked: the seeking of fellowship is driven by desire, and the fellowship vocabulary appears where desire is most intensely present.
- **Evil (R057, 5 shared verses):** The pairing with evil at the highest level reflects the large proportion of fellowship vocabulary in contexts of wrong fellowship (idolatrous joining, moral complicity, companionship with evildoers, occult charming). Fellowship's most frequent co-occurrence context is not with righteous characteristics but at the boundary with evil.
- **Strength/Might (R187, 5 shared verses; R198, 3 shared verses):** This pairing is not immediately obvious from the fellowship definition. It may reflect the wound-fellowship groups (Isa 53:5, Pro 20:30, Phili 3:10) where suffering and power are adjacent themes.

**New finding:** The co-occurrence pattern reveals that fellowship operates most densely at the moral boundary zone — where the desire-for-connection meets the choice between righteousness and evil. The characteristic is not primarily a positive-association characteristic (it does not co-occur most with love, peace, or joy) but a *boundary* characteristic: it is most active where the relational joining capacity must choose its direction. This is structurally consistent with the six modes of operation (finding 062-OPER-001) — fellowship is morally neutral at the joining level and morally determined by its object.

findings.session_b_note: The co-occurrence pattern reveals that goodness occupies a central position in the inner-being landscape — it co-occurs with characteristics across the full spectrum of the programme's analytical dimensions. The top-25 co-occurrence list includes: strength (R187, 32), love (R103, 28), desire (R043, 27), authority (R197, 25), praise (R121, 22), despair (R044, 22), will (R173, 21), distress (R051, 20), peace (R117, 18), knowledge (R100, 17), innocence (R090, 17). This is an exceptionally broad co-occurrence signature — goodness appears alongside cognitive (knowledge), emotional positive (praise, peace, joy), emotional negative (despair, distress), volitional (will, desire), moral (innocence), and relational (love) characteristics. The breadth confirms that goodness is not a specialist characteristic operating in a narrow domain but one that permeates the whole landscape. The R044 (despair) co-occurrence at 22 is notable — goodness and despair appear together frequently, likely in psalmic lament contexts where the two are in tension or contrast. (OBS-067-OBS-019, OBS-067-OBS-020, SBF-067-Q122)

findings.session_b_note: Three surprising co-occurrences: (a) **Strength (R187, 105) and authority (R197, 69)** — love and power as the second and third highest co-occurrence registers. This is analytically unexpected — strength and authority are C20 cluster characteristics, not C17. The data suggests that love and power are not merely adjacent but structurally co-present in biblical contexts. The 1Cor 13 framework places love above gifts of power ('tongues of angels, gifts of prophecy') — the comparison implies they occupy the same evidential terrain. SD-026 (already raised) addresses this. (b) **Despair (R044, 55)** — despair appearing in the top 10 co-occurrences with love. The lament/petition pattern (despair crying to love for rescue) generates this co-occurrence. Love and despair are structurally linked as the inner state that appeals to love and the love that responds to despair. (c) **Guilt (R073, 32)** — less surprising given SD-028 (forgiveness-love chain) but notable that guilt appears in the top 25 — love and guilt are structurally related at the verse level through the forgiveness-love causal chain.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-103-006: Love's structural position in the programme is that of the central node in the inner-being vocabulary's relational architecture. Co-occurrence data: 196 with compassion, 105 with strength, 68 with pea…
findings.finding_value: Love's structural position in the programme is that of the central node in the inner-being vocabulary's relational architecture. Co-occurrence data: 196 with compassion, 105 with strength, 68 with peace, 62 with faith — confirming love's connections to the full range of C17 characteristics and extending to C20 (strength/authority). Shared anchor data: 48 verses shared across multiple registries, with Exo 34:6 (5 registries) and Gal 5:22 (5 registries) as the highest-density shared anchors — confirming love as the vocabulary cluster around which the programme's most significant cross-registry verses gather. Sequential position: love stands downstream of divine action (received) and upstream of the ethical-moral life (generative of commandment-keeping, Spirit-fruits, community identity). Causal productivity: love generates joy, rest, grief, obedience, praise — the programme's most causally productive characteristic. Vocabulary sharing: term sharing ratio 0.701, the highest in C17 — love shares vocabulary with compassion, mercy, kindness, goodness, desire, and peace. The primary gap: distinctions from adjacent characteristics (compassion, mercy, kindness) remain partially drawn; Session D is the resolution context.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-103-010: Love's comprehensive constitutional location (all five levels) is structurally consistent with its position as the programme's central co-occurrence node. A characteristic that operates at every const…
findings.finding_value: Love's comprehensive constitutional location (all five levels) is structurally consistent with its position as the programme's central co-occurrence node. A characteristic that operates at every constitutional level will co-occur with the broadest range of other characteristics — because any verse that names soul, heart, mind, spirit, or body is potentially within love's evidential terrain. The co-occurrence breadth (top 25 covering registries from C17 through C20 and beyond) reflects the constitutional breadth: strength and authority (C20) co-occur with love because the same verses that address God's inner character include both love and power vocabulary — the divine portrait (Exo 34:6) is constitutionally comprehensive. The vocabulary sharing ratio (0.701 — highest in C17) similarly reflects the constitutional comprehensiveness: love shares vocabulary with compassion (at the somatic/racham level), with goodness (at the heart/tov level), with desire (at the ahav/phileō root level), with peace (at the soul-rest level). Constitutional breadth and vocabulary breadth are the same phenomenon viewed from different angles.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-103-014: The faculty engagement breadth in T3 is consistent with love's structural position as the programme's central sequential node in T6. A characteristic that engages all eleven faculties will necessarily…
findings.finding_value: The faculty engagement breadth in T3 is consistent with love's structural position as the programme's central sequential node in T6. A characteristic that engages all eleven faculties will necessarily stand at the intersection of the programme's full inner-being vocabulary — because any characteristic that engages one faculty will co-occur with love insofar as love also engages that faculty. The memory-faculty engagement explains part of the co-occurrence with despair (R044 — 55 shared verses): lament appeals to the memory of God's love (Lam 3:22) as its ground. The identity-faculty engagement explains the co-occurrence with calling (R019 — 51 shared): identity-as-beloved and identity-as-called are grammatically co-ordinate (Rom 1:7). The moral-sensitivity engagement explains co-occurrence with guilt (R073 — 32 shared): moral sensitivity calibrated by love recognises guilt as the state that precedes the forgiveness that generates love (Luk 7:47). Faculty engagement and structural relationships thus form a coherent explanatory system: the faculty profile generates the co-occurrence pattern.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-103-019: The formation process and the structural relationships are mutually reinforcing systems. The formation pathway (divine love received → Spirit infusion → soul purification → community expression) maps …
findings.finding_value: The formation process and the structural relationships are mutually reinforcing systems. The formation pathway (divine love received → Spirit infusion → soul purification → community expression) maps onto the sequential structural position: love's formation follows the same sequence as love's structural position in the programme — first received (downstream of divine action), then formed (mediating), then expressed (generative of ethical life). The growth-capacity of love (1Th 3:12 — Q&A-092) explains the programme's most puzzling co-occurrence finding: strength and authority (C20, 105 and 69 shared verses respectively). Love growing under the Lord's enabling encounters contexts of power — covenantal love among the people of God is exercised within structures of authority, governance, and strength. The love-power co-occurrence reflects the formation context: love formed within communities is formed within structures of authority. The eschatological trajectory (toward perfect love and direct knowledge) describes the structural relationships' completion: when love reaches its eschatological form, the partial sequential relationships (love received → love given → ethical life) are resolved into the direct love-knowledge of the new covenant (Jer 31:34).

findings.session_b_note: The co-occurrence pattern reveals that mercy occupies a central hub position in the inner-being landscape — it connects to the two poles of human moral condition (guilt/R073 at 75 shared verses) and divine response (compassion/R023 at 76 shared verses), to the power/authority cluster (R187, R196, R197, R198 all in top 25 — SD001 confirmed), and to the relational-emotional cluster (love/R103, peace/R117, despair/R044, distress/R051). *New finding: mercy's co-occurrence pattern positions it as a structural hub connecting the guilt-facing and the grace-giving poles of the inner-being economy — it bridges the human condition (guilt, despair, distress) with the divine provision (love, calling, peace).* OBS-111-021, OBS-111-022.

findings.finding_value: Reading T6 as a whole reveals mercy as structurally integrative — its cross-registry position is not peripheral but central. The T6 synthesis: (a) co-occurrence positions mercy as a hub between the guilt-facing pole (R073 guilt at 75) and the grace-giving pole (R023 compassion at 76) and the power cluster (R187, R196, R197, R198); (b) mercy appears consistently in the middle of inner-being sequences as the bridge from negative condition to positive outcome (Q&A-149); (c) mercy is produced by love and compassion and produces forgiveness, joy, shame, identity, comfort; (d) mercy has constituent status within wisdom (Jam 3:17) and has constituent elements within itself (atonement as mechanism, compassion as motivation, holiness as relational frame); (e) the vocabulary root architecture is theologically coherent (Q&A-157), each root family tracing the full arc of the mercy-event; (f) 16 shared anchor verses confirm mercy's appearance at the intersection of multiple analytical domains (Q&A-165); (g) boundaries with compassion and lovingkindness are partially drawn but require Session D. The T6 synthesis: mercy functions as the structural integrator of the inner-being relational economy — it is the characteristic through which negative conditions are bridged to positive states across the widest range of cross-registry connections in C17.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-012: T1's four-element structure (disposition, mechanism, petition-response, spatial locus) maps to T6's finding that mercy is a structural hub. Each of mercy's four elements connects to a different cluste…
findings.finding_value: T1's four-element structure (disposition, mechanism, petition-response, spatial locus) maps to T6's finding that mercy is a structural hub. Each of mercy's four elements connects to a different cluster of adjacent characteristics: the disposition element connects to compassion/love/anger adjacencies; the mechanism element connects to forgiveness/guilt/atonement adjacencies; the petition-response element connects to prayer/calling/despair adjacencies; the spatial locus connects to holiness/mind/soul adjacencies. Mercy's definitional complexity (T1) is what enables its structural hub position (T6).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-017: T2's soul-level atoning operation (the nephesh addressed by kipper) maps to T6's sequential positioning of mercy (mercy as bridge from negative condition to positive outcome). The constitutionally spe…
findings.finding_value: T2's soul-level atoning operation (the nephesh addressed by kipper) maps to T6's sequential positioning of mercy (mercy as bridge from negative condition to positive outcome). The constitutionally specific operation on the nephesh (T2) is what makes mercy the bridge across the most fundamental negative condition (guilt as soul-condition addressed by atonement). T6's co-occurrence with guilt (R073 at 75) and its cross-registry sequential bridging function are the relational expression of T2's constitutional operation at the soul level. Mercy bridges guilt to forgiveness (T6) because it operates constitutionally on the soul-level guilt-condition (T2).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-021: T3 shows mercy as a faculty-comprehensive characteristic and T6 shows mercy as a structurally integrative hub characteristic. Reading together: the faculty-comprehensiveness (T3) is what enables the s…
findings.finding_value: T3 shows mercy as a faculty-comprehensive characteristic and T6 shows mercy as a structurally integrative hub characteristic. Reading together: the faculty-comprehensiveness (T3) is what enables the structural hub position (T6). A characteristic that activates all (or nearly all) inner faculties is positioned to connect to the widest range of adjacent characteristics — which is exactly what T6's co-occurrence and cross-registry data shows. Mercy's structural hub position in T6 is the cross-registry expression of its faculty-comprehensiveness in T3. The one missing faculty (creativity, T3.5.2 — S) corresponds to the one connection not evidenced in T6 — creative production is not a named output of mercy in the cross-registry data.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-024: T4's asymmetric relational chain (God→human→human) and T6's sequential positioning of mercy as bridge-between-conditions are structurally related. T6 shows mercy appearing between negative conditions …
findings.finding_value: T4's asymmetric relational chain (God→human→human) and T6's sequential positioning of mercy as bridge-between-conditions are structurally related. T6 shows mercy appearing between negative conditions (guilt, despair, distress) and positive outcomes (forgiveness, joy, peace, identity). T4 shows mercy flowing asymmetrically from greater-to-lesser. Reading together: the bridge function T6 identifies is made possible by the asymmetric relational structure T4 describes — mercy can bridge from negative to positive precisely because it flows from a position of greater (God, or the human who has received from God) toward a position of lesser (the guilty, the suffering, the despairing). T4's power-asymmetry requirement is T6's bridge-enabling mechanism.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-026: T5 reveals mercy's formative arc (received → forms capacity → generates pastoral ability) and T6 reveals mercy's structural position as producer of adjacent characteristics (forgiveness, joy, shame, i…
findings.finding_value: T5 reveals mercy's formative arc (received → forms capacity → generates pastoral ability) and T6 reveals mercy's structural position as producer of adjacent characteristics (forgiveness, joy, shame, identity, comfort, peace). Reading T5 and T6 together: the characteristics T6 identifies as mercy's structural outputs (forgiveness, joy, shame, identity) are the same states T5 identifies as mercy's formative sequences. T6's causal and sequential relationships describe the cross-registry structural outcomes of T5's formative process. Mercy's formative arc (T5) moves the person through inner states (joy, shame, identity) that are themselves registered in the co-occurrence data (T6) as adjacent characteristics that appear alongside mercy. The formative sequence is the intra-personal version of the cross-registry adjacency.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-028: T6's finding that mercy is a structurally integrative hub characteristic (Q&A-165) and T7's finding that mercy's vocabulary arc is a theological narrative (Q&A-180) are convergent findings at differen…
findings.finding_value: T6's finding that mercy is a structurally integrative hub characteristic (Q&A-165) and T7's finding that mercy's vocabulary arc is a theological narrative (Q&A-180) are convergent findings at different analytical levels. T6 shows the cross-registry structural integration; T7 shows the lexical-semantic integration. Reading together: mercy's structural integration (T6 — it appears at the intersection of guilt/guilt-resolution, power/compassion, formation/wisdom domains) is lexically grounded in vocabulary breadth and root-level coherence (T7 — root families trace the full mercy arc). T6's term-sharing ratio (0.708) is the quantitative expression of T7's vocabulary arc comprehensiveness. The two tiers together confirm that mercy is both lexically and structurally the most integrative characteristic in C17 — its vocabulary embraces the full semantic arc of the mercy event, and its structural position in the inner-being landscape bridges the widest range of adjacent characteristics.

findings.session_b_note: The co-occurrence pattern reveals contrition as a convergence characteristic — it consistently appears at the intersection of multiple inner-being registers: heart (the moral-evaluative centre), fear (the companion affective posture), and pride (the structural opposite). findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-030-006: T6 as a whole positions contrition within the inner-being landscape as a convergence characteristic with multiple structural connections. The co-occurrence pattern places contrition at the nexus of he…
findings.finding_value: T6 as a whole positions contrition within the inner-being landscape as a convergence characteristic with multiple structural connections. The co-occurrence pattern places contrition at the nexus of heart (R183), fear (R061), pride (R123), sorrow (R151), and fellowship (R062) — all meeting in contrition's primary anchor verses. The causal structure is rich: contrition is causally produced by divine-human encounter; it causally produces divine nearness; it is constitutive of genuine repentance (R135). The vocabulary is sufficiently distinctive (dkh/ktt/nkh root families) that contrition maintains lexical identity even amid these structural connections. The shared anchor analysis confirms Isa 57:15 as the convergence verse — simultaneously registering in divine identity, human moral failure, and creaturely posture registers. T6 synthesis: contrition is a structurally central characteristic that connects multiple inner-being registers (dependence, fear, pride, heart, sorrow, fellowship) while maintaining a distinctive vocabulary and position as the penitential sub-form of creaturely dependence before God.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-030-012: The definition tier (T1) establishes contrition's primary dimension (Dependence/Creatureliness) and its structural opposite (pride); the structural relationships tier (T6) confirms and enriches this t…
findings.finding_value: The definition tier (T1) establishes contrition's primary dimension (Dependence/Creatureliness) and its structural opposite (pride); the structural relationships tier (T6) confirms and enriches this through correlation data. T6's convergence position finding (Q&A-147 — contrition appears where heart, fear, and pride dynamics are simultaneously active) is a structural consequence of T1's definition: a characteristic defined by the collapse of self-sufficiency before God will necessarily appear in the same verses as the characteristics that are most involved in self-sufficiency (pride) and in creaturely orientation toward God (fear, heart). The causal sequence (contrition precedes divine nearness; contrition follows encounter with divine holiness) maps onto the sequential relationships in T6, confirming T1's directional analysis.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-030-021: The faculty tier (T3) establishes that contrition deepens the perceptive capacity for divine address and opens the conscience to receive its verdict; the structural relationships tier (T6) shows that …
findings.finding_value: The faculty tier (T3) establishes that contrition deepens the perceptive capacity for divine address and opens the conscience to receive its verdict; the structural relationships tier (T6) shows that contrition consistently co-occurs with fear (R061 — trembling at God's word) and is causally related to it (Isa 66:2). The faculty engagement (T3) explains the co-occurrence (T6): contrition opens the person to divine address (T3.1) and this openness to divine word is what fear of God (trembling at God's word) also names — they are the same inner orientation named from different perspectives. T3's faculty account of contrition's perceptive opening and T6's co-occurrence data for fear (R061) are mutually explanatory.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-030-024: The relational tier (T4) establishes contrition's primary vertical direction; the structural relationships tier (T6) maps the horizontal co-occurrence pattern. Together they reveal contrition's full r…
findings.finding_value: The relational tier (T4) establishes contrition's primary vertical direction; the structural relationships tier (T6) maps the horizontal co-occurrence pattern. Together they reveal contrition's full relational landscape: primarily vertical (T4) but embedded in a horizontal network of related characteristics (T6 — heart, fear, pride, sorrow, fellowship). The co-occurrence at key verses (Isa 53:5 shared with R062 fellowship and R151 sorrow; Isa 66:2 shared with R061 fear) shows that contrition's primary vertical relationship (human before God) is always mediated through a cluster of associated inner-being characteristics. The structural connections (T6) are the horizontal context within which the vertical relational event (T4) occurs.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-030-026: The formative tier (T5) shows that contrition's formation produces the settled lowliness and word-permeability that Isa 66:2 designates; the structural relationships tier (T6) shows that contrition is…
findings.finding_value: The formative tier (T5) shows that contrition's formation produces the settled lowliness and word-permeability that Isa 66:2 designates; the structural relationships tier (T6) shows that contrition is constitutive of genuine repentance (T6.3). Together T5 and T6 reveal the inner logic of contrition's formative productivity: contrition forms the character that makes genuine repentance possible (T6.3 constitutive relationship) and sustains the inner posture (lowliness, word-permeability) that the structural connections (fear, heart) express in their own vocabularies. The formation account (T5) explains why contrition has such dense structural connections (T6) — it is the inner-being event that produces the character from which the connected characteristics flow.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-030-028: The structural relationships tier (T6) identifies contrition's convergence position (co-occurring with heart, fear, pride, sorrow, fellowship) and its shared anchor verses; the evidential tier (T7) co…
findings.finding_value: The structural relationships tier (T6) identifies contrition's convergence position (co-occurring with heart, fear, pride, sorrow, fellowship) and its shared anchor verses; the evidential tier (T7) confirms that the shared anchor verses (Isa 53:5, Isa 57:15, Psa 34:18) are also the exegetically richest verses in the corpus. The co-occurrence pattern (T6) is not arbitrary — it is grounded in specific verses (T7) that are architecturally complex enough to carry multiple characteristics simultaneously. Isa 57:15 as the convergence verse (T6.6 and T7.2.5) is both the verse with the most shared registries and the most complete single-verse expression of contrition. T6's structural network and T7's verse-level analysis are mutually confirming: the verses that carry the most structural connections are the same verses that are analytically richest.

findings.session_b_note: The co-occurrence pattern reveals fellowship as a relational-formative hub — it consistently appears with desire (the motivating state directing it), unity (its corporate outcome), spirit (its mediating agent), and comfort (its affective product through suffering). findings.finding_value: T6 positions fellowship as a structurally central hub characteristic — it connects desire (R43 — strongest co-occurrence signal), unity (R167 — corporate outcome), spirit (R184 — mediating agent), comfort (R192 — affective product of shared suffering), contrition and sorrow (R30, R151 — shared anchor Isa 53:5), yielding (R180 — shared anchor 2Pe 1:4), covenant (R34 — shared anchor Mal 2:14). Fellowship is structurally upstream of unity (fellowship is the participatory inner reality; unity is its corporate structural expression) and downstream of desire (desire directs fellowship). The vocabulary analysis (T6.4) reveals the root-level connection between wound and companionship (both from chavar) as the deepest structural finding: fellowship and suffering-wounding share the same etymological root, revealing that the deepest fellowship is structurally connected to the deepest wounding.

The love-103 signal (8 shared verses) confirms the downstream love-response as a recurring correlation. OBS-064-011.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-006: T6 reveals compassion as the structural centre of the C17 cluster rather than a peripheral member. The love co-occurrence (196/351 = 55.8% of all OWNER verses) is uniquely dominant — compassion and lo…
findings.finding_value: T6 reveals compassion as the structural centre of the C17 cluster rather than a peripheral member. The love co-occurrence (196/351 = 55.8% of all OWNER verses) is uniquely dominant — compassion and love co-occur in more than half of all active verses, raising the programme-level question whether they are truly separable at the data level. Three structural observations from the co-occurrence landscape: (1) compassion sits at C17's centre of gravity (love, mercy, kindness as top three co-occurrences — all within-cluster); (2) compassion generates a human-response cluster (peace, faith, will, surrender, seeking co-occurring at significant levels — the pattern of divine compassion generating human inner-being responses); (3) compassion is constitutively responsive to human distress (despair, guilt, distress, evil all present in the co-occurrence table — compassion operates most characteristically in the presence of need). The CHASAD root crossing compassion (C17) and shame (C06) is the programme's most structurally unexpected finding — a root family that bridges two clusters. Exod 34:6 as the programme's most multiply-anchored verse (6 registries) must be treated as a cluster-level synthesis anchor. The compassion/mercy boundary (SD-009) is the most critical unresolved distinction. T6.7 (dimensional sharing) is programme-stage limited — formally deferred.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-012: T1's primary dimension (Relational Disposition) and T6's co-occurrence landscape are mutually confirming. The love co-occurrence dominance (196 verses) is the co-occurrence expression of T1's relation…
findings.finding_value: T1's primary dimension (Relational Disposition) and T6's co-occurrence landscape are mutually confirming. The love co-occurrence dominance (196 verses) is the co-occurrence expression of T1's relational-disposition classification: love and compassion co-occur at this extraordinary rate because they share the relational-disposition register. T1's finding that compassion is constitutively outward-facing explains why the co-occurrence landscape shows the C17 cluster (love, mercy, kindness) as the primary co-occurrence family. T6's unresolved compassion/mercy distinction (SD-009) is the most critical consequence of T1's definitional incompleteness — the boundary between compassion and mercy as adjacent Relational Disposition characteristics is the definitional question T1 cannot answer without T6 data.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-017: T2's somatic-constitutional location explains several T6 structural connections. The shared anchor at Isa 53:5 (with R030 contrition) confirms that the somatic wound vocabulary intersects both compass…
findings.finding_value: T2's somatic-constitutional location explains several T6 structural connections. The shared anchor at Isa 53:5 (with R030 contrition) confirms that the somatic wound vocabulary intersects both compassion and contrition at the constitutional-somatic level — both characteristics have somatic-body language as part of their evidential ground. The CHASAD root's crossing of compassion and shame clusters (T6.4 — most unexpected structural finding) is partly explainable from T2: if CHASAD names a covenantal-soul disposition, it can operate in both the positive register (chesed — steadfast love/compassion) and the negative register (bōsheth — shame as the opposite soul-condition of exposed vulnerability). T2's constitutional portrait (soul-body interface) is the constitutional ground for the root-level cluster-crossing that T6 identifies.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-021: T3's finding that compassion is the motivational ground of conscientiousness explains the co-occurrence pattern in T6. Conscience (T3.9) and moral evaluation (T3.8) are the faculties that register the…
findings.finding_value: T3's finding that compassion is the motivational ground of conscientiousness explains the co-occurrence pattern in T6. Conscience (T3.9) and moral evaluation (T3.8) are the faculties that register the pitiable need as a moral claim; compassion is the affective-motivational response that converts that moral knowledge into action. The co-occurrence of will (R173 — 25 verses) and surrender (R156 — 21 verses) in T6 is the co-occurrence expression of T3's volitional faculty finding: compassion engages and redirects the will toward the suffering other. The sequential relationship confirmed in T6 (compassion → mercy — constitutionally causal) is the relational expression of T3's finding that compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action: the mercy-act is the action that compassion's motivation produces.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-024: T4's scope-by-need finding (compassion crosses covenantal boundaries) and T6's co-occurrence landscape (the human-response cluster — peace, faith, will, surrender — co-occurring with compassion) revea…
findings.finding_value: T4's scope-by-need finding (compassion crosses covenantal boundaries) and T6's co-occurrence landscape (the human-response cluster — peace, faith, will, surrender — co-occurring with compassion) reveal a structural pattern: divine compassion reaching across boundaries generates a characteristic cluster of human inner-being responses regardless of the covenantal position of the recipient. The Nineveh response (repentance and turning) and the pattern of peace/faith/will/surrender co-occurring with compassion both confirm this: compassion-received generates a recognisable inner-being response cluster that is structurally consistent across relational positions. T6's mapping of the human-response cluster is the co-occurrence evidence for T4's structural finding about scope and response.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-026: T5's three mechanisms of change explain the structural pattern visible in T6's co-occurrence landscape. The encounter/sudden mechanism (splanchnizō producing immediate transformation) corresponds to t…
findings.finding_value: T5's three mechanisms of change explain the structural pattern visible in T6's co-occurrence landscape. The encounter/sudden mechanism (splanchnizō producing immediate transformation) corresponds to the high co-occurrence with despair (28 verses) and distress (16 verses) — these are the conditions that trigger the sudden compassion-event. The covenantal-sustaining mechanism corresponds to the high co-occurrence with love (196 verses), mercy (76 verses), and covenant (17 verses) — these are the characteristics that share the sustaining, gradual register with chesed. The participatory-ontological mechanism corresponds to the sequential relationship (compassion → mercy confirmed as constitutionally causal in T6.2) — the deepest formation mechanism produces the person who naturally extends mercy as the externalised form of the compassion-character formed within. Formation mechanisms (T5) explain co-occurrence patterns (T6).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-028: T6's structural connections and T7's vocabulary analysis are mutually confirming at the most analytically significant points. The CHASAD root crossing two clusters (T6.4 — most unexpected structural f…
findings.finding_value: T6's structural connections and T7's vocabulary analysis are mutually confirming at the most analytically significant points. The CHASAD root crossing two clusters (T6.4 — most unexpected structural finding) is confirmed and extended by T7's vocabulary analysis: the CHASAD root includes shame as the negative semantic pole embedded within the root itself (T7.1 P5), not as an external antonym. This means the cluster-crossing T6 identifies is not an external structural anomaly but an internal semantic feature: the compassion vocabulary contains its own opposite at the root level. Exod 34:6 as the programme's most multiply-anchored verse (T6.6 — 6 registries) is also T7's most evidentially rich single text — the verse that carries the most structural connections is the same verse that is most analytically central to the vocabulary analysis. The love co-occurrence dominance (T6.1 — 196/351 verses) is confirmed by T7's vocabulary arc: the vocabulary's fullest range (womb to almsgiving) overlaps extensively with the love vocabulary's range, which is why they co-occur across more than half of all active verses.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-006: T6 produces the most structurally significant finding in the review set for any single tier: grace is not produced by any other inner-being characteristic. It is the originating point of a causal chai…
findings.finding_value: T6 produces the most structurally significant finding in the review set for any single tier: grace is not produced by any other inner-being characteristic. It is the originating point of a causal chain, not its product. This categorically distinguishes grace from every other characteristic reviewed — all others can be produced by at least one other characteristic; grace cannot. This structural uniqueness is confirmed by T2.9's origin analysis (grace originates with God — it does not originate in the human constitutional system) and is analytically consistent across T6.2 (seeking is the posture before grace arrives, not its producer), T6.3 (S-rating on "is grace produced by another characteristic"), and T6.4 (the vocabulary's structural completeness without a generative human-side term). The co-occurrence pattern reveals grace at the intersection of divine initiative and creaturely need: seeking (R140 — 40 verses, dominant) as the creature's pre-grace posture; moral failure cluster (evil, guilt, sin, transgression) as the creaturely context; power cluster (strength, might) confirming the 2Cor 12:9 connection. The love co-occurrence (R103 — 14 verses) is the primary within-cluster signal raising the grace-love boundary question (SD013). All major boundary distinctions (grace-love, grace-mercy, grace-justice, grace-chesed) remain open at T6.5 — the most unresolved boundary cluster in the review set. T6.7 (dimensional sharing) is programme-stage limited.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-012: T1's dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) and T6's co-occurrence pattern are mutually confirming. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (R140 — 40 verses) is the co-occurrence ex…
findings.finding_value: T1's dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) and T6's co-occurrence pattern are mutually confirming. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (R140 — 40 verses) is the co-occurrence expression of T1's finding that grace requires the receptor's inner posture of appeal: seeking is the relational posture before grace arrives, and the vocabulary encodes this (tachanum — built into the same root as chen). T6's structural uniqueness finding (grace is not produced by any other characteristic) is T1's definitional consequence: because grace is constitutively the uncaused inclination of the greater toward the lesser, it cannot be produced by anything in the lesser's constitutional system. T1's definition predicts T6's structural uniqueness.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-021: T3's faculty findings explain several patterns in T6's co-occurrence landscape. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (R140 — 40 verses) is partly explained by T3.6's agency-constituting finding: seekin…
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty findings explain several patterns in T6's co-occurrence landscape. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (R140 — 40 verses) is partly explained by T3.6's agency-constituting finding: seeking requires the constituted agency that grace provides for its own reception (SD026 — grace giving the capacity for supplication). The power cluster co-occurrences (strength R187 — 15 verses, might R198 — 10 verses) confirm T3.7's agency-constituting finding at the cross-registry level: grace producing agency is registered as co-occurring with power/strength across the corpus. T3.8's moral clarity finding explains the guilt co-occurrence (R073 — 10 verses): the moral clarity grace produces is most visible at the point of moral failure, and the co-occurrence reflects this — grace and guilt appear together because grace produces the moral clarity that accurately names the guilt it addresses.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-024: T4's relational architecture and T6's co-occurrence network express the same structural reality from relational and cross-registry perspectives. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (T6 — R140, 40 vers…
findings.finding_value: T4's relational architecture and T6's co-occurrence network express the same structural reality from relational and cross-registry perspectives. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (T6 — R140, 40 verses) is the co-occurrence expression of T4.2 (the human-to-God supplication direction): seeking is the relational posture, and R140 is the registry that names it. The sequential relationship confirmed in T6.2 (grace precedes and enables faith, repentance, supplication, mourning — SD003, SD006, SD026, SD038) is the causal expression of T4's architectural finding: grace is the enabling condition for every positive human-to-God relational posture. The boundary questions in T6.5 (grace-love, grace-mercy, grace-chesed) correspond to T4.5's scope analysis: the characteristics that share grace's scope (particularly love and mercy) are the same characteristics whose relational scope overlaps with grace's at T4.5.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-026: T5's five formation mechanisms explain the structural pattern visible in T6's co-occurrence and sequential landscape. The encounter mechanism (sudden grace-event) corresponds to the sequences confirme…
findings.finding_value: T5's five formation mechanisms explain the structural pattern visible in T6's co-occurrence and sequential landscape. The encounter mechanism (sudden grace-event) corresponds to the sequences confirmed in T6.2 (grace precedes and causes the immediate responses of mourning, fear, supplication — SD038, SD026). The word mechanism (Act 20:32) corresponds to the faith co-occurrence (R059 — 10 verses): the proclaimed word that carries grace produces faith as its response. The inference mechanism (Rom 8:32 — assurance derived by reasoning) corresponds to the hope and peace co-occurrences (R117 — 10 verses): reasoned assurance from grace produces the inner peace and hope co-occurring registries name. The mediated-transformation mechanism (tenderheartedness → forgiving) produces the love co-occurrence (R103 — 14 verses) as tenderheartedness is the inner precondition of the forgiving that love and grace share. T5's mechanisms generate T6's structural connections.

findings.session_b_note: The co-occurrence pattern reveals that covenant occupies a structurally central position in the inner-being landscape — it is co-present with characteristics across multiple dimensions and domains. Three observations: (1) Central hub status: covenant co-occurs with the widest range of inner-being characteristics of any word in the C17 cluster expected — it is not specialist but generalist in its inner-being neighbourhood. This is consistent with the DIM-34-SD001 hypothesis (covenant as C17 structural backbone — OBS-034-002). (2) Inner organ dominance: the strongest co-occurrences are with the inner organs (mind 39, Soul 19, heart 14) — confirming that covenant's primary inner-being site is the core constitutional organs, not peripheral characteristics. (3) Relational-grace cluster coherence: the C17 cluster characteristics (love, compassion, faithfulness, kindness) all appear in the top co-occurrence table — covenant and the relational-grace vocabulary are structurally inseparable in the verse evidence. This co-occurrence coherence supports treating C17 as a genuine cluster rather than an administrative grouping.

The co-occurrence data (Q&A-147) shows covenant occupying a central hub position in the inner-being landscape — co-present with the widest range of characteristics across multiple dimensions. T6 as a whole establishes that covenant is not one characteristic in a relational cluster but the architectural backbone of the cluster — the structural condition of possibility for the other C17 characteristics.

findings.finding_value: M01-A's co-occurrence with wisdom, obedience, humility, trust, and love reveals that reverential fear of God is a foundational characteristic — it is the ground from which these others grow. The direction of the co-occurrence is consistently: fear as ground, wisdom/obedience/humility/trust as fruit. This places M01-A at the deep structural layer of the inner-being landscape rather than as one among many equal characteristics.

The co-occurrence pattern places M01 in a structurally central position in the inner-being landscape: reverential fear (M01-A) is adjacent to and foundational for wisdom, obedience, humility, and trust. Disordered fear (M01-B's social register, M01-F, G) is adjacent to and opposed by faith/trust and love. The cluster occupies a pivotal position — ordered fear enables the full range of positive inner-being characteristics; disordered fear suppresses them.

The co-occurrence pattern reveals that anger rarely operates as an isolated single state. It is consistently embedded in a complex of related characteristics: anger co-occurs with grief (they can coexist in the same moment), with jealousy (jealousy is a frequent trigger and companion), with pride (wounded honour as a frequent anger-source), and with judgment/wrath (the three named components of the cluster internally co-occur). The pattern suggests anger is the affective expression of a broader moral-relational complex involving assessment of wrongdoing, wounded relational investment, and consequential response.

The co-occurrence pattern reveals M03 as a deeply embedded cluster in the inner-being landscape — grief is not an isolated characteristic but one that regularly co-occurs with the full range of other inner-being states. Most significantly: grief co-occurs with prayer (M21), repentance (M11), hope (M18), and joy (M04) in the positively-directed registers; and with fear (M01) and weakness (M24) in the distress registers. This suggests that grief is a primary inner-being transitional state — a state through which the person moves toward other states, both by God's action (mourning into dancing, distress into deliverance) and by the person's own response (grief into prayer, godly grief into repentance).

**[CHAR-1]** E — Gladness and exultation are regularly paired in the evidence as a natural inner-state cluster — they appear to co-occur so frequently that they may constitute a characteristic pair. Exultation appears to be the more intense, more directional member of the pair; gladness the more diffuse and sustained. The pattern suggests they are related but distinct inner states that naturally accompany each other in worship and celebration contexts.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The co-occurrence pattern reveals that Joy does not operate in isolation but as part of a cluster of positive inner-being states that mutually reinforce each other. Gladness and Joy are the closest and most frequently co-occurring pair — confirming the characteristic-map analysis that they are distinct but adjacent inner-being states. The formula "joy and gladness" throughout the prophetic and historical books is a literary and theological convention reflecting their natural paired experience. The Exultation-Joy pairing (gil + sa.mach) confirms that at the highest moments of divine encounter, Joy rises toward Exultation. The Wonder co-occurrence at the resurrection appearances shows that Joy and Wonder arise simultaneously at the most extraordinary divine events.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Suffering-Joy co-occurs most consistently with Joy (Characteristic 2) — confirming the analytical judgment that they are related but distinct: Suffering-Joy is Joy in its most paradox-sustaining, Spirit-enabled form operating in the specific context of suffering. The co-occurrence reveals they are on a continuum rather than entirely separate. M04-F's adjacent absence-of-comfort (mav.li.git) shows the characteristic negatively defined: what Suffering-Joy is not is the state of grief-without-comfort that replaces it when the Spirit's enabling is absent.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The Joy/Gladness co-occurrence confirms the boundary established in the characteristic map and in Characteristic 2's Phase 9: the two characteristics are distinct but naturally adjacent inner states that arise together in the same circumstances. Joy is the active-participatory face; Gladness is the warm-settled cognitive face; they co-occur because genuine encounter with divine goodness produces both the active rejoicing (Joy) and the settled recognition (Gladness) simultaneously. The Praise co-occurrence confirms Gladness as a fundamentally doxological characteristic at its divine-recognition level — recognising God as good naturally overflows into praise-declaration.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Three analytically significant co-occurrence patterns: (1) **Joy-Delight co-occurrence** (Jer 7:34 etc.) confirms adjacency while also confirming distinction — they are silenced together because they are distinct but related forms of positive inner orientation; (2) **Delight-Obedience integration** (M04-M) shows the most distinctive Delight co-occurrence not found in other M04 characteristics: Delight and obedience are constitutively linked in this corpus; pleasing God through commandment-keeping is the form Delight takes in the obedience register; (3) **Delight-Love adjacency** (Jer 31:20; 1Th 2:8) reveals Delight as the pleasurable dimension of Love — they co-occur because Love-without-Delight is obligation without pleasure, and Delight-without-Love lacks the relational commitment that gives Delight its relational grounding.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The tov-na.im pairing of Psa 133:1 ("how good and pleasant") confirms Pleasure as the experiential-felt quality that accompanies and completes Gladness's evaluative-cognitive goodness: Gladness says "this is genuinely good"; Pleasure says "and it feels agreeable." The Pleasure-Peace pairing (Pro 3:17) confirms Pleasure as the inner experiential quality of wisdom's path — wisdom's good is experienced as both pleasant (inner felt quality) and peaceful (inner settled state). The co-occurrence reveals Pleasure as consistently the felt-experiential dimension of what other characteristics evaluate or choose.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The consistent pairing of Wonder with thanks and praise (Psa 9:1; 107:8, 15, 21, 31) confirms Wonder as the motivational source of doxological praise — not merely an inner feeling but the characteristic that drives the praise-response. The pairing of Wonder and fear (Exo 34:10; Mar 10:32) confirms their adjacency while preserving their distinction: fear is the threat-response to encountered power; Wonder is specifically the astonishment-response to what exceeds categories. The Tell-Remember-Meditate triad's consistent co-occurrence with Wonder confirms memory and proclamation as Wonder's defining co-practices.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The co-occurrence patterns reveal the cluster's internal architecture: Joy and Gladness are the most closely paired because they are the two faces of positive inner experience — Joy is the active-participatory face, Gladness the settled-warm face — and genuine encounter with God typically produces both simultaneously. The Joy/Exultation pair confirms that exultation is Joy at its highest intensity. The Joy/Suffering-Joy lexical sharing (agalliao) confirms that Suffering-Joy is not a separate inner-being reality but Joy in its most paradox-sustaining Spirit-enabled form. The Gladness/Pleasure pairing (Psa 133:1's tov + na.im) confirms that Gladness evaluates what is good while Pleasure feels what is agreeable — they are the cognitive and experiential faces of the same reality. The cluster's co-occurrence pattern is structured: not random adjacency but systematic relationships between characteristics that reflect their genuine phenomenological kinship.

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-1]** E — CHAR-1 is a relational characteristic that attracts co-occurrence with its primary causes (contempt producing shame), its outer form (humiliation), and its structural opposites (honour, innocence). The pattern reveals CHAR-1 as positioned at the intersection of three axes: the moral axis (guilt → shame → correction or hardening), the relational axis (contempt/dishonour → shame → withdrawal or endurance), and the divine-encounter axis (sin → guilt-shame → gateway to God or seared conscience). CHAR-1's place in the inner-being landscape is as the emotional-moral register of the person's standing — it co-occurs with whatever challenges, strips, or exposes that standing.

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 co-occurs most significantly with CHAR-1 (shame as experienced inner state): enforced humiliation typically produces the felt inner shame-experience (Jer 48:39 — "turned his back in shame, Moab has become a derision" shows both simultaneously). CHAR-2 also co-occurs with CHAR-5 (contempt producing shame): the violent treatment of the vineyard servants (VCG-01) overlaps with the contempt-mechanism of CHAR-5.

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 co-occurs most significantly with CHAR-5 (shame produced by contempt): the contempt-mechanism (CHAR-5) is frequently the source of the worth-denial (CHAR-3). CHAR-3 also co-occurs with CHAR-1 (felt shame) as the relational cause of CHAR-1's felt experience in the dishonoured person.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 co-occurs with CHAR-1 in the M07-B seared-conscience register (the loss of the capacity for shame = the loss of CHAR-4's functioning). The absence of CHAR-1's corrective shame-experience is simultaneously the loss of CHAR-4's evaluative operation. CHAR-4 also co-occurs with CHAR-6 (innocence as structural counter to shame) — the blameless conscience of CHAR-6 is the positive form of what CHAR-4's functioning conscience is oriented toward.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — CHAR-5 co-occurs most significantly with CHAR-3 (dishonour as relational worth-denial): contempt-produced shame is a specific form of worth-denial, and the two characteristics share vocabulary (atimazō, exoutheneō) and often describe the same event from different analytical angles. CHAR-5 also co-occurs with CHAR-2 (enforced humiliation): VCG-02's violent rejection (servants beaten) is simultaneously CHAR-5 (contempt producing shame in the recipient) and CHAR-2 (enforced downward movement of standing). CHAR-5 is causally related to CHAR-1: the contempt received (CHAR-5) produces the felt inner shame-experience (CHAR-1) in the recipient.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-6 co-occurs most significantly with CHAR-1 (shame as experienced inner state) in its M07-C register: the guilt-shame of M07-C (the face that cannot be lifted before God, Ezr 9:6) is the condition that CHAR-6 structurally counters. Where CHAR-6 is present, M07-C's guilt-shame is absent; where CHAR-6 is absent, M07-C's guilt-shame is appropriate and present. CHAR-6 also co-occurs with CHAR-4 (shamefulness as moral-evaluative judgment): CHAR-4's functioning conscience is the evaluative operation; CHAR-6 is the positive moral condition that results when the conscience's evaluation finds no deliberate wrongdoing.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — Within M07, the co-occurrence patterns reveal four consistent pairings. (1) Chars 1 and 2 co-occur most frequently — the felt inner shame and the enforced outer humiliation regularly appear in the same verse as inner and outer faces of the same event (Jer 48:39 — "Moab has turned his back in shame" shows both). (2) Chars 3 and 5 co-occur regularly — dishonour-as-worth-denial and contempt-as-specific-mechanism frequently describe the same act from different analytical angles (atimazō in Mar 12:4 covers both). (3) Chars 1 and 6 are structurally paired opposites — guilt-shame (Char 1 M07-C) and innocence (Char 6) are the polar states of the conscience: Psa 119:80 ("may my heart be blameless... that I may not be put to shame") expresses their direct structural relationship. (4) Chars 4 and 6 co-occur logically — the functioning conscience that identifies the shameful (Char 4) is the same conscience whose clean condition constitutes innocence (Char 6). The cluster's internal co-occurrence structure: 1+2 (experience and mechanism), 3+5 (relational act and contempt-mechanism), 1+6 (guilt-shame and its counter), 4+6 (conscience's evaluative and integrity modes).

---
