questions.section: T6 — Structural Relationships with Other Characteristics
questions.question_text: Does the sharing extend to root-level architecture — a shared root generating terms across two or more characteristics?
questions.review_note: Same two-stage dependency as T6.4.1, plus a lemma/root match across two characteristic-candidates' term families.

findings.session_b_note:
The data partially evidences this and the finding is significant:

**The aphiēmi root across multiple semantic directions within the registry:** All three G0863 variations (G, H, I) derive from the same root — aphiēmi — and are present in this registry. This root generates: the forgiveness-sense (G0863H), the leaving/forsaking-sense (G0863G), and the permitting-sense (G0863I). The shared root architecture within the registry is already acknowledged in OBS-064-026: "the same aphiēmi that releases sin (forgiveness) releases family and property (discipleship)."

**The aphiēmi root connection to calling (R019):** DIM-064-SD009 identifies the leaving-act shared with calling (019) — the discipleship-leaving (G0863G) connects the forgiveness vocabulary to the calling vocabulary at the root level. Mar 10:29 (anchor for group 5376-001) is the leaving-act in response to the call — the same root (aphiēmi) appears in the forgiveness registry and is structurally connected to the calling registry through shared act-structure.

*New finding:* The aphiēmi root is not merely an intra-registry structural element but a **cross-registry root connector** — linking forgiveness (G0863H) to calling/discipleship (G0863G as leaving-act) through shared root architecture. This cross-registry root connection has not been formally identified as a vocabulary-sharing finding in the existing analysis. The zero shared_term_count reflects the XREF mechanism's limitation, not the actual root-level connection.

findings.finding_value: T6 confirmed that goodness has the most extensive vocabulary-sharing and cross-registry connection pattern of any characteristic analysed so far in the programme. T7 confirms through the vocabulary arc (Q&A-177) that this extensiveness is a lexical reality, not a programme classification artefact: the three root families (TOV, AGATHO, CHRESTO) each generate multiple terms distributed across multiple registries because the semantic ranges genuinely overlap. The vocabulary sharing (T6.4) is not the result of how the programme has drawn its boundaries — it reflects the actual lexical distribution of the Hebrew and Greek goodness vocabulary, which crosses conceptual boundaries that English vocabulary maintains more distinctly. The three-stage vocabulary arc (H2896A breadth → agathōsunē precision → chrēstotēs precision) tracks the same movement as the cross-registry distribution pattern: H2896A generates the widest distribution (TOV root to R103, to R42, to multiple other registries); the NT precision terms (G0019, G5544) generate narrower distributions (R65 and R99 respectively). As the vocabulary narrows to precision, the cross-registry connections narrow correspondingly. T6's structural pattern and T7's lexical arc describe the same underlying phenomenon: goodness vocabulary begins broad and specialises, and its cross-registry connections follow the same trajectory.

findings.finding_value: Love's structural position in the programme is that of the central node in the inner-being vocabulary's relational architecture. Co-occurrence data: 196 with compassion, 105 with strength, 68 with peace, 62 with faith — confirming love's connections to the full range of C17 characteristics and extending to C20 (strength/authority). Shared anchor data: 48 verses shared across multiple registries, with Exo 34:6 (5 registries) and Gal 5:22 (5 registries) as the highest-density shared anchors — confirming love as the vocabulary cluster around which the programme's most significant cross-registry verses gather. Sequential position: love stands downstream of divine action (received) and upstream of the ethical-moral life (generative of commandment-keeping, Spirit-fruits, community identity). Causal productivity: love generates joy, rest, grief, obedience, praise — the programme's most causally productive characteristic. Vocabulary sharing: term sharing ratio 0.701, the highest in C17 — love shares vocabulary with compassion, mercy, kindness, goodness, desire, and peace. A characteristic that operates at every constitutional level will co-occur with the broadest range of other characteristics — because any verse that names soul, heart, mind, spirit, or body is potentially within love's evidential terrain. The co-occurrence breadth (top 25 covering registries from C17 through C20 and beyond) reflects the constitutional breadth: strength and authority (C20) co-occur with love because the same verses that address God's inner character include both love and power vocabulary — the divine portrait (Exo 34:6) is constitutionally comprehensive. The vocabulary sharing ratio (0.701 — highest in C17) similarly reflects the constitutional comprehensiveness: love shares vocabulary with compassion (at the somatic/racham level), with goodness (at the heart/tov level), with desire (at the ahav/phileō root level), with peace (at the soul-rest level). Constitutional breadth and vocabulary breadth are the same phenomenon viewed from different angles.

findings.finding_value: The structural relationship data and the evidential foundation are the most mutually confirming pair in the synthesis matrix. The co-occurrence breadth (T6.1) is directly explained by the vocabulary breadth (T7.1.10 — the widest semantic arc in the programme): a vocabulary that spans from divine being to love of darkness will co-occur with every other inner-being characteristic because it occupies every register of the inner-being vocabulary. The shared anchor density (48 verses — T6.6) is explained by the primary anchor's function (Lam 3:22 — T7.2.5/T7.2.6): the programme anchors the most significant cross-registry verses at love because love is the definitional centre from which adjacent characteristics derive their meaning. The vocabulary sharing ratio (0.701 — T6.4) is explained by the root-level connections (T7.1.2): the racham root connects love, compassion, and mercy; the ahav root connects love and desire; the tov root connects love and goodness. The structural relationship data is, at its core, the observable programme-level effect of the lexical architecture that the evidential foundation analysis reveals. Structural breadth and lexical breadth are the same reality at different levels of analysis.

findings.finding_value: T6 reveals compassion as the structural centre of the C17 cluster rather than a peripheral member. The love co-occurrence (196/351 = 55.8% of all OWNER verses) is uniquely dominant — compassion and love co-occur in more than half of all active verses, raising the programme-level question whether they are truly separable at the data level. Three structural observations from the co-occurrence landscape: (1) compassion sits at C17's centre of gravity (love, mercy, kindness as top three co-occurrences — all within-cluster); (2) compassion generates a human-response cluster (peace, faith, will, surrender, seeking co-occurring at significant levels — the pattern of divine compassion generating human inner-being responses); (3) compassion is constitutively responsive to human distress (despair, guilt, distress, evil all present in the co-occurrence table — compassion operates most characteristically in the presence of need). The CHASAD root crossing compassion (C17) and shame (C06) is the programme's most structurally unexpected finding — a root family that bridges two clusters. Exod 34:6 as the programme's most multiply-anchored verse (6 registries) must be treated as a cluster-level synthesis anchor. The compassion/mercy boundary (SD-009) is the most critical unresolved distinction. T6.7 (dimensional sharing) is programme-stage limited — formally deferred.

findings.finding_value: T6 produces the most structurally significant finding in the review set for any single tier: grace is not produced by any other inner-being characteristic. It is the originating point of a causal chain, not its product. This categorically distinguishes grace from every other characteristic reviewed — all others can be produced by at least one other characteristic; grace cannot. This structural uniqueness is confirmed by T2.9's origin analysis (grace originates with God — it does not originate in the human constitutional system) and is analytically consistent across T6.2 (seeking is the posture before grace arrives, not its producer), T6.3 (S-rating on "is grace produced by another characteristic"), and T6.4 (the vocabulary's structural completeness without a generative human-side term). The co-occurrence pattern reveals grace at the intersection of divine initiative and creaturely need: seeking (R140 — 40 verses, dominant) as the creature's pre-grace posture; moral failure cluster (evil, guilt, sin, transgression) as the creaturely context; power cluster (strength, might) confirming the 2Cor 12:9 connection. The love co-occurrence (R103 — 14 verses) is the primary within-cluster signal raising the grace-love boundary question (SD013). All major boundary distinctions (grace-love, grace-mercy, grace-justice, grace-chesed) remain open at T6.5 — the most unresolved boundary cluster in the review set. T6.7 (dimensional sharing) is programme-stage limited.

They confirm each other from different analytical directions: T2 establishes that there is no constitutional source for grace within the human person; T6 establishes that there is no characteristic-level source for grace within the programme's inner-being landscape. The vocabulary's structural completeness (T7 — but relevant here as T6.4) reflects this constitutional uniqueness: because grace originates entirely from outside the human system, its vocabulary must encode the full two-sided circuit (giving and receiving) from within a single root, with no gap left for a generative human-side term.

Its five-dimensional breadth (MC, RD, Cognition, Transformation, DHC) means it shares dimensional territory with virtually every adjacent characteristic. Its co-occurrence breadth (14 registries ≥6 shared verses) and shared-anchor density (12 shared anchors across 9 registries) confirms the hub position empirically. The sequential relationships (giving→worship, suffering→giving, faithlessness→giving-over) show it operating as both a causal initiator and a causal consequence in relation to other characteristics. The aman root architecture reveals that R060, R059, and R044 are conceptually entangled at the root level — the programme's separation is analytical, not lexical. The distinction from nearest neighbours (hesed/R099, love/R103) is of kind — dispositional vs. actional — confirming that R060 holds a distinct structural position as the actional realisation of what the dispositional characteristics name. What T6 reveals as a whole: this characteristic is not isolated in the inner-being landscape; it is a connector through which multiple adjacent characteristics are expressed, related, and developed.

findings.finding_value: The structural landscape analysis (T6 — hub position, aman root architecture entangling R059/R044/R060, distinction of kind from nearest neighbours) and the vocabulary/methodological analysis (T7 — full vocabulary arc, grammatically actional, primary anchor Hos 11:8) produce the final convergent finding. The aman root architecture (T6.4.2, Q&A-157) and the vocabulary arc (T7.1.10, Q&A-179) are describing the same reality: the programme's separation of registries by word is an analytical convenience that cuts across a root-level unity. The vocabulary arc — enacted pole (na.tan/verb) + constituted pole (emunah/hesed/pistis/nouns) — names the same reality that the root architecture identifies: the aman root generates both the dispositional terms and the contextual terms, while na.tan provides the enacted verbal expression. The grammatically actional character of na.tan (T7.1.2, Q&A-171) is the structural reason for its distinction-of-kind from the nominal faithfulness vocabulary (T6.5.3, Q&A-162). What this pair reveals as the final synthesis: the vocabulary evidence and the structural landscape evidence independently converge on the same conclusion — this characteristic is the enacted form of what the faithfulness vocabulary names dispositionally, and this distinction is fundamental to understanding both the characteristic itself and its position in the inner-being landscape.

findings.finding_value:
Root-sharing reveals three structural bridges:

1. **Wisdom-knowledge-understanding bridge (cha.kham/ya.da/bin):** The three primary characteristic-triad sub-groups share their root families broadly — confirming they are structurally continuous, not discrete. They describe the same inner reality from three complementary perspectives.

2. **Evaluation-planning bridge (cha.shav):** The same root covers evaluative thinking (M15-D VCG03/04) and purposive devising (M15-E VCG05), confirming that evaluation and planning are cognitive partners within the cluster.

3. **Word-reflection-evaluation bridge (logos family):** G3056, G1260, G1261, G3053 connect M15-H (word), M15-F (reflective reasoning), and M15-D (evaluative argumentation) — suggesting that the cluster's communicative, reflective, and evaluative activities share a common conceptual foundation in the logos-reason tradition.

Three root families are especially significant: (1) **The tov root** — tov as noun, adjective, comparative, and negation spans Gladness (Char 3) and portions of Delight and Pleasure, making it the most structurally foundational root in M04; (2) **The agalliao/agalliasis root** — generates Joy's most intense register and Suffering-Joy's entire primary register; the root-family structure reveals these as one characteristic's two contextual forms rather than two entirely separate characteristics; (3) **The pa.la/pe.le/miph.la.ah root** — the Wonder root family dedicated to M04-I, the most root-concentrated vocabulary in the cluster; Wonder's root-family loyalty (the root not shared across multiple characteristics, unlike tov) confirms Wonder as the most lexically bounded characteristic in M04.

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. The *bosh* root (H0954) generates *bosh*, *bo.shet*, *bu.shah*, *bosh.nah* — all within CHAR-1. The *aischun-* root generates *aischunē*, *aischunō*, *kataischunō* — also largely within CHAR-1 with some extension to M07-D. The *ke.lim.mah/ka.lam* root spans CHAR-1 (inner experience) and CHAR-2 (outer humiliation), revealing at the root level that the experience and the abasement are linguistically proximate phenomena.

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 shares vocabulary significantly with CHAR-1: ka.lam, bosh, bo.shet, ke.lim.mah all appear in both. The distinction is the verse-emphasis: when the term names the enforced outer mechanism, it is CHAR-2; when it names the felt inner collapse, it is CHAR-1. Vocabulary sharing reflects the fact that inner and outer are aspects of the same shame-event differently observed.

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 shares atimazō and atimia with CHAR-1 (where these terms name the felt experience of dishonour) and with CHAR-2 (where they name the enforced downward movement). The head-covering kataischunō (1Cor 11:4-5) appears in CHAR-1 for the shame-experience register and in CHAR-3 for the relational-disrespect register. Vocabulary sharing is significant and reflects the close analytical relationship between the cluster's characteristics.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 shares aischunē (G0152) with CHAR-1 (where it names the felt experience vs. CHAR-4 where it names the moral quality of conduct — 2Cor 4:2; Phili 3:19). CHAR-4 shares atimia (G0819) with CHAR-1 and CHAR-3 (where it names the relational worth-denial vs. CHAR-4 where it names the quality of disordered passions). The vocabulary sharing reflects the semantic overlap between the shameful quality and the shame-experience in the biblical vocabulary.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — CHAR-5 shares exoutheneō with M06's contempt vocabulary. Atimazō (G0818) is shared with CHAR-3 (dishonour). The vocabulary sharing confirms that CHAR-5 is analytically positioned at the intersection of contempt (M06) and dishonour (CHAR-3): it is the received form of the contempt-act, experienced as worth-denial.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-6 shares its vocabulary (niq.qa.von, qe.ha.von) with M12 (purity/holiness) as the terms' primary register. This is the principal vocabulary-sharing relationship for CHAR-6: the same terms that name CHAR-6's inner-moral-innocence function are also the primary vocabulary of M12's purity register. The sharing reflects the fact that CHAR-6 is retained in M07 because of its shame-polarity function, while M12 holds the terms in their primary purity-holiness register.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's vocabulary sharing confirms the analytical distinctness of the six despite their shared semantic field. Most significant shared vocabulary: atimazō/atimia appears in Chars 1, 2, and 3 — naming the inner experience, the outer mechanism, and the relational act respectively. Aischunē appears in Chars 1 and 4 — the felt experience vs the evaluative quality. Exoutheneō appears in Chars 3 and 5 — worth-denial and contempt-dismissal overlap. The bosh-family (primarily Char 1, with secondary presence in Chars 2 and 4) is the cluster's most widely distributed primary family. Vocabulary sharing is extensive but analytical distinctness is maintained by verse-emphasis: the same term names the inner experience (Char 1), the outer mechanism (Char 2), the relational act (Char 3), the evaluative quality (Char 4), or the contempt-source (Char 5). The programme's characteristic structure imposes the analytical distinctions that the vocabulary does not make on its own.

---

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. The Hebrew g-'-h root is the most extensive cross-characteristic root sharing evidenced. From this root: ga.ah (H1342, to rise/soar — Job 10:16, vc=33945, M08-A2-VCG-02), ga.on (H1347, pride/majesty — extensive M08-A3 use), ga.a.vah (H1346, arrogance/pride — M08-A4-VCG-03 extensive), ga.vah (H1361, to exalt/be proud — M08-A1 extensive), ga.vo.ah (H1364, high/haughty — M08-A1-VCG-03), ge.eh (H1343, proud — M08-A4-VCG-02), ge.ah (H1344, pride — M08-A4-VCG-04), ge.ut (H1348, majesty/pride — M08-A3-VCG-02), ge.vah (H1466, pride/height — M08-A4-VCG-04). This single root generates the majority of CHAR-1's Hebrew vocabulary and simultaneously generates terms used in the M22 divine-majesty register. The rum (r-w-m) root similarly generates terms across M08 (CHAR-1), M22 (divine exaltation), and the positive "God lifts up the humble" register (M39 adjacent). Two root families span both human self-elevation (CHAR-1) and divine genuine exaltation (M22).

**[CHAR-2]** E — The z-d root family (zid, za.don, zed) is primarily distinctive to CHAR-2 within M08, without the cross-register spanning of CHAR-1's roots. The closest root-level sharing is the conceptual overlap between za.don/zed (insolent disregard for divine law) and CHAR-1's ga.on/ge.eh vocabulary (self-elevation above divine limits) — both root families describe the self exceeding its proper creaturely station, but through different conceptual paths (za.don through wilful law-contempt; ga.on through dispositional self-elevation). They share a conceptual family without sharing specific roots.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. The kauchaomai root (Greek) and the ha.lal root (Hebrew) both span M08-CHAR-3 and M22 (divine praise/glorying). The register-distinction is direction (self-directed vs God-directed), not root. This is the carry-forward observation from the brief: M08-C ↔ M22 register-adjacency through shared vocabulary. The Phase 7 VCG design addressed this by separating the three VCG registers within CHAR-3: VCG-01 (condemned self-boasting), VCG-02 (Pauline examined), VCG-03 (God-directed glorying — M22 cross-register). The same root/word, different directions.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes, at the prefix level. Huperfroneō (CHAR-4) and huperēfanos (CHAR-1's Greek primary term) both use the huper- (above, over) prefix — confirming that both characteristics operate in the "above proper station" semantic domain, with huperēfanos naming the visible social expression (appearing above others) and huperfroneō naming the cognitive expression (thinking above what is warranted). The huper- prefix family spans CHAR-1 (huperēfanos), CHAR-4 (huperfroneō), and the relational register (huperoraō, huperairō). This root-level architecture confirms M08's self-elevation characteristics as organised around the same spatial-metaphorical core (above/over), differentiated by faculty (disposition, cognition, social visibility).

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes. The ga.on/ga.vah root (g-'-h family) spans M08-CHAR-1 (dispositional self-elevation), M08-CHAR-5 (proud-might subset), and M22 (divine majesty) — the same root family generates terms across three registers. The huper- prefix spans CHAR-1, CHAR-4, and CHAR-5 in Greek. The ma.rom/rum root spans M08-CHAR-5 and M22 (God's exaltation). The carry-forward observation (M08-E ↔ M23) is evidenced at the root level: ga.on, ma.rom, shal.le.tet, and archō all carry their primary lexical register in M23 (strength/power/dominion); they remain in M08-CHAR-5 because the §3.D verses evidence the M23 faculty corrupted into self-exaltation.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Yes, with significant structural implications. The g-'-h root (to rise, swell) is the primary Hebrew root of M08, generating vocabulary for CHAR-1 (ga.on, ga.vah, ga.a.vah, ge.eh, ga.vo.ah, etc.) and CHAR-5 (ga.on proud-might subset, ga.vah heart-elevation). The r-w-m root (rum — to be high) generates vocabulary for CHAR-1 (rum verb/H7311A) and spans M22 (God's exaltation). The z-d root is specific to CHAR-2. The kauchaomai family spans CHAR-3 VCG-01/02/03 and M22. The huper- Greek prefix spans CHAR-1 (huperēfanos), CHAR-4 (huperfroneō), and CHAR-5 (hupsēlofroneō). The cluster-synthesis: M08's Hebrew root architecture is dominated by the g-'-h and r-w-m families, which simultaneously span the M22 divine-majesty register — confirming that the cluster's vocabulary is etymologically parasitic on the vocabulary of divine genuine greatness.

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-2]** E — The hupo- prefix (under) is shared between hupakoē (CHAR-2 Submission) and hupotagē (CHAR-2 Submission) — both operate within CHAR-2 but at the root level share the positioning-under architecture that distinguishes submission from other characteristics. The hupakouō root (under-hearing) connects etymologically to akouō (hearing) which appears across multiple programme characteristics as an enabling function. The vocabulary's root-level architecture (hupo — under) is distinctive and essentially defines the characteristic's constitutional structure: positioning under a legitimate authority.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The dkk root (crushed/ground) is specific to CHAR-3 Contrition within the M09 cluster — no other M09 characteristic uses this root. However, the semantic domain of crushing/breaking overlaps conceptually with the tapein- (low-lying, base) root of CHAR-1 Humility. The root-level architecture is distinct (dkk vs tapein-) but semantically adjacent — both roots involve downward movement or diminishment of the person's inner state.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The metriopatheō root (metrios — measured; patheō — to feel) is specific to CHAR-4 and does not share root-level architecture with CHAR-1 (tapein- or ka.na roots) or CHAR-2 (hupo- roots). The vocabulary is terminologically distinct across the M09 characteristics at the root level.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The semnos root (from sebomai — to reverence, worship) is not shared at the root level with other M09 characteristics. However, the sebomai root connects to the worship-godliness vocabulary (eusebeia — 1Ti2:2) — the root architecture confirms the link between dignity and godliness at the vocabulary level: semnotēs is the outward character-quality of the godliness-directed person.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The root nadab (to give voluntarily, to offer freely) connects na.div to the broader free-will offering vocabulary in the OT (nadab — freewill offerings are a category of OT worship). Within M09, the na.div root is specific to CHAR-6 — no other M09 characteristic uses this root. The root-level connection to M04 and M29 is semantic-domain adjacency rather than shared root — na.div (freely-giving will) and M29's volitional terms and M04's joy terms are conceptually adjacent without sharing the nadab root.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The tapein- Greek root generates all four of the primary Greek terms for this characteristic (tapeinos, tapeinofrosunē, tapeinoō, tapeinōsis) and they remain within CHAR-1 Humility rather than generating terms for other characteristics. The ka.na root is used consistently for Humility in the M09 corpus. The Hebrew root vocabulary does not evidence shared root-level generation across characteristics within the M09 cluster in the way some other clusters evidence. The most significant root-sharing is between CHAR-1 Humility and CHAR-3 Contrition — both operate in the domain of the person's posture before God in recognition of failure, but with different terms (ka.na vs dak.ka) evidencing genuinely distinct inner-being phenomena.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Root-level sharing is limited but analytically significant where present. Humility (CHAR-1) and Submission (CHAR-2) share the positional-downward semantic architecture (tapein- = low-lying; hupo- = under) without sharing an identical root — each characteristic generates its own root-family. Contrition (CHAR-3) and Humility (CHAR-1) share the semantic domain of inner diminishment (dak.ka — crushed; ka.na — bent/subdued) without sharing the same root, confirming their conceptual adjacency within distinct terminological identities. Willing-heartedness (CHAR-6): the nadab root connects to the freewill-offering vocabulary of OT worship — specific to CHAR-6 within M09. questions.section: T6 — Structural Relationships with Other Characteristics
questions.question_text: What does the vocabulary sharing show about the conceptual relationship between the characteristics?

findings.session_b_note:
From the root-level evidence:

**The aphiēmi root reveals a conceptual unity of releasing acts:** The same root generates forgiveness (releasing a debt-claim), discipleship (releasing family/property for a higher loyalty), permitting (releasing access to another), and abandonment (releasing what should be held — the wrong use). The conceptual relationship these characteristics share: they all involve the **volitional releasing of a claim, bond, or access** — a category of inner-being acts defined by the structure of intentional release. Forgiveness is the instance of this releasing-act directed toward moral debt; discipleship-leaving is the instance directed toward prior obligations; permitting is the instance directed toward granting access.

**The salach-root reveals a conceptual unity of divine-exclusive acts:** H5545, H5546, H5547 all share the salach root and are all divine-exclusive. The root itself encodes divine prerogative — the salach-cluster is conceptually unified as the vocabulary of divine pardoning that humans can seek but not independently exercise.

*Gap noted:* Whether the aphiēmi root connection to other registries (calling, reconciliation) constitutes a formally significant vocabulary-sharing relationship requires further programme-level investigation. The zero XREF count suggests this has not yet been captured in the database.

findings.session_b_note:
Three insights emerge from the vocabulary-sharing pattern:

**High sharing ratio (57.7%) reveals structural embeddedness rather than lexical uniqueness.** Compassion does not have a sharply bounded vocabulary that distinguishes it cleanly from adjacent characteristics. Its vocabulary is deeply interwoven with love, mercy, grace, kindness, and comfort. This is not a weakness in the programme's categorisation — it reflects the data's genuine structure. Compassion in Scripture is not a lexically isolated phenomenon; it is constitutively embedded in a cluster of adjacent characteristics that share its deepest roots.

**Root-level sharing (RACHAM, CHASAD, CHIN/CHEN) reveals conceptual relationships at a deeper level than lexical sharing.** These shared roots suggest not merely that compassion and love sometimes use the same words, but that they draw on the same foundational anthropological realities — the womb, the covenant bond, the disposition of favour. The conceptual relationship is not one of overlap between distinct categories but of shared constitutional ground.

**The CHASAD root crossing two clusters (compassion/love and shame) is the most structurally significant finding.** The same root family names both covenantal loyalty-love and shame/exposure. SD-008 identifies this as a programme-level question: if the depth of mercy presupposes the depth of shame (the root family spans both), then the inner-being connection between compassion and shame is structural rather than incidental. This has implications for how the programme understands the relationship between compassion and the conditions of moral failure it most consistently addresses.

findings.finding_value: T2 confirmed that goodness's origin is singular (God) but its delivery is multiple (encounter, word, Spirit). T6 confirmed that goodness's vocabulary is distributed across multiple registries through shared root families. These two findings are structurally related: the vocabulary distribution (T6.4 — TOV root to R103, AGATHO root to R65, CHRESTO root to R99) reflects the multiple delivery mechanisms of T2. The TOV root's distribution to love (R103) corresponds to the encounter-relational delivery mechanism; the AGATHO root's distribution to generosity (R65) corresponds to the action-expression level of the constitutional movement; the CHRESTO root's shared presence across R67 and R99 corresponds to the dispositional-kindness register of chrēstotēs. The vocabulary distribution is not arbitrary — it tracks the constitutional and relational architecture of how goodness operates and reaches the person. The single-origin of goodness (T2.9.2) is expressed through a vocabulary distributed across the programme's relational-characteristic cluster, reflecting the multiple pathways of the one goodness.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-028: T6 confirmed that goodness has the most extensive vocabulary-sharing and cross-registry connection pattern of any characteristic analysed so far in the programme. T7 confirms through the vocabulary ar…
findings.finding_value: T6 confirmed that goodness has the most extensive vocabulary-sharing and cross-registry connection pattern of any characteristic analysed so far in the programme. T7 confirms through the vocabulary arc (Q&A-177) that this extensiveness is a lexical reality, not a programme classification artefact: the three root families (TOV, AGATHO, CHRESTO) each generate multiple terms distributed across multiple registries because the semantic ranges genuinely overlap. The vocabulary sharing (T6.4) is not the result of how the programme has drawn its boundaries — it reflects the actual lexical distribution of the Hebrew and Greek goodness vocabulary, which crosses conceptual boundaries that English vocabulary maintains more distinctly. The three-stage vocabulary arc (H2896A breadth → agathōsunē precision → chrēstotēs precision) tracks the same movement as the cross-registry distribution pattern: H2896A generates the widest distribution (TOV root to R103, to R42, to multiple other registries); the NT precision terms (G0019, G5544) generate narrower distributions (R65 and R99 respectively). As the vocabulary narrows to precision, the cross-registry connections narrow correspondingly. T6's structural pattern and T7's lexical arc describe the same underlying phenomenon: goodness vocabulary begins broad and specialises, and its cross-registry connections follow the same trajectory.

findings.session_b_note: Vocabulary sharing at this density reveals that love is not a bounded standalone characteristic but the semantic centre of a vocabulary cluster. The characteristics surrounding love (compassion, mercy, kindness, goodness, desire, peace) share vocabulary with it because they are all expressions or dimensions of a common inner-being reality — oriented-attachment-to-the-good-and-to-persons. The registries do not name wholly distinct phenomena; they name distinguishable aspects of a single broadly relational inner-being reality. The practical implication: Session D synthesis for love cannot treat the other C17 characteristics as merely adjacent — they are lexically and conceptually continuous with love. The distinctions drawn in the programme's registry structure are analytical tools, not natural kinds.

findings.finding_value: Love's structural position in the programme is that of the central node in the inner-being vocabulary's relational architecture. Co-occurrence data: 196 with compassion, 105 with strength, 68 with peace, 62 with faith — confirming love's connections to the full range of C17 characteristics and extending to C20 (strength/authority). Shared anchor data: 48 verses shared across multiple registries, with Exo 34:6 (5 registries) and Gal 5:22 (5 registries) as the highest-density shared anchors — confirming love as the vocabulary cluster around which the programme's most significant cross-registry verses gather. Sequential position: love stands downstream of divine action (received) and upstream of the ethical-moral life (generative of commandment-keeping, Spirit-fruits, community identity). Causal productivity: love generates joy, rest, grief, obedience, praise — the programme's most causally productive characteristic. Vocabulary sharing: term sharing ratio 0.701, the highest in C17 — love shares vocabulary with compassion, mercy, kindness, goodness, desire, and peace. The primary gap: distinctions from adjacent characteristics (compassion, mercy, kindness) remain partially drawn; Session D is the resolution context.

findings.finding_value: The structural relationship data and the evidential foundation are the most mutually confirming pair in the synthesis matrix. The co-occurrence breadth (T6.1) is directly explained by the vocabulary breadth (T7.1.10 — the widest semantic arc in the programme): a vocabulary that spans from divine being to love of darkness will co-occur with every other inner-being characteristic because it occupies every register of the inner-being vocabulary. The shared anchor density (48 verses — T6.6) is explained by the primary anchor's function (Lam 3:22 — T7.2.5/T7.2.6): the programme anchors the most significant cross-registry verses at love because love is the definitional centre from which adjacent characteristics derive their meaning. The vocabulary sharing ratio (0.701 — T6.4) is explained by the root-level connections (T7.1.2): the racham root connects love, compassion, and mercy; the ahav root connects love and desire; the tov root connects love and goodness. The structural relationship data is, at its core, the observable programme-level effect of the lexical architecture that the evidential foundation analysis reveals. Structural breadth and lexical breadth are the same reality at different levels of analysis.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-006: T6 reveals compassion as the structural centre of the C17 cluster rather than a peripheral member. The love co-occurrence (196/351 = 55.8% of all OWNER verses) is uniquely dominant — compassion and lo…
findings.finding_value: T6 reveals compassion as the structural centre of the C17 cluster rather than a peripheral member. The love co-occurrence (196/351 = 55.8% of all OWNER verses) is uniquely dominant — compassion and love co-occur in more than half of all active verses, raising the programme-level question whether they are truly separable at the data level. Three structural observations from the co-occurrence landscape: (1) compassion sits at C17's centre of gravity (love, mercy, kindness as top three co-occurrences — all within-cluster); (2) compassion generates a human-response cluster (peace, faith, will, surrender, seeking co-occurring at significant levels — the pattern of divine compassion generating human inner-being responses); (3) compassion is constitutively responsive to human distress (despair, guilt, distress, evil all present in the co-occurrence table — compassion operates most characteristically in the presence of need). The CHASAD root crossing compassion (C17) and shame (C06) is the programme's most structurally unexpected finding — a root family that bridges two clusters. Exod 34:6 as the programme's most multiply-anchored verse (6 registries) must be treated as a cluster-level synthesis anchor. The compassion/mercy boundary (SD-009) is the most critical unresolved distinction. T6.7 (dimensional sharing) is programme-stage limited — formally deferred.

findings.finding_value: T2's somatic-constitutional location explains several T6 structural connections. The shared anchor at Isa 53:5 (with R030 contrition) confirms that the somatic wound vocabulary intersects both compassion and contrition at the constitutional-somatic level — both characteristics have somatic-body language as part of their evidential ground. The CHASAD root's crossing of compassion and shame clusters (T6.4 — most unexpected structural finding) is partly explainable from T2: if CHASAD names a covenantal-soul disposition, it can operate in both the positive register (chesed — steadfast love/compassion) and the negative register (bōsheth — shame as the opposite soul-condition of exposed vulnerability). T2's constitutional portrait (soul-body interface) is the constitutional ground for the root-level cluster-crossing that T6 identifies.

findings.finding_value: T6's structural connections and T7's vocabulary analysis are mutually confirming at the most analytically significant points. The CHASAD root crossing two clusters (T6.4 — most unexpected structural finding) is confirmed and extended by T7's vocabulary analysis: the CHASAD root includes shame as the negative semantic pole embedded within the root itself (T7.1 P5), not as an external antonym. This means the cluster-crossing T6 identifies is not an external structural anomaly but an internal semantic feature: the compassion vocabulary contains its own opposite at the root level. Exod 34:6 as the programme's most multiply-anchored verse (T6.6 — 6 registries) is also T7's most evidentially rich single text — the verse that carries the most structural connections is the same verse that is most analytically central to the vocabulary analysis. The love co-occurrence dominance (T6.1 — 196/351 verses) is confirmed by T7's vocabulary arc: the vocabulary's fullest range (womb to almsgiving) overlaps extensively with the love vocabulary's range, which is why they co-occur across more than half of all active verses.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-006: T6 produces the most structurally significant finding in the review set for any single tier: grace is not produced by any other inner-being characteristic. It is the originating point of a causal chai…
findings.finding_value: T6 produces the most structurally significant finding in the review set for any single tier: grace is not produced by any other inner-being characteristic. It is the originating point of a causal chain, not its product. This categorically distinguishes grace from every other characteristic reviewed — all others can be produced by at least one other characteristic; grace cannot. This structural uniqueness is confirmed by T2.9's origin analysis (grace originates with God — it does not originate in the human constitutional system) and is analytically consistent across T6.2 (seeking is the posture before grace arrives, not its producer), T6.3 (S-rating on "is grace produced by another characteristic"), and T6.4 (the vocabulary's structural completeness without a generative human-side term). The co-occurrence pattern reveals grace at the intersection of divine initiative and creaturely need: seeking (R140 — 40 verses, dominant) as the creature's pre-grace posture; moral failure cluster (evil, guilt, sin, transgression) as the creaturely context; power cluster (strength, might) confirming the 2Cor 12:9 connection. The love co-occurrence (R103 — 14 verses) is the primary within-cluster signal raising the grace-love boundary question (SD013). All major boundary distinctions (grace-love, grace-mercy, grace-justice, grace-chesed) remain open at T6.5 — the most unresolved boundary cluster in the review set. T6.7 (dimensional sharing) is programme-stage limited.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-017: T2's constitutional origin finding (grace does not originate in the human constitutional system) and T6's structural uniqueness finding (grace is not produced by any other inner-being characteristic) …
findings.finding_value: T2's constitutional origin finding (grace does not originate in the human constitutional system) and T6's structural uniqueness finding (grace is not produced by any other inner-being characteristic) are the same finding from constitutional and structural perspectives. They confirm each other from different analytical directions: T2 establishes that there is no constitutional source for grace within the human person; T6 establishes that there is no characteristic-level source for grace within the programme's inner-being landscape. The vocabulary's structural completeness (T7 — but relevant here as T6.4) reflects this constitutional uniqueness: because grace originates entirely from outside the human system, its vocabulary must encode the full two-sided circuit (giving and receiving) from within a single root, with no gap left for a generative human-side term.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-028: T6's structural uniqueness (grace is not produced by any inner-being characteristic — categorically the originating point of the causal chain) and T7's vocabulary structural completeness (every dimens…
findings.finding_value: T6's structural uniqueness (grace is not produced by any inner-being characteristic — categorically the originating point of the causal chain) and T7's vocabulary structural completeness (every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term, including the structural negative acharistos) confirm and explain each other. T6 establishes that grace stands outside the characteristic-production network; T7 establishes that the vocabulary encodes this structural position with unique completeness — including the negative (acharistos) and the NT coinage (charitoō) as markers of grace's conceptual uniqueness. The shared anchor verses (T6.6) are also T7's most evidentially rich texts: Eph 2:8 (which anchors multiple co-occurring registries) carries the most complete single-verse expression of grace's structural position (sovereign gift, not of works, producing faith). T6 and T7 mutually confirm that grace's structural uniqueness in the programme landscape corresponds to a lexical uniqueness in the vocabulary — both point to the same underlying analytical claim: grace is categorically distinct from every other inner-being characteristic.

findings.session_b_note: The vocabulary sharing reveals that covenant and faithfulness are not merely adjacent characteristics but lexically co-generated — they share the same root and therefore the same conceptual DNA. The 'firm covenant' (amanah) and 'faithfulness' (emunah) are not two separate inner-being realities that happen to be related; they are two aspects of the same root reality. A covenant is firm because it is grounded in faithfulness; faithfulness is the character quality that makes covenant possible and sustainable. This conceptual co-generation means that in the inner-being analysis, covenant and faithfulness should be understood as constitutively paired — neither is fully understood without the other. Similarly, the karat root reveals that covenant-making and covenant-dissolution are conceptually paired: the vocabulary of cutting encompasses both the establishing cut (karat berit) and the severing cut (divorce, cutting off). Covenant carries its negation within its own root vocabulary.

The structural centrality of covenant (T6) is the co-occurrence consequence of its semantic comprehensiveness (T7). The two findings confirm each other: wide vocabulary arc → wide co-occurrence → structural hub position. Covenant's place at the centre of the inner-being landscape (T6) is not arbitrary but lexically grounded (T7).

findings.session_b_note: The aman root architecture (Q&A-157) reveals that faithfulness (R060), faith/trust (R059), and despair/unfaith (R044) are conceptually entangled at the root level — they are differentiated aspects of a single semantic family, not independent characteristics. findings.finding_value: The structural landscape analysis (T6 — hub position, aman root architecture entangling R059/R044/R060, distinction of kind from nearest neighbours) and the vocabulary/methodological analysis (T7 — full vocabulary arc, grammatically actional, primary anchor Hos 11:8) produce the final convergent finding. The aman root architecture (T6.4.2, Q&A-157) and the vocabulary arc (T7.1.10, Q&A-179) are describing the same reality: the programme's separation of registries by word is an analytical convenience that cuts across a root-level unity. The vocabulary arc — enacted pole (na.tan/verb) + constituted pole (emunah/hesed/pistis/nouns) — names the same reality that the root architecture identifies: the aman root generates both the dispositional terms and the contextual terms, while na.tan provides the enacted verbal expression. The grammatically actional character of na.tan (T7.1.2, Q&A-171) is the structural reason for its distinction-of-kind from the nominal faithfulness vocabulary (T6.5.3, Q&A-162). What this pair reveals as the final synthesis: the vocabulary evidence and the structural landscape evidence independently converge on the same conclusion — this characteristic is the enacted form of what the faithfulness vocabulary names dispositionally, and this distinction is fundamental to understanding both the characteristic itself and its position in the inner-being landscape.

findings.finding_value: The vocabulary sharing within M01 reveals that its sub-groups are facets of a single characteristic rather than independent phenomena. The same root generates the reverential posture of M01-A, the acute alarm of M01-B, the divine-name formula of M01-A-VCG-06, and the commanded-release corpus of M01-B-VCG-06. This root-level unity is itself a theological datum: Scripture uses a single vocabulary family to span from "fear of God as the whole duty of man" (Ecc 12:13) to "fear of the enemy before battle" (Deu 20:1) — implying that these are not separate inner experiences but related expressions of a constitutively unified characteristic.

**Contrast: B vs M03:** The che.mah / bitterness vocabulary interface with M03 (grief/bitterness) reveals that anger and grief share a deep affective root in the experience of perceived violation. Grief and anger are not simply adjacent — they arise from the same appraisal structure (wrongdoing / loss) and can shade into each other. The vocabulary overlap at the bitterness point reflects the inner-being reality that anger-grief and grief-anger are experientially porous.

The vocabulary sharing with M24 (Weakness) reveals that at the lexical level, Scripture does not always sharply distinguish between grief (M03) and vulnerability/suffering (M24) — many terms carry both registers. This suggests that in the biblical world, the inner experience of grief and the inner experience of weakness and suffering are phenomenologically close — they are felt similarly in the body (pressing, constriction, depletion) and the vocabulary reflects this. The distinction the programme maintains between M03 and M24 is an analytical one based on primary register (loss-related vs vulnerability-related), but the shared vocabulary warns against over-sharpening that boundary.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The shared vocabulary (su.s, gil) across exultation, gladness, and volitional delight confirms that these characteristics are not sharply bounded in the Hebrew inner-being vocabulary — they form a cluster of related inner states sharing the same high-intensity positive register. The distinctions between them (Exultation's surging directedness, Gladness's warm diffuseness, Volitional Delight's will-faculty engagement) are real but operate within a shared semantic field.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The extensive vocabulary sharing between Joy (Characteristic 2), Gladness (Characteristic 3), and Exultation (Characteristic 1) confirms that these three characteristics form a semantic cluster: they are distinct inner-being states that share the same Hebrew and Greek lexical family because they are cognate experiences. Joy and Gladness are so lexically close (sa.mach / sim.chah appear in the same passages, often in synonymous parallelism) that the distinction between them is primarily phenomenological (active-participatory vs. warm-diffuse) rather than lexical. This has implications for Phase 9 findings: the Joy/Gladness boundary should be expected to appear as an important analytical question in Session D synthesis.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The shared agalliao/agalliasis root between Characteristic 2 (Joy) and Characteristic 7 (Suffering-Joy) confirms that these are the most closely related characteristics in M04 — they are not merely adjacent but share the same lexical family at its most intense register. The difference is contextual rather than lexical: the same term (agalliao) names Joy's most intense form in favourable circumstances and Suffering-Joy's primary form in adverse circumstances. The context of suffering is the distinguishing marker of Characteristic 7, not a distinct vocabulary.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Tov's pervasive presence across moral, relational, and circumstantial registers confirms that Gladness (as the evaluative-cognitive recognition of genuine goodness) is the broadest-scope positive inner characteristic in M04 — it is the characteristic most directly connected to the concept of goodness itself, which is why its primary term (tov) ranges across the widest semantic field of any M04 term. The vocabulary sharing with Joy (sa.mach/sim.chah frequently appear alongside tov in the same passages) confirms the Joy/Gladness adjacency already established.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The tov-root sharing between Delight (M04-G-VCG-02) and Gladness (Characteristic 3) is the most conceptually significant: both characteristics claim portions of the tov corpus, which means they are using the same primary Hebrew term to name different inner-being states. The difference is that Gladness uses tov in its evaluative-cognitive and circumstantial registers, while Delight uses tov in its experiential-orientation registers (Psa 73:28 — "it is good to be near God"; Psa 118:8–9 — taking refuge in the Lord as better). The conceptual relationship revealed: Delight and Gladness are the two closest characteristics in M04, sharing a root and a lexical corpus while remaining analytically distinct through their different primary dimensions (Delight's affective-volitional vs. Gladness's cognitive-evaluative).

**[CHAR-5]** E — The ni.cho.ach sharing across M04-K-VCG-01 (Pleasure), M04-M (obedience-orientation), and M04-P (corrupt worship) confirms that the same worship-pleasure mechanism is operative across three different moral contexts — what differs is the object and the inner orientation, not the mechanism itself. The a.nog sharing across Pleasure (M04-K) and Delight (M04-G) confirms the closest vocabulary relationship between these two characteristics. The tov sharing across Pleasure (M04-K-VCG-03) and Gladness (Characteristic 3) confirms the root-level kinship identified in the Gladness analysis.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The thaumazō sharing between Wonder (M04-I-VCG-03 — Rev 17:6, 7) and Delight's beast-captivation (M04-N-VCG-02 — Rev 13:3; 17:8) is analytically significant: both Rev 13:3 and Rev 17:6–7 describe the same human response (marvelling) to the same adversarial powers; but one instance (thaumazō in Rev 13:3; 17:8) is classified under Delight (captivation-delight) and the other (Rev 17:6 — John's marvelling) is classified under Wonder (dark astonishment at evil). This confirms that the same vocabulary term can serve distinct inner-being characteristics depending on its object and the nature of the inner engagement.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Three cluster-level revelations: (1) **The tov root's bridging function** confirms that Gladness (evaluative-cognitive goodness), Delight (experiential-orientation toward goodness), and Pleasure (felt-agreeableness of goodness) are not three independent characteristics but three facets of a single underlying reality — the perception, orientation, and experience of genuine goodness; (2) **The agalliao sharing** confirms that Joy and Suffering-Joy are contextually differentiated forms of the same intense inner-being state rather than categorically different characteristics — the difference is the constitutive role of suffering, not a different vocabulary; (3) **The thaumazō sharing between Wonder (dark astonishment — Rev 17:6) and Delight (beast-captivation — Rev 13:3; 17:8)** confirms that the same adversarial strategy can exploit both Wonder and Delight through the same vocabulary term — the adversary does not need distinct mechanisms to corrupt distinct characteristics but can deploy the same vocabulary-term toward different corrupt ends depending on the inner disposition of the receiver.

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-1]** E — The vocabulary sharing reveals that the distinction between CHAR-1 (inner experience) and CHAR-2 (outer humiliation) is an analytical distinction that the Hebrew does not always make morphologically — the same root can name both. The word-field of shame in Hebrew treats inner experience and outer abasement as aspects of the same reality. The analytical separation of these into distinct characteristics is programme-necessary for analytical precision, but the vocabulary confirms they are related faces of the same phenomenon.

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 shares vocabulary significantly with CHAR-1: ka.lam, bosh, bo.shet, ke.lim.mah all appear in both. The distinction is the verse-emphasis: when the term names the enforced outer mechanism, it is CHAR-2; when it names the felt inner collapse, it is CHAR-1. Vocabulary sharing reflects the fact that inner and outer are aspects of the same shame-event differently observed.

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 shares atimazō and atimia with CHAR-1 (where these terms name the felt experience of dishonour) and with CHAR-2 (where they name the enforced downward movement). The head-covering kataischunō (1Cor 11:4-5) appears in CHAR-1 for the shame-experience register and in CHAR-3 for the relational-disrespect register. Vocabulary sharing is significant and reflects the close analytical relationship between the cluster's characteristics.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 shares aischunē (G0152) with CHAR-1 (where it names the felt experience vs. CHAR-4 where it names the moral quality of conduct — 2Cor 4:2; Phili 3:19). CHAR-4 shares atimia (G0819) with CHAR-1 and CHAR-3 (where it names the relational worth-denial vs. CHAR-4 where it names the quality of disordered passions). The vocabulary sharing reflects the semantic overlap between the shameful quality and the shame-experience in the biblical vocabulary.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — CHAR-5 shares exoutheneō with M06's contempt vocabulary. Atimazō (G0818) is shared with CHAR-3 (dishonour). The vocabulary sharing confirms that CHAR-5 is analytically positioned at the intersection of contempt (M06) and dishonour (CHAR-3): it is the received form of the contempt-act, experienced as worth-denial.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-6 shares its vocabulary (niq.qa.von, qe.ha.von) with M12 (purity/holiness) as the terms' primary register. This is the principal vocabulary-sharing relationship for CHAR-6: the same terms that name CHAR-6's inner-moral-innocence function are also the primary vocabulary of M12's purity register. The sharing reflects the fact that CHAR-6 is retained in M07 because of its shame-polarity function, while M12 holds the terms in their primary purity-holiness register.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's vocabulary sharing confirms the analytical distinctness of the six despite their shared semantic field. Most significant shared vocabulary: atimazō/atimia appears in Chars 1, 2, and 3 — naming the inner experience, the outer mechanism, and the relational act respectively. Aischunē appears in Chars 1 and 4 — the felt experience vs the evaluative quality. Exoutheneō appears in Chars 3 and 5 — worth-denial and contempt-dismissal overlap. The bosh-family (primarily Char 1, with secondary presence in Chars 2 and 4) is the cluster's most widely distributed primary family. Vocabulary sharing is extensive but analytical distinctness is maintained by verse-emphasis: the same term names the inner experience (Char 1), the outer mechanism (Char 2), the relational act (Char 3), the evaluative quality (Char 4), or the contempt-source (Char 5). The programme's characteristic structure imposes the analytical distinctions that the vocabulary does not make on its own.

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-1]** E — The vocabulary sharing between CHAR-1 and M22 reveals that arrogant self-elevation is conceptually parasitic on divine genuine exaltation: the creature uses the same vocabulary — the same spatial metaphor of upward elevation — that Scripture reserves for God's legitimate exaltation, but applies it to the creature's illegitimate claim. Isa 2:11 (vc=34601, M08-A3-VCG-04) states the resolution: "the Lord alone will be exalted in that day" — the shared vocabulary creates a narrative tension that is resolved eschatologically when the proper subject of the elevation terms (God alone) is re-established and the improper subject (the creature) is brought low. This conceptual parasitism also explains why the Phase 5.5 set-aside was structurally necessary: the same terms appear in both M08 and M22 because CHAR-1 is the creature's mirror-inversion of M22, operating with M22's vocabulary in the wrong direction and with the wrong subject.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The relative distinctiveness of CHAR-2's vocabulary (z-d root family) from CHAR-1's vocabulary (g-'-h and r-w-m roots) confirms the analytical distinction between the two characteristics: they are constitutively related (CHAR-1 generates CHAR-2's dispositional ground) but lexically distinguished (the zid "boiling" vocabulary specifically names the act-of-transgression that goes beyond the dispositional-elevation named by ga.on/rum). The vocabulary confirms that Scripture distinguishes the inner disposition (CHAR-1) from the transgressive act (CHAR-2) through different root families.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The vocabulary sharing between CHAR-3 and M22 reveals that boasting/glorying and praising/glorying are the same inner-being impulse directed differently: toward the self (CHAR-3 VCG-01) or toward God (M22). The impulse to exult in, celebrate, and publicly affirm something is a created human capacity; the direction of its expression determines whether it is M08 (self-directed) or M22 (God-directed). This conceptual relationship makes CHAR-3 the most direct M08 ↔ M22 bridge: the condemned boasting of VCG-01 and the God-directed glorying of VCG-03 are the same faculty expressed in opposite directions. The VCG-03 verses are in CHAR-3's corpus because they address the boasting-impulse's redirection — they belong here as the examined contrast, while their fully God-directed form will be addressed when M22 opens.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The huper- prefix shared between CHAR-1's huperēfanos and CHAR-4's huperfroneō reveals that these two characteristics are the same spatial-metaphorical movement (self-elevation above proper station) applied to two different faculties: CHAR-1 in the dispositional-social register (appearing above others) and CHAR-4 in the cognitive register (thinking above what is warranted). CHAR-4 is the cognitive form of CHAR-1 at the vocabulary level — confirmed by the shared prefix root.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The vocabulary sharing between CHAR-5 and M23 reveals that CHAR-5 is structurally parasitic on M23's legitimate strength faculty: the same ga.on that names God's genuine majesty (M22) and legitimate human strength (M23) names the creature's self-exaltation based on that strength (CHAR-5). The conceptual relationship is the same as between CHAR-1 and M22 (rum spanning both): CHAR-5 is what happens to M23's strength-faculty when it becomes the ground for self-aggrandisement rather than God-serving stewardship. This makes CHAR-5 the M08 characteristic most directly dependent on M23's content for understanding — CHAR-5 is M23's misuse-pole, as CHAR-1 is M22's misuse-pole.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster-level vocabulary sharing reveals the programme's most significant cross-cluster conceptual relationship: M08 (pride) is etymologically derived from M22 (divine majesty) vocabulary, and M08-CHAR-5 is etymologically derived from M23 (strength/dominion) vocabulary. The creature uses the vocabulary of God's legitimate exaltation (M22) to name its illegitimate self-exaltation (M08-CHAR-1, CHAR-5). The vocabulary sharing is not accidental — it reflects the theological logic that pride is the creature's attempt to claim the Creator's own vocabulary of greatness. The cluster-synthesis: M08's cross-cluster vocabulary relationships confirm that pride is definitionally parasitic on divine greatness — it uses the same conceptual categories (exaltation, strength, majesty, height) that describe God's genuine attributes and claims them for the creature's self-elevation.

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-2]** E — The vocabulary analysis reveals that CHAR-2 Submission and CHAR-1 Humility are conceptually adjacent but terminologically distinct at the primary level. Both involve positioning downward (tapeinos-root vs hupo-root), but with different relational targets: tapein- is about the person's general posture relative to their own standing; hupo- (submission) is about the person's positioning under a specific legitimate authority. The shared Philippi context (Phili2:3 humility; Phili2:8 obedience) confirms conceptual adjacency without terminological conflation.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The semantic-domain sharing (crushing/lowering) confirms the conceptual adjacency of CHAR-3 Contrition and CHAR-1 Humility: both operate in the inner-being space of the person who is not elevated or self-asserting before God, but contrition occupies the acute-crisis end (dkk — crushed, pulverised) while humility occupies the stable-dispositional end (tapein-, ka.na — lower, humble). The vocabulary confirms the distinction established at Phase 5: same semantic domain, different intensity-form and temporal character.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The vocabulary analysis confirms that CHAR-4 is terminologically distinct from CHAR-1 and CHAR-2 at the root level — each characteristic has its own distinct vocabulary. The conceptual relationship (CHAR-4 as expression of CHAR-1's self-knowledge in the relational-engagement register) is evidenced by shared-weakness-ground rather than shared root vocabulary. The characteristics are conceptually related but terminologically independent.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The root-link between semnotēs (semnos/sebomai — reverence-worthiness) and godliness (eusebeia) confirms the conceptual relationship evidenced at 1Ti2:2: dignity is the characterological expression of genuine godliness in the person's social existence. The vocabulary confirms that semnotēs is not an independent social virtue but the manner-quality that godliness takes when expressed in human social and relational existence.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The vocabulary analysis confirms the M04 and M29 register-adjacency as *semantic-domain sharing rather than terminological sharing*. Na.div (CHAR-6) and M04/M29 vocabulary share the conceptual domain of the freely-motivated, joy-infused inner orientation without sharing specific root terms. The relationship is conceptual adjacency: willing-heartedness is the volitional face of what joy (M04) is the affective face of — both describe the person whose inner life moves freely and gladly toward God.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The vocabulary analysis reveals that Humility (CHAR-1) and Contrition (CHAR-3) are conceptually related but terminologically distinct: both operate in the inner person's response to moral failure and God's word, but dak.ka (contrition) names the more acute, broken, grief-laden form while ka.na (voluntary humbling) and the tapein- family name the stable posture and volitional act. The vocabulary boundary confirms the analytical distinction made at Phase 5: contrition is the acute crisis-form and humility is the stable dispositional-form. The shared vocabulary space between CHAR-1 and CHAR-2 (Submission) is more relational than root-level — both involve the person taking a lowered posture before an authority, but the terms are distinct (tapein- vs hupakoē/hupotagē).

**[CLUSTER]** E — The vocabulary sharing analysis reveals that M09's conceptual coherence operates primarily at the semantic-domain level rather than through shared roots. The "low-lying/under" semantic domain (tapein-, hupo-, ka.na, dak.ka) connects CHAR-1, CHAR-2, and CHAR-3 as the cluster's downward-movement characteristics. The "freely-giving/springing" semantic domain (na.div, and cross-cluster to M04/M29 vocabulary) connects CHAR-6 to M04 and M29 without root-level sharing. The "reverence-worthiness" domain (semnos/sebomai) connects CHAR-5 to godliness (eusebeia) rather than to other M09 characteristics — confirming that semnotēs is the characterological manner-quality of the godly person rather than primarily a non-self-assertive inner posture. Meekness (CHAR-4)'s vocabulary (metriopatheō; okneō) is Greek philosophical-register and stands terminologically isolated from the OT-Hebrew downward-movement vocabulary of the other characteristics. The cluster's two testamental vocabularies reveal an OT Hebrew core (crisis and spontaneous inner movement — CHAR-3, CHAR-6) and a Greek NT expansion (dispositional and social-ordering — CHAR-1 NT development, CHAR-4, CHAR-5).
