findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-1]** E — The vocabulary sharing reveals that CHAR-1 (Wilful sinning), CHAR-2 (Unintentional sinning), CHAR-3 (Confession), CHAR-4 (Conscience suppression), CHAR-13 (Sin as divine record), and CHAR-16 (Sinner as moral character) are not conceptually independent phenomena but *perspectival facets* of the same underlying moral reality — sinning as the human condition of wrongdoing before God. The distinction the programme draws between them is analytical (differentiating the act from the character, the record from the confession) while the vocabulary treats them as a unified field. The act (CHAR-1) and the character (CHAR-16) share the same root because in Scripture the act and its moral weight on the actor are not ultimately separable.

**[CHAR-10]** E — The apostasia/pa.sha conceptual parallel (T6.4.2) reveals that departure-from-established-commitment is a cross-register theme in M10: CHAR-8 covers it in the political-military register (pa.sha — breaking political submission), CHAR-10 covers it in the covenantal-identity register (apostasia — forsaking the Mosaic covenant). Both are named by "standing-away-from" conceptual structures applied to different binding relationships. The vocabulary isolation of deleazō and sunupokrinomai confirms their cross-cluster nature: they belong primarily to M14 and M08 respectively and are present in M10 only as sinful-outcome mechanisms.

**[CHAR-11]** E — The vocabulary sharing (same roots; condition vs act grammatical differentiation) reveals that CHAR-11 is not conceptually separate from the other M10 sinning characteristics but is the *condition-register* of the same semantic field. Sin (hamartia/cha.ta) names both the condition (CHAR-11) and the specific acts (CHAR-1 through CHAR-10): the characteristic is distinguished not by having a different vocabulary but by deploying the shared vocabulary in its noun-power-condition mode rather than its verb-act mode. This confirms CHAR-11's position as the foundational register of the M10 cluster's vocabulary.

**[CHAR-12]** E — The vocabulary sharing confirms that CHAR-12 is not a conceptually separate domain but a specific *register* within the broader hamartia/hamartanō semantic field: the enslaving-power register (noun used as power-subject: "sin enslaves"; "imprisoned under sin") exists alongside the act-register (hamartanō as discrete sinning), the condition-register (CHAR-11 — under sin), and the habit-register (CHAR-6 — habitual practice). CHAR-12 is identified not by unique vocabulary but by its specific deployment of the shared vocabulary in the power-governing-force register.

**[CHAR-13]** E — The vocabulary sharing confirms that CHAR-13 is not a separate semantic domain but the *objective-record register* of the same cha.ta/hamartia semantic field that all M10 characteristics share. The characteristics are distinguished not by different vocabularies but by different registers of the same vocabulary: CHAR-1 (the act), CHAR-6 (the habitual pattern), CHAR-11 (the structural condition), CHAR-12 (the enslaving power), CHAR-13 (the retained objective record) are all names for different aspects of what the cha.ta root names as a totality. CHAR-13's distinctiveness is the record-dimension — sin as a retained moral fact — not a different vocabulary.

**[CHAR-14]** E — The shared vocabulary (chat.tat/hamartia/paraptōma across M10) confirms that CHAR-14 operates within the same semantic field as all other M10 characteristics — it addresses the same sin that the other characteristics describe. CHAR-14's unique vocabulary contribution (kip.pu.rim — covering-atonement) is the specific conceptual mechanism that distinguishes the characteristic's distinctive operation: the covering/atoning function is CHAR-14's unique terminological contribution to M10 alongside the shared sin-vocabulary.

**[CHAR-15]** E — The total vocabulary sharing (only cha.ta used; no specialised vocabulary for the inherited-condition dimension) reveals that CHAR-15 is not a distinct semantic domain but the *temporal-generational register* of the shared cha.ta sinning vocabulary. The generational sin-condition is evidenced not through distinctive terminology but through the *context* of ancestral attribution (Isa 43:27 — "your first father") and prolonged duration (Isa 64:5 — "a long time"). CHAR-15's distinctiveness is contextual-temporal, not lexical.

**[CHAR-16]** E — The shared root confirms that CHAR-16 is not a separate semantic domain but the *person-type* expression of the shared cha.ta/hamartia field. What distinguishes CHAR-16 vocabularily is the agent-noun form (chat.ta/hamartōlos): these terms name the person constituted by the root's semantic content rather than the act, condition, or record. CHAR-16's vocabulary uniqueness is thus its grammatical form (agent-noun) applied to the shared root — naming the sinner rather than the sinning.

**[CHAR-17]** E — The distinctive *ʾāšam* root vocabulary (a.sham/ash.mah — guilt-realisation and guilt-condition) confirms that CHAR-17 is a semantically distinct characteristic within M10: it has its own primary vocabulary that does not appear in CHAR-1, CHAR-13, or CHAR-16's primary terms. The shared a.von root connects CHAR-17 to the broader guilt-iniquity field but does not dissolve the distinction. CHAR-17 is the *ʾāšam*-characteristic of M10: the subjective guilt-recognition and guilt-condition register that the *ʾāšam* root uniquely names.

**[CHAR-18]** E — The shared a.von root reveals that CHAR-18 (crime) and CHAR-17 (guilt/punishment) are the same moral reality named at different levels. The a.von root covers the entire arc: the crime committed (CHAR-18 — H5771G), the guilt-liability it generates (CHAR-17 — H5771H), and the punitive-consequence it deserves (CHAR-17 — H5771I). This root-architecture confirms what T6.2's constitutive relationship finding names: CHAR-18 and CHAR-17 are two faces of the same moral reality, distinguished by the crime-dimension (objective, accumulated, in the divine record — CHAR-18) and the guilt-experience dimension (subjective, conscience-registered — CHAR-17).

**[CHAR-19]** E — The vocabulary distinctiveness confirms that CHAR-19 is conceptually irreducible within M10: no other characteristic shares its primary vocabulary family (pe.sha/pa.sha root). The three-term formula (Exo 34:7 — iniquity, transgression, sin) positions CHAR-19 as one of the three fundamental moral-failure categories alongside CHAR-18 (iniquity) and CHAR-1 (sin); the three are distinct enough to require separate vocabularies. CHAR-19 is the boundary-crossing register; CHAR-18 is the accumulated-crime register; CHAR-1 is the missing-the-mark register — each requires its own term-family.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The vocabulary sharing (identical primary term and root) reveals that CHAR-1 and CHAR-2 are analytically distinguished facets of a single Hebrew semantic field. The distinction the programme draws between them (wilful vs unintentional) is carried not by different vocabulary but by the qualifier — *bishgagah* (unintentionally) in CHAR-2 vs no qualifier (or explicit knowledge markers) in CHAR-1. The conceptual relationship is one of *same act, different inner quality*: both are cha.ta, but CHAR-2 is cha.ta-in-ignorance while CHAR-1 is cha.ta-in-knowledge. The vocabulary unity confirms that Scripture treats them as belonging to the same moral domain, differentiated by inner-being quality rather than by kind.

**[CHAR-20]** E — The vocabulary distinctiveness (zero root-level sharing with any other M10 characteristic) confirms that CHAR-20 is a genuinely distinct conceptual domain within M10 that cannot be derived from or reduced to other M10 characteristics. The ma.al/ba.gad vocabulary uniquely names the covenantal-relational-betrayal dimension of moral failure. The cross-register flags (M13 Truth/Faithfulness; M31 Faith/Unbelief) confirm: CHAR-20 sits at the intersection of M10 (sin/guilt) and M13 (faithfulness) and M31 (faith) — it is the sin-characteristic that most directly engages the faithfulness-cluster.

**[CHAR-21]** E — The vocabulary pattern reveals CHAR-21 as M10's richest (nine term-families) and most vocabulary-diverse characteristic. The partial overlap with CHAR-18 through a.vah/a.von confirms the conceptual adjacency: both characteristics address moral distortion but CHAR-18 focuses on the accumulated crime-weight while CHAR-21 focuses on the inner structural twisting. The NT's unique ftheirō/fthora vocabulary for CHAR-21 confirms it as the characteristic that most comprehensively engages the NT's corruption-theology language.

**[CHAR-22]** E — The adikos/adikēma vocabulary sharing with M26's *dik-* root confirms CHAR-22 as M10's M26-interface characteristic: injustice is definitionally the negation of justice/righteousness. The M26 cross-register flag on all CHAR-22 terms is linguistically grounded — adikos literally means "not-just." CHAR-22 is the only M10 characteristic whose primary NT vocabulary is the direct lexical negation of an adjacent cluster's positive characteristic.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The vocabulary sharing reveals that sinning (CHAR-1/2), its naming as confession (CHAR-3), and the guilt-state (CHAR-17) are not conceptually independent phenomena but *facets of a single moral episode viewed from different analytical positions*. The same root appears in all four because Scripture treats the sinning, the guilt, the naming, and the record as belonging to a unified moral reality. CHAR-3 is distinguished not by different vocabulary but by the grammatical and relational configuration: the first-person, self-applied, past-tense naming. The characteristic is the same moral domain, viewed from the confessor's speech-act position.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The vocabulary sharing (and especially the inverted form: *chatati* in CHAR-3 vs *lo chatati* in CHAR-4) reveals that conscience suppression and confession are *mirror characteristics*: they use the same vocabulary in opposite directions. The confessor says "I have sinned" (*chatati*); the conscience-suppressed person says "I have not sinned" (*lo chatati*). This structural inversion within the same vocabulary confirms that CHAR-4 is defined most precisely as the *absence or inversion of CHAR-3* — the characteristic that takes the place of confession when the conscience fails to operate.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The shared vocabulary (cha.ta across CHAR-1/2/3/4/5/6) confirms that all these characteristics share the same semantic domain — the domain of sinning and its inner-being dimensions. CHAR-5's conceptual relationship to the others is defined by its grammatical configuration: the same sinning-vocabulary deployed in the non-departure-from construction reveals CHAR-5 as the characteristic that *holds sinning in place* rather than committing it (CHAR-1), confessing it (CHAR-3), or suppressing awareness of it (CHAR-4). CHAR-5 is the will-act that prevents the movement from any of these toward the turn.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The vocabulary sharing (identical root, shared vocabulary domain) reveals that all sinning characteristics operate within the same semantic field. CHAR-6 is not a different *kind* of sinning but a different *temporal configuration* of the same sinning vocabulary: the person-type (hachotet) and continuous-present (hamartanōn) forms are the vocabulary of sustained and formed sinning, marking habitual defection as the temporal-dispositional end of the sinning spectrum rather than a qualitatively distinct act.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The vocabulary sharing (shared H2398 root, differentiated by stem) reveals that contagious sin is not a different *kind* of sinning from the other characteristics but the same sinning root operating in its *causative mode*. The Hiphil causative is the grammatical marker of the scale-amplification: the same moral failure (sinning against God) that operates at the personal level (Qal) operates at the communal-causative level (Hiphil). CHAR-7 is conceptually the communal-causative extension of the personal sinning characteristics — same moral content, different grammatical configuration and relational scope.

**[CHAR-8]** E — The shared root (H6586 pa.sha) between CHAR-8 and CHAR-19 reveals that political revolt and personal moral transgression are *the same inner dynamic operating in different relational registers*. The root names the wilful breaking-away from a binding relationship — whether that relationship is political-authority (CHAR-8) or personal-moral-covenantal (CHAR-19). The conceptual relationship is: CHAR-8 is the political-domain expression of the same transgressive will-act that CHAR-19 names in the personal-moral domain.

**[CHAR-9]** E — The vocabulary isolation of blasfēmia within M10 reveals that CHAR-9 is conceptually distinct from all other M10 characteristics: the other characteristics are forms of sinning/transgressing/failing morally in the OT Hebrew vocabulary domain; CHAR-9 is specifically the *speech-act* form of moral failure, named by a Greek term that encodes the speech-medium as constitutive of the characteristic. The characteristic is conceptually related to the others (sinful speech is sinful) but occupies a distinct conceptual niche: sin specifically through and as speech.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The vocabulary sharing between ra.sha-as-person-type (M10b) and ra.sha-as-legal-status (M10 cross-register) reveals a conceptual relationship of derivation: the legal guilt status (M10) is derived from and grounded in the inner moral character orientation (M10b). The legal declaration "wicked" (M10b-A-VCG-01) names a status that is consequential upon the inner disposition — the forensic verdict follows from and confirms the moral character. This conceptual derivation has implications for understanding both clusters: the sin-act that generates legal guilt (M10) is not merely external behaviour but the outward expression of the inner moral person-orientation (M10b-A).

**[CHAR-2]** E — The vocabulary sharing between adikia (CHAR-2) and the forensic-legal register (M10) reveals the same conceptual relationship as CHAR-1's ra.sha cross-register: constitutional inner unrighteousness (adikia as CHAR-2) is the inner condition from which moral-legal offense (adikia in the M10 forensic register) flows. The shared root expresses that the inner condition and its outward-legal expression are aspects of a single reality. The kakia/kakos root-sharing with CHAR-6 (kakopoios — evildoer) reveals that the inner settled badness (kakia — CHAR-2) and the outward evil-doing person-type (kakopoios — CHAR-6) are root-related — the constitutional badness (kakia) produces and characterises the evildoer (kakopoios).

**[CHAR-3]** E — The to.e.vah vocabulary sharing between CHAR-3 (moral-character abomination) and CHAR-4 (idolatrous abomination) reveals that the biblical authors used a single concept-term (to.e.vah) to cover both moral-character and idolatrous violations — treating them as aspects of a single category of divine revulsion. The programmatic separation into CHAR-3 and CHAR-4 is analytically necessary (the inner-being content differs significantly) but the vocabulary sharing confirms that in the biblical mind the two registers are species of the same genus (that which provokes divine revulsion by violating divine holiness). The ra.sha vocabulary sharing within CHAR-3's corpus (Pro 15:8; 15:9; 17:15 — VCG-01 and VCG-03) confirms the conceptual relationship between CHAR-1 (wickedness) and CHAR-3 (abomination): the wicked person is specifically the person whose inner condition triggers abomination-verdict.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The to.e.vah sharing with CHAR-3 confirms that both characteristics are species of the same genus: divine revulsion at human moral-spiritual failure, with CHAR-3 addressing the moral-character register and CHAR-4 the idolatrous-devotion register. The shiq.quts sharing with M27 reveals that CHAR-4's inner-being dimension (the heart's devotion to idols) is directly linked to the concrete-object dimension (the idol as a thing of loathing): the inner devotion cannot be separated from the objects to which it attaches. The vocabulary connecting inner-being (to.e.vah as quality of the inner person's practice) with object-category (shiq.quts as the detestable idol-object) confirms that CHAR-4 describes a specifically object-directed inner attachment — the characteristic cannot be understood without reference to both the inner devotion and the external object to which it is misdirected.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The a.ven root sharing with M27 and M03 reveals that the biblical writers used a single vocabulary field (emptiness-trouble-iniquity) to cover both the agent's inner scheming and the victim's received affliction — these are opposite ends of the same harm-event, treated as aspects of the same concept. The ro.a/ra.sha root sharing confirms the conceptual relationship between CHAR-5 (active scheming process) and CHAR-1 (settled wicked identity): both are aspects of the same root concept of evil, with CHAR-5 naming the process and CHAR-1 naming the character-state that the process produces. The vocabulary sharing reveals these characteristics as analytically distinct but conceptually related aspects of a single moral-theological domain.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The blasfēmeō sharing with M06 confirms that CHAR-6 and M06 address the same speech-contempt domain from different analytical angles: CHAR-6 as the inner-wickedness expression; M06 as the contemptuous relational act. The kakopoios/kakos root sharing confirms the conceptual relationship between CHAR-6 (evil-doer as charged identity in VCG-03) and CHAR-2 (evil as constitutional inner nature): the person accused as kakopoios is accused of being what CHAR-2's person-type is constitutionally — the two characteristics are conceptually related through the same evil-doer concept at the person-type level.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's vocabulary sharing reveals three conceptual relationships. First: Chars 3 and 4's shared to.e.vah vocabulary confirms their identity as two sub-registers of the same abomination category — divided by content (moral character vs. idolatrous devotion) but united by the same relational mechanism (divine revulsion responding to boundary violation). Second: the ra.a/ro.a root connection between Chars 1 and 5 confirms that wickedness-as-identity and iniquity-as-process are analytically related — the same root generates the person-type (Char 1) and the quality of their deeds (Char 5). Third: the ka- root connection between Chars 2 and 6 confirms that the constitutional evil-nature (Char 2) and its speech-expression (Char 6) are conceptually continuous — the evil-doer accusation (kakopoios) names through hostile speech exactly what the constitutional evil-nature (kakia) describes structurally.
findings.notes: outcome=E

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-1]** E — The shared ta.me root vocabulary reveals that the four M10c characteristics are not separate, unrelated conditions — they are differentiated registers of one broadly unified inner-being domain: defilement and impurity. Characteristic 1 (ritual), Characteristic 2 (moral-inner), Characteristic 3 (corporate-covenantal), and Characteristic 4 (external spiritual agency) share the same lexical architecture because they are addressing the same fundamental category — the condition of being unclean in its various registers — from different angles. The shared vocabulary is evidence of conceptual unity beneath register differentiation.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The shared root vocabulary reveals the four M10c characteristics as differentiated registers of one broad defilement domain. The same roots (ta.me, akathartos) deploy differently in different contexts: in the Levitical bodily-mechanism context = Characteristic 1; in the NT moral-inner context = Characteristic 2; in the corporate-covenantal prophetic context = Characteristic 3; in the spiritual-agency context = Characteristics 1 or 4. The shared vocabulary signals that the programme's four characteristics are not four separate conditions but four registers of one domain — the condition of defilement/impurity as it operates across different dimensions of creaturely existence.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The shared ta.me root reveals the four M10c characteristics as differentiated registers of one lexical domain: all four use the same root to name what is fundamentally the same condition (defilement/uncleanness) as it operates in different dimensions (ritual/bodily, moral-inner, corporate/covenantal, external-spiritual-agency). The shared vocabulary confirms conceptual unity beneath register differentiation. The nid.dah sharing between Characteristics 1 and 3 is particularly revealing: the same bodily-impurity paradigm (menstruation) serves both as the archetype of the ritual defilement state (Characteristic 1) and as the metaphor for the corporate moral uncleanness that God finds repugnant (Eze 36:17, Characteristic 3). The metaphorical extension of the bodily paradigm into the corporate moral domain is the vocabulary arc that most directly shows the connection between the two registers.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The shared akathartos root reveals all four M10c characteristics as differentiated registers of one unified defilement domain. The same root concept (not-clean, defilement) applies to: bodily-ritual status (Characteristic 1), inner moral condition (Characteristic 2), corporate-covenantal defilement of sacred space (Characteristic 3), and the character of external spiritual agents (Characteristic 4). The shared vocabulary confirms that the programme's four characteristics are registers of one domain — defilement/impurity as it operates in different dimensions of creaturely existence.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The vocabulary sharing reveals the M10c cluster as lexically and conceptually unified. The four characteristics are not four separate conditions with their own distinct vocabulary — they are four registers of one condition (defilement/uncleanness) named by the same root vocabulary deployed in different contexts. The most analytically significant example: G0169 akathartos operates in three of the four characteristics with three different referents — (1) the person's ritual status (Char 1 — Act 10:14/28: "common or unclean"), (2) the inner moral condition (Char 2 — 2Cor 6:17: "touch no unclean thing"), and (3) the character of the external spiritual agent (Char 4 — "unclean spirit" — pneuma akatharton). The same Greek word applies to a ritual-status condition, an inner-moral condition, and an adversarial spiritual being — revealing that the cluster's unity is not merely formal but operates at the level of the same fundamental concept of defilement-as-incompatibility-with-holiness operating across different domains. The nid.dah sharing between Characteristics 1 and 3 shows the bodily-impurity paradigm functioning as the metaphorical vehicle for understanding corporate moral repugnance — vocabulary sharing as conceptual bridge between registers.

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 shares vocabulary significantly with CHAR-1: ka.lam, bosh, bo.shet, ke.lim.mah all appear in both. The distinction is the verse-emphasis: when the term names the enforced outer mechanism, it is CHAR-2; when it names the felt inner collapse, it is CHAR-1. **[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 shares atimazō and atimia with CHAR-1 (where these terms name the felt experience of dishonour) and with CHAR-2 (where they name the enforced downward movement). The head-covering kataischunō (1Cor 11:4-5) appears in CHAR-1 for the shame-experience register and in CHAR-3 for the relational-disrespect register. Vocabulary sharing is significant and reflects the close analytical relationship between the cluster's characteristics.

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 shares aischunē (G0152) with CHAR-1 (where it names the felt experience vs. CHAR-4 where it names the moral quality of conduct — 2Cor 4:2; Phili 3:19). CHAR-4 shares atimia (G0819) with CHAR-1 and CHAR-3 (where it names the relational worth-denial vs. CHAR-4 where it names the quality of disordered passions). The vocabulary sharing reflects the semantic overlap between the shameful quality and the shame-experience in the biblical vocabulary.

**[CHAR-5]** E — CHAR-5 shares exoutheneō with M06's contempt vocabulary. Atimazō (G0818) is shared with CHAR-3 (dishonour). The vocabulary sharing confirms that CHAR-5 is analytically positioned at the intersection of contempt (M06) and dishonour (CHAR-3): it is the received form of the contempt-act, experienced as worth-denial.

questions.section: T6 — Structural Relationships with Other Characteristics
questions.question_text: Which adjacent characteristic most closely resembles this one, and what precisely distinguishes them?

findings.session_b_note:
The data identifies mercy (R111, 16 shared verses) and grace (R068, implied through DIM-064-SD017) as the closest adjacent characteristics. The distinction work is partially done:

**Forgiveness vs. Mercy:**
- DIM-064-SD016 flags this as a Session D question: "does the programme's treatment of mercy and kindness situate them in the same divine-attribute cluster as forgiveness, and does their co-location in Psa 86:5 suggest a systematic relationship where forgiveness is the specific relational act that mercy and hesed generate?"
- The partial distinction implied by the data: mercy (hesed) is the **dispositional ground** — the settled loving-kindness orientation of God toward his covenant people; forgiveness is the **specific relational act** through which that disposition is expressed toward guilt-bearing persons. Mercy is broader (covering all relational generosity); forgiveness is narrower (addressing the specific condition of moral debt).
- Psa 86:5 — "good and forgiving, abounding in steadfast love" — places them as co-equal divine attributes in apposition, not in causal sequence. This complicates a simple upstream-downstream model.

**Forgiveness vs. Grace:**
- DIM-064-SD017: "grace is the upstream disposition from which forgiveness flows." The distinction: grace = dispositional source (what God is — disposed to give freely); forgiveness = specific relational act (what grace produces in the context of guilt). Grace is dispositional and broad; forgiveness is specific and targeted at the debt-condition.

*Gap noted:* The precise boundary between forgiveness and mercy has not been drawn — it is the most significant unresolved distinction in the programme for this characteristic. Session D is named as the target for this resolution.

findings.session_b_note:
The data identifies mercy (R111) as the most closely resembling adjacent characteristic, based on:
- Direct XREF relationship (G1653, G1656, G3628 as XREF terms in R23)
- Shared anchor verses (Rom 9:15, Jas 5:11, Num 6:25)
- Co-occurrence of 76 shared verses
- SD-009 naming this as the most direct test of whether R23 and R111 are genuinely separable

**What the data suggests about the distinction (partial):** SD-016's three-stage model implies a directional distinction: compassion is the inner somatic-movement (splanchnizō), mercy is the soul-level dispositional form (eleos), and almsgiving (eleēmosunē) is the external act. On this model, compassion and mercy are not parallel alternatives but sequential stages — compassion precedes and generates mercy. If this is correct, the distinction is one of constitutional level and sequence rather than of kind.

However, SD-009 raises the specific counter-evidence of Rom 9:15, where oikteirō (compassion) and eleeō (mercy) are deployed in parallel — suggesting they may be synonymous in that context. The parallel structure does not resolve whether the terms are truly interchangeable or whether the parallelism is rhetorical.

**What is missing (P):** The precise inner-being boundary between compassion and mercy is not established in the current data and is explicitly deferred to Session D (SD-009). This is the most critical unresolved distinction question in the registry.

findings.session_b_note:
The closest adjacent characteristics, based on the co-occurrence and shared anchor data:

**Unity (R167, 4 shared verses):** Unity names the state of oneness; fellowship names the participatory experience that generates or constitutes that oneness. The distinction: unity is a state, fellowship is a process and participation. A group can have unity without fellowship being its name; fellowship always involves genuine shared participation, not merely structural unity.

**Love (R103, 3 shared verses):** Love is the motivating inner-quality from which fellowship may flow; fellowship is the structural relational reality love creates or sustains. Love can exist without being expressed as fellowship; fellowship without love risks becoming formal compliance.

**Covenant (R34, flagged in DIM-62-SD001 and SP-062-007):** Covenant names the bond structure; fellowship names the lived inner reality of participating within that bond. Covenant is contractual-covenantal; fellowship is experiential-participatory.

**Gap:** These distinctions are inferential from the data pattern rather than from direct verse-level comparison. Session D boundary analysis (DIM-62-SD001) is required for precise distinction work.

findings.finding_value: T1's boundary analysis (Q&A-019-021) identified three structural opposites and named the boundary problem with adjacent characteristics as partially unresolved. T6's structural relationships data confirms and deepens this: the boundary between goodness and love (R103), kindness (R99), and generosity (R65) is structurally unresolved at the root level — the vocabulary sharing (T6.4) and co-occurrence data (T6.1) reveal that these registries are adjacent precisely because they share root families and co-anchor at the same verses. T1's definition of goodness as constituted by the Mic 6:8 tri-fold (justice + kindness + humility — Q&A-152) directly names kindness as a component of goodness — which means the goodness-kindness boundary (T1.3 partially answered, T6.5 partially answered) is not between two separate characteristics but between a whole and one of its constituents. This reading resolves the boundary partially: kindness may be a constituent mode of goodness rather than a peer characteristic. Session D testing required.

findings.session_b_note: The closest adjacent characteristic from co-occurrence data is compassion (R023, 196 shared verses). What distinguishes them from the data: compassion is love's responsive form under the condition of the other's suffering — the rachamim/womb-movement is activated by the beloved's need or distress. Love without suffering context does not require the racham-movement; love in the presence of suffering always produces it. Stated differently: compassion is the subset of love that is suffering-triggered; love is the broader orientation of which compassion is one mode (OBS-103-029, OBS-103-042). However: the data does not fully distinguish chesed from compassion at the verse level — both can be present simultaneously (Lam 3:22). The distinction is partial. Gap: the precise boundary between love and compassion requires dedicated Session D analysis of both registries' verse corpora together.

findings.finding_value: T6 reveals compassion as the structural centre of the C17 cluster rather than a peripheral member. The love co-occurrence (196/351 = 55.8% of all OWNER verses) is uniquely dominant — compassion and love co-occur in more than half of all active verses, raising the programme-level question whether they are truly separable at the data level. Three structural observations from the co-occurrence landscape: (1) compassion sits at C17's centre of gravity (love, mercy, kindness as top three co-occurrences — all within-cluster); (2) compassion generates a human-response cluster (peace, faith, will, surrender, seeking co-occurring at significant levels — the pattern of divine compassion generating human inner-being responses); (3) compassion is constitutively responsive to human distress (despair, guilt, distress, evil all present in the co-occurrence table — compassion operates most characteristically in the presence of need). The CHASAD root crossing compassion (C17) and shame (C06) is the programme's most structurally unexpected finding — a root family that bridges two clusters. Exod 34:6 as the programme's most multiply-anchored verse (6 registries) must be treated as a cluster-level synthesis anchor. The compassion/mercy boundary (SD-009) is the most critical unresolved distinction. T6.7 (dimensional sharing) is programme-stage limited — formally deferred.

findings.finding_value: T6 produces the most structurally significant finding in the review set for any single tier: grace is not produced by any other inner-being characteristic. It is the originating point of a causal chain, not its product. This categorically distinguishes grace from every other characteristic reviewed — all others can be produced by at least one other characteristic; grace cannot. This structural uniqueness is confirmed by T2.9's origin analysis (grace originates with God — it does not originate in the human constitutional system) and is analytically consistent across T6.2 (seeking is the posture before grace arrives, not its producer), T6.3 (S-rating on "is grace produced by another characteristic"), and T6.4 (the vocabulary's structural completeness without a generative human-side term). The co-occurrence pattern reveals grace at the intersection of divine initiative and creaturely need: seeking (R140 — 40 verses, dominant) as the creature's pre-grace posture; moral failure cluster (evil, guilt, sin, transgression) as the creaturely context; power cluster (strength, might) confirming the 2Cor 12:9 connection. The love co-occurrence (R103 — 14 verses) is the primary within-cluster signal raising the grace-love boundary question (SD013). All major boundary distinctions (grace-love, grace-mercy, grace-justice, grace-chesed) remain open at T6.5 — the most unresolved boundary cluster in the review set. T6.7 (dimensional sharing) is programme-stage limited.

findings.finding_value: T4's relational architecture and T6's co-occurrence network express the same structural reality from relational and cross-registry perspectives. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (T6 — R140, 40 verses) is the co-occurrence expression of T4.2 (the human-to-God supplication direction): seeking is the relational posture, and R140 is the registry that names it. The sequential relationship confirmed in T6.2 (grace precedes and enables faith, repentance, supplication, mourning — SD003, SD006, SD026, SD038) is the causal expression of T4's architectural finding: grace is the enabling condition for every positive human-to-God relational posture. The boundary questions in T6.5 (grace-love, grace-mercy, grace-chesed) correspond to T4.5's scope analysis: the characteristics that share grace's scope (particularly love and mercy) are the same characteristics whose relational scope overlaps with grace's at T4.5.

findings.session_b_note: The most closely adjacent characteristics from the co-occurrence and C17 cluster data are: (1) Hesed/love (R103, 37 shared verses): the closest structural neighbour. Distinction: covenant is the relational structure (the bond that holds commitment across time); hesed is the relational quality (the love that sustains the bond from within). Covenant without hesed is merely legal; hesed without covenant is unstable. The distinction is structural (covenant) vs. qualitative (hesed). This distinction is supported by Deu 7:9 — "keeps covenant and steadfast love" — where they are paired but distinguished. (2) Faithfulness (R060, 10 shared verses, XREF-connected via H0548): faithfulness is a character quality; covenant is the structured bond that faithfulness holds together. Faithfulness is the inner character of the covenant-keeping person; covenant is the formal framework within which that faithfulness is exercised. (3) Oath (H7621 in R019 — XREF, OBS-034-006): the oath is the performative speech act that constitutes the covenant; the covenant is the ongoing relational bond established by the oath. Oath is the entry mechanism; covenant is the resulting bond. Gap: the precise boundaries of these distinctions require Session D cross-registry analysis — the current data provides the directional finding but not the fully precise boundary definition. Per SB-9: cross-word synthesis conclusions not permitted; raising as SD pointers.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-099-006: T6 reveals that kindness sits at the structural centre of a dense network of related characteristics rather than on the edge. Its most consistent co-occurrences (faithfulness, justice, compassion, for…
findings.finding_value: T6 reveals that kindness sits at the structural centre of a dense network of related characteristics rather than on the edge. Its most consistent co-occurrences (faithfulness, justice, compassion, forgiveness, humility, patience) are not merely adjacent virtues but appear to be partially constituent of kindness itself — the Mic 6:8 triad (justice/kindness/humility) and the Eph 4:32 cluster (kindness/tenderheartedness/forgiveness) function as composite wholes where each element reinforces and partly defines the others. The causal network is explicit and directional: divine kindness → praise + repentance in the recipient → reproduced human kindness toward others → sustained covenant relationships. This causal chain means kindness is not only a characteristic that one possesses but one that is structurally self-propagating through its own operation. The semantic-root finding is analytically significant: the CHESED root family spans the noun (chesed — kindness), the verb (chasad — be kind), the person (chasid — the kind one), the negative (shame/reproach for its failure), and a proper name (Chesed) — a root family that covers definition, action, identity, consequence, and proper-noun instantiation within a single family. T6's most significant intra-tier finding: Mic 6:8 anchors eight registries simultaneously, which confirms that kindness is not a standalone quality but a node in a structural web of C17 cluster characteristics — its full meaning requires these other registries to be seen.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-028: T6's structural relationship findings and T7's lexical and literary findings are mutually confirming at the level of the semantic root. The T6 finding that the CHESED root family covers noun (chesed),…
findings.finding_value: T6's structural relationship findings and T7's lexical and literary findings are mutually confirming at the level of the semantic root. The T6 finding that the CHESED root family covers noun (chesed), verb (chasad), person (chasid), shame-negative (H2617B), and proper noun (Chesed) is a T7 lexical observation that has structural significance: a root family that spans all these categories is not merely a lexical curiosity but evidence that kindness (as the CHESED root names it) is a comprehensive inner-being reality — it has a noun form (what it is), a verb form (what it does), a person form (who embodies it), a consequence form (what happens when it fails), and a proper-noun instantiation (when it names a person). The T6 co-occurrence finding that kindness clusters with faithfulness, justice, and compassion maps directly onto the T7 semantic range finding that chesed itself encompasses goodness/kindness/faithfulness — the co-occurrence cluster is partly a reflection of the internal semantic complexity of chesed: different registries are studying different dimensions of what is, in the original Hebrew, a single concept. T7's primary anchor verse (Lam 3:22) is T6's most significant causal statement: the inexhaustibility of chesed (T7) is the precondition for the causal chain's stability (T6) — if chesed could run out, the chain would break.

findings.session_b_note: The closest neighbours requiring distinction work: (1) Rest (nuach/menuchah — major component of R117 itself): rest and peace co-reside in this registry, which creates an internal distinction challenge. Rest is the cessation-of-striving dimension; peace is the positive wholeness-condition that rest may produce or accompany. Rest can be given and withdrawn (Deu 28:65 — no resting place); peace encompasses more than the cessation of striving (shalom includes welfare, friendship, covenant, and messianic embodiment). Rest is a component of peace's semantic range but not co-extensive with it; (2) Joy (R97, 21 shared verses): joy and peace are frequently paired (Gal 5:22 — adjacent Spirit-fruits; Isa 55:12 — "go out in joy... led forth in peace"). Joy is the positive affective response; peace is the positive existential condition. Joy can be present without complete peace (James 1:2 — "count it all joy... when you meet trials of various kinds" — joy in trials doesn't require peaceful resolution); peace at its fullest produces joy but is not joy itself. Gap: the boundary between peace and rest (as internal to R117) requires Session D clarity — is rest a dimension of peace or a distinct characteristic captured by the same registry?

findings.session_b_note: The two closest adjacent characteristics are R099 (kindness/hesed) and R103 (love). Hesed (R099): both hesed and na.tan-in-its-covenantal-mode express the outward enactment of covenantal commitment. The distinction within the data: hesed describes the quality of the commitment (steadfast, covenant-loyal); na.tan describes the act by which that commitment is expressed (giving as its enacted form). Its five-dimensional breadth (MC, RD, Cognition, Transformation, DHC) means it shares dimensional territory with virtually every adjacent characteristic. Its co-occurrence breadth (14 registries ≥6 shared verses) and shared-anchor density (12 shared anchors across 9 registries) confirms the hub position empirically. The aman root architecture reveals that R060, R059, and R044 are conceptually entangled at the root level — the programme's separation is analytical, not lexical. The distinction from nearest neighbours (hesed/R099, love/R103) is of kind — dispositional vs. actional — confirming that R060 holds a distinct structural position as the actional realisation of what the dispositional characteristics name. What T6 reveals as a whole: this characteristic is not isolated in the inner-being landscape; it is a connector through which multiple adjacent characteristics are expressed, related, and developed.

The characteristic's actional nature (it is a verb, not a noun) means it produces other characteristics as its outputs (worship, hope, wisdom) and is produced by others as its inputs (love, compassion, trust). This producing/produced-by structure is precisely what makes it a hub: it sits at the intersection of multiple causal chains. The distinction of kind from nearest neighbours (T6.5, Q&A-162 — dispositional vs. actional) confirms that its structural position in the landscape is as the enacted form of what dispositional characteristics name. What this pair reveals: the definition of faithfulness-as-giving (actional) is the structural reason for its hub position. Because it is an act that can express any of the adjacent dispositions, it sits at the centre of the dispositional cluster. It is the verbal form of a field of nouns.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness vs. Faithfulness (e.mu.nah/pistis)]** Faithfulness is consistently paired with righteousness (Deu 32:4; Psa 85:10) — they are related but distinct. Faithfulness names reliability, steadfastness, covenant-keeping through time; righteousness names moral conformity to the right standard. Faithfulness is temporal and relational (staying true over time to a commitment); righteousness is moral and relational (being right in relation to the standard). A person can be faithful (reliable) without being righteous (morally conforming); a person can be righteous (morally right) in a specific instance without being faithful (sustained over time).

findings.finding_value: **[F — Moral Reckoning vs. Cognition generally]** The reckoning faculty in F is specifically moral-evaluative cognition — it differs from general cognition in that its object is always moral worth, moral standing, or moral reality. The distinction is in the object and outcome of the cognitive act, not in the cognitive process itself.

**Cross-cluster finding 8 — The A2/C tension (Ezekiel vs. NT security)**
The cluster holds an unresolved tension: the Ezekiel forfeiture model (A2-002: righteousness can be forfeited; non-transferable; non-accumulative) stands in tension with the NT's declared security of the justified person (C: Rom 8:34 — "who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who intercedes"). This tension is visible when A2 and C are held simultaneously. findings.finding_value:
[E] M01-A's nearest neighbour within the programme is **reverence / awe** (if separately classified) and **trust / faith** (as the complement that fear-of-God enables). The distinction from trust: reverential fear is the *posture* that grounds right relationship with God; trust is the *reliance* that flows from it. Fear and trust coexist and are mutually enabling (Psa 112:7-8; Psa 115:11) but are analytically distinct — fear names the posture of creaturely asymmetry before God; trust names the reliance that the security of that relationship produces.

---

[E] M01-A (reverential fear) and M01-F (anticipatory dread) are nearest neighbours on the temporal axis. The distinction: M01-A is a stable dispositional orientation; M01-F is a forward-looking affective condition. Fear-of-God in M01-A produces confidence (Pro 14:26); anxiety in M01-F colonises the inner life with dread. They can involve the same vocabulary (pa.chad appears in both) but are constitutively distinct in their inner-person operation.

M01-B (acute fear) and M01-E (trembling) are nearest neighbours. The distinction: M01-B is primarily an inner-state with volitional consequences; M01-E is primarily the somatic expression of that inner state. They co-occur (1Sa 28:5: fear in the heart and trembling paired) but are analytically distinct: M01-B is the inner fear-event; M01-E is the body's registration of it.

[E] M01-B (acute fear) and M01-E (trembling) are nearest neighbours. The distinction: M01-B is primarily an inner-state with volitional consequences; M01-E is primarily the somatic expression of that inner state. They co-occur (1Sa 28:5: fear in the heart and trembling paired) but are analytically distinct: M01-B is the inner fear-event; M01-E is the body's registration of it.

---

[E] M01-D (dismay) and M01-E (trembling) are nearest neighbours in the somatic register. The distinction: M01-D is the dissolution of inner coherence (the shattering, not the shaking); M01-E is the bodily trembling that registers the fear. Dismay collapses function; trembling expresses the inner state while function remains (partially) intact.

M01-A (reverential fear) and M01-F (anticipatory dread) are nearest neighbours on the temporal axis. The distinction: M01-A is a stable dispositional orientation; M01-F is a forward-looking affective condition. Fear-of-God in M01-A produces confidence (Pro 14:26); anxiety in M01-F colonises the inner life with dread. They can involve the same vocabulary (pa.chad appears in both) but are constitutively distinct in their inner-person operation.

M01-D (dismay) and M01-E (trembling) are nearest neighbours in the somatic register. The distinction: M01-D is the dissolution of inner coherence (the shattering, not the shaking); M01-E is the bodily trembling that registers the fear. Dismay collapses function; trembling expresses the inner state while function remains (partially) intact.

Within M01 itself, the nearest-neighbour pairs are: A/F (dispositional vs. anticipatory), B/E (inner fear/somatic expression), D/E (dissolution vs. trembling). Across the programme's broader landscape, the nearest neighbour to M01-A (reverential fear of God) is likely M18 (Awe/Wonder) if such a cluster is designated — the distinction being that M01-A is specifically relational (directed toward God in covenant posture) while M18's awe may be more broadly generated.

[E] **Contrast: M02 vs M06:** The nearest neighbour is M06 Hate, Contempt and Hostility. The distinction: anger (M02) is reactive and thermally intense — it arises in response to a perceived violation and is aimed at the wrong-act or wrong-condition. Hate (M06) is dispositional and directed aversion toward a person or thing — it is maintained as a settled orientation, not necessarily thermally hot. Anger can exist without hate (the parent angry at a child's behaviour without hating the child); hate can exist without anger (cold contempt is hate without the heat of anger). Cross-routing flag from Phase 7: Neh 4:7 sits at this boundary — the coalition's hostility toward Israel's restoration is closer to M06's hostile-enmity register than to M02's burning heat.

---

[E] **Contrast: M02 vs M28:** The near neighbour for the jealousy register is M28 Envy, Greed and Lust. The distinction: jealousy (M02-E) is protectively possessive — it fires at the threat to what is already claimed. Envy (M28) is covetously acquisitive — it desires what belongs to another. The Hebrew qin.ah carries both dimensions but the dominant M02-E-VCG-04 register is possessive-relational; the M28 register is covetous. The boundary is the presence or absence of a prior claim: jealousy presupposes a claim; envy presupposes the absence of the desired object.

The closest adjacent characteristic is M24 Weakness (Vulnerability and Suffering). The distinction is: M03 grief is constitutively relational — it arises from the loss of or damage to something or someone bonded to and valued; M24 weakness names the constitutional vulnerability and depletion of the person as such, regardless of relational content. Grief presupposes love; weakness does not. A person can be weak without having lost anything they love; a person cannot grieve without having loved something that is now absent or damaged.

The second closest is M01 Fear: the anguish register of M03 (tsu.qah, qe.pha.dah — BOUNDARY) overlaps with M01's terror register. The distinction is: M03 is oriented toward loss (the loved thing that is gone or threatened); M01 is oriented toward threat (the danger that is approaching). Both produce inner constriction but from different relational orientations.

**[CHAR-1]** E — **Gladness** (M04 Characteristic 3) is the closest adjacent characteristic — both are positive inner states, both use overlapping vocabulary (gil_verb; su.s appears in both), both are Godward in their primary orientation. The distinction: Exultation is characterised by **surging intensity, directedness, and triumph** — it rises toward its object; Gladness is characterised by **warmth, brightness, and settled positivity** — it pervades the inner being without the surge. Psa 14:7 — "let Jacob rejoice (gil), let Israel be glad (sa.me.ach)" — places them in synonymous parallel, suggesting they are experienced together, but the different terms signal different qualities of the same positive inner territory.

**[CHAR-2]** E — **Gladness** (Characteristic 3) is the closest adjacent characteristic. The distinction has been established across Phase 9: (1) **Activity vs. warmth** — Joy is active and participatory (rejoices *in* something, engaged, directional); Gladness is warm, diffuse, and settled (the heart is glad, the inner condition is bright); (2) **Independence from circumstance** — Joy can transcend and persist through adverse circumstances (Hab 3:18; 2Cor 6:10; 1Pe 1:6); Gladness is more characteristically responsive to circumstances assessed as good (M04-O; M04-L); (3) **Communal structure** — Joy has a constitutively communal dimension (feast-joy; sunchairo); Gladness is more characteristically individual or circumstantially responsive; (4) **Object-specificity** — Joy consistently names its object ("rejoice in the Lord," "rejoice at his birth"); Gladness is more characteristically a condition without always specifying an object.

**[CHAR-7]** E — **Joy** (Characteristic 2) is the closest — confirmed by the shared agalliao vocabulary, the co-occurrence patterns, and the sequential relationship. The precise distinction: (1) **Context** — Joy (Characteristic 2) rejoices in what is genuinely celebratable and good; Suffering-Joy rejoices specifically in the context of what is genuinely adverse and painful; (2) **Mechanism** — Joy can arise through multiple mechanisms (word comprehension, divine encounter, volitional cultivation, feast practice); Suffering-Joy's primary mechanism is Spirit-impartation and eschatological grounding; (3) **Constitutive role of suffering** — for Suffering-Joy, the suffering is not merely the context but the constitutive occasion of the characteristic: "insofar as you share Christ's sufferings" (1Pe 4:13) — the sharing of suffering is the condition and form of the joy; (4) **Eschatological concentration** — Suffering-Joy has a higher eschatological concentration than Joy; every instance of its primary (agalliao) evidence is grounded in eschatological reality.

**[CHAR-3]** E — **Joy** (Characteristic 2) is the closest adjacent characteristic. The distinction has been progressively established across both Phase 9 runs: (1) **Activity vs. settled warmth** — Joy is active, participatory, and engaged (rejoices *in* something, commanded to constant orientation); Gladness is settled, warm, and diffuse (the inner condition of one who has assessed that things are genuinely good); (2) **Independence from circumstance** — Joy can transcend adverse circumstances (Phili 4:4 "always"; Hab 3:18); Gladness in its circumstantial face (M04-O) is more characteristically responsive to assessed-good circumstances — Jon 4:3, 8 (circumstances reversed → Gladness collapses); (3) **Primary faculty** — Joy's primary dimension is affective; Gladness's primary dimension is cognitive-evaluative; (4) **Command-susceptibility** — Joy is more directly commandable (Phili 4:4; 1Th 5:16; the Deuteronomic feast-commands); Gladness's evaluative face is less directly commandable — one must be formed in the capacity for accurate evaluation.

**[CHAR-4]** E — **Gladness** (Characteristic 3) is the closest adjacent characteristic, sharing the tov vocabulary and overlapping in certain registers (Psa 73:28; 84:10; 118:8–9 appear in both clusters' evidence). The precise distinctions: (1) **Object-focus vs. diffuseness** — Delight is always delight *in* a specific object (law, God, person, wisdom, idol); Gladness is diffuse warmth, an inner state of being-glad that is not necessarily anchored to a single treasured object; (2) **Affective-volitional vs. cognitive-evaluative** — Delight's primary dimension is affective-volitional (the pleasurable orienting of affect and will toward the object); Gladness's primary dimension is cognitive-evaluative (the assessment that something is genuinely good); (3) **Resting vs. assessing** — Delight rests in its object; Gladness assesses that things are good; (4) **Breadth** — Delight has 247 verses across 5 sub-groups; Gladness has 133 verses across 2 sub-groups; Delight is the broader characteristic, encompassing a corrupt register (M04-P) that Gladness does not have as a primary concern.

**[CHAR-5]** E — **Delight** (Characteristic 4) is the closest adjacent characteristic. Precise distinctions: (1) **Object-focus vs. ambient** — Delight focuses on a specific treasured object (sha.a.shu.im, cha.phets directed toward God, law, persons); Pleasure is the more ambient quality of agreeableness received from what surrounds the person without necessarily focusing on a single treasured object; (2) **Volitional vs. receptive** — Delight has a strong volitional component (cha.phets/eudokeo); Pleasure is more purely receptive (na.im/ni.cho.ach); (3) **Constitutional depth** — Delight operates primarily at the inner being/soul level (Rom 7:22; Mat 12:18); Pleasure operates across a wider constitutional range including explicit body-level (Pro 16:24; Deu 28:54, 56); (4) **Shared vocabulary** — a.nog appears in both, marking the overlap zone: Psa 37:4's a.nog in Delight (directed toward God as specific object) vs. Deu 28:54's a.nog in Pleasure (ambient luxury-ease) — the same root, different directional structure.

**[CHAR-6]** E — **Exultation** (Characteristic 1) is the closest adjacent in terms of the response to God's extraordinary acts. Precise distinctions: (1) **Arrested vs. surging** — Wonder stills the inner being; Exultation surges upward; (2) **Receptive-perceptive vs. active-emotive** — Wonder is the response to what is seen/encountered; Exultation is the active upward thrust of the inner being; (3) **Cognitive boundary vs. emotive peak** — Wonder arises at the limit of comprehension; Exultation arises at the peak of received salvation/victory; (4) **Proclamatory vs. participatory** — Wonder's characteristic expression is telling/declaring; Exultation's characteristic expression is jubilation and shouting; (5) **Not requiring Spirit** — Wonder is available to the natural person encountering the extraordinary; Exultation in its highest register may require Spirit-production.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's five primary boundary pairs with precise distinguishing criteria: (1) **Joy (Char 2) / Gladness (Char 3)** — confirmed as the cluster's closest and most analytically demanding boundary; Joy is active-participatory, commands engagement, can transcend adverse circumstances, and is communally constituted; Gladness is settled-warm, cognitively-evaluative, primarily responsive to circumstances assessed as good, and less directly commandable. The formulaic pairing shows they co-arise from the same conditions; the phenomenological distinction is consistent; (2) **Delight (Char 4) / Gladness (Char 3)** — closest through the tov-root sharing; distinguished by object-focus vs. diffuseness (Delight is always toward a specific object; Gladness is a diffuse evaluative warmth) and affective-volitional vs. cognitive-evaluative primary faculty; (3) **Delight (Char 4) / Pleasure (Char 5)** — closest through the a.nog vocabulary; distinguished by directed vs. ambient orientation (Delight is directed toward a specific treasured object; Pleasure is the ambient quality of what is agreeable in the surroundings); (4) **Wonder (Char 6) / Exultation (Char 1)** — closest in their shared context (God's extraordinary acts); distinguished by arrested-cognitive vs. active-emotive-surging response; (5) **Joy (Char 2) / Suffering-Joy (Char 7)** — closest through shared agalliao vocabulary; distinguished by the constitutive role of suffering and degree of Spirit-dependence.

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-1]** E — CHAR-2 (Humiliation as enforced abasement, M07-D) is the closest neighbour. Both involve shame; both involve downward movement of standing. The precise distinction is: CHAR-1 is the *felt inner experience* — the collapse of dignity and confidence as an inner event; CHAR-2 is the *enforced outer movement* — the mechanism by which a person's standing is brought down by an external agent. A person can experience CHAR-1 (inner shame) without CHAR-2 (no external enforced abasement); and a person can undergo CHAR-2 (be publicly humiliated) without necessarily experiencing CHAR-1 in its full inner form (if they are morally insensitive or resilient). The servant who endures beating and spitting (Isa 50:6) undergoes CHAR-2 (physical humiliation) while CHAR-1 is present but borne (voluntarily accepted).

**[CHAR-2]** E — The nearest neighbour distinction with CHAR-1: CHAR-2 is the outer-mechanism; CHAR-1 is the inner-experience. The distinction is of kind (mechanism vs. experience). CHAR-2 is also distinct from CHAR-5 (contempt producing shame): CHAR-5's mechanism is specifically contempt/dismissal; CHAR-2's mechanism is enforced downward movement (which can be produced by contempt but also by military defeat, divine judgment, natural loss).

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 is most closely related to CHAR-5 (shame produced by contempt): both involve the treatment of persons as of diminished worth. The distinction: CHAR-3 names the relational verdict (worth-denial as the act and its structural effect); CHAR-5 names the specific mechanism (contempt/dismissal as the producing agent and its received shame as the specific outcome in the recipient). CHAR-3 is broader — worth-denial can be produced by contempt (CHAR-5), by structural assignment (VCG-02), or by hypocrisy and favoritism (VCG-01) without being contempt in the strict sense.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 is most closely related to CHAR-1 in its moral-consequence register (M07-B — shame as the consequence of moral failure). The distinction: CHAR-1-M07-B is about shame as the experience that follows moral failure; CHAR-4 is about the conscience's recognition of what is shameful as a quality of conduct or desire. CHAR-4 is the evaluative faculty; CHAR-1-M07-B is the experiential consequence. They frequently occur together: the same act that CHAR-4 identifies as shameful produces CHAR-1's shame-experience in the person who commits it.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — CHAR-5 is most closely related to CHAR-3 (dishonour as relational worth-denial) and to M06 (contempt as the producing mechanism). The distinction between CHAR-5 and CHAR-3: CHAR-5 names the specific mechanism (contempt as the producing force) and the received shame as the specific outcome; CHAR-3 names the relational verdict of worth-denial more broadly (which can arise from causes other than contempt). The distinction between CHAR-5 and M06: M06 holds the contempt-projection (the contempt-er's inner act); CHAR-5 holds the contempt-received shame (the recipient's inner experience). CHAR-5 and M06 are relational complements — they are the two faces of the same contempt-shame dynamic.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-6 is most closely related to M12 (purity/holiness) through shared vocabulary, but the analytical distinction is clear: M12 holds the purity/holiness register of niq.qa.von and qe.ha.von as the primary meaning of these terms; CHAR-6 holds the innocence-as-counter-to-shame function of the same terms in every verse of the 8-verse corpus. The distinction is one of purpose and register: M12 = moral and ritual purity as the characteristic; CHAR-6 = innocence as specifically the protection against and structural counter to shame.

---

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-2]** E — The closest adjacent characteristic is CHAR-1 Humility. Both involve the person taking a lower posture. The precise distinction: Humility (CHAR-1) is the inner disposition of self-lowering before God and others generally — a self-regarding posture about the person's own standing that is stable and dispositional across all contexts. Submission (CHAR-2) is the will's yielding to a specific legitimate authority — relational-responsive, directional toward a particular authority, and constituted in the relationship with that authority. A person who is humble in general character will tend to be submissive to legitimate authority; but the two are distinguishable: Gal2:5 (Paul withholding submission from false teachers) requires discernment about legitimate authority that is not the same question as whether Paul is personally humble.

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-1 Humility is the closest adjacent characteristic, confirmed by Isa57:15's direct pairing ("contrite and lowly in spirit"). The precise distinction: *Humility (CHAR-1)* is the stable inner disposition of self-lowering before God — ongoing, dispositional, applicable across all life-contexts. *Contrition (CHAR-3)* is the acute, crisis-precipitated inner state specifically following confrontation with moral failure or divine holiness — intense, episodic, affectively loaded with the weight of the specific moral reality that occasions it. The distinction: humility is the stable posture; contrition is the acute form of that posture under the specific conditions of moral crisis.

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-1 Humility is the closest adjacent characteristic, confirmed by the co-occurrence analysis (T6.1.1) and the Phase 7 multi-faceted designation (Mat11:29 — "gentle and lowly in heart"). The precise distinction: *Humility (CHAR-1)* is the inner posture of self-lowering before God and others — it is constitutively about the person's orientation of self-placement. *Meekness/Gentleness (CHAR-4)* is the quality of the person's engagement with others in their weakness and need — it is constitutively about the manner of relational contact. The distinction: humility is an inner posture relative to self; meekness/gentleness is the relational quality of engagement with others that the humble posture enables.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The M08 (Pride) cluster is the closest structural opposite rather than resemblant adjacent characteristic — the carry-forward OPEN observation is that semnotēs and M08 proud self-display are structural opposites. The closest resemblant adjacent characteristic within M09 is CHAR-1 Humility: both involve the person not asserting their worth or standing through self-promotion. The distinction: *Humility (CHAR-1)* is the active self-lowering before God and others — the person places themselves in the lower position. *Dignity (CHAR-5)* is the settled inner gravity that does not need to assert, claim, or display — it is non-assertive not through active self-lowering but through grounded self-possession. Humility is active; dignity is settled. Humility positions downward; dignity rests in position.

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-2 Submission is the most structurally adjacent within M09, as both are volitional characteristics. The precise distinction: *Submission (CHAR-2)* is the will's yielding to a specific legitimate authority in response to its claim — the will orients *toward* what is commanded; *Willing-heartedness (CHAR-6)* is the will's spontaneous free movement toward giving and service — the will moves *from* its own inner motivation rather than in response to an external command. The distinction: submission is command-responsive; willing-heartedness is spontaneously self-generating. A person can be submissive (yielding when commanded) without being willing-hearted (freely motivated without command); and willing-hearted (freely giving before commanded) without the specific authority-submission of CHAR-2.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The closest adjacent characteristic is CHAR-3 Contrition (M09-E in the sub-group structure — dak.ka, crushed and broken spirit). Both operate in the register of the person's inner posture before God in acknowledgment of their true standing. The precise distinction: *Humility (CHAR-1)* is the stable dispositional posture of the whole person — ongoing, sustained, characterological, applicable across all of life's contexts (Mic6:8 — "walk humbly with your God" — comprehensive and continuous). *Contrition (CHAR-3)* is the acute, emotion-laden, crisis-precipitated inner brokenness specifically following confrontation with moral failure (Psa34:18 — "he saves the crushed in spirit"; Isa57:15 — pairs contrition with lowliness but as a distinct, acute state). The distinction is one of *temporal form and affective intensity*: humility is sustained and dispositional; contrition is acute and crisis-localized.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The five intra-cluster boundary distinctions documented across the per-characteristic batches form the cluster's analytical contribution to the programme's inner-being taxonomy. Summary of the most important boundaries. *CHAR-1 / CHAR-3*: same semantic domain; distinguished by temporal form and affective intensity — humility is stable and dispositional; contrition is acute, affectively loaded, crisis-precipitated. *CHAR-1 / CHAR-2*: distinguished by relational structure — humility is the general self-lowering posture; submission is the specifically authority-directed yielding. *CHAR-1 / CHAR-4*: distinguished by register — humility is the inner posture of self-lowering; meekness/gentleness is the quality of relational engagement that the posture enables. *CHAR-2 / CHAR-6*: distinguished by source — submission is command-responsive; willing-heartedness is spontaneously self-generating. *CHAR-1 / CHAR-5*: distinguished by kind and stance — humility is the active downward movement; dignity is the stable non-assertive settled position. Cluster-level: these five boundaries together define M09's internal taxonomy of non-self-assertive inner existence, distinguishing six genuinely distinct characteristics that are mutually adjacent, mutually defining, and mutually confirming — none of the six is redundant with the others.

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-1]** E — CHAR-2 (Unintentional sinning) most closely resembles CHAR-1 in vocabulary (both use cha.ta, both use the Lev 4/5 cultic-atonement framework). The precise distinction is the quality of the will's engagement: CHAR-1 requires that the person knows what they are doing and does it — the will is engaged with knowledge of the wrong. CHAR-2 occurs when the wrong is not consciously intended — the Lev 4:22/27 formulation ("doing unintentionally any one of all the things that by the commandments of the Lord his God ought not to be done") defines CHAR-2. The distinction is at the point of inner awareness: CHAR-1 involves the will acting against known moral reality; CHAR-2 involves the will acting without that awareness, so that conscience engages only after the fact.

**[CHAR-10]** E — CHAR-6 (Habitual defection) most closely resembles the enticement-mechanism of CHAR-10 in its dispositional outcome: 2Pe 2:14 — "hearts trained in greed... insatiable for sin" — the formed character of the enticers resembles CHAR-6's settled dispositional pattern. The precise distinction: CHAR-6 is the formed settled sinning disposition as a condition; CHAR-10's enticement mechanism is the *process* through which that formation occurs. CHAR-6 is the endpoint; CHAR-10 names the pathway. CHAR-6's "habitual defection" is the dispositional state that sustained CHAR-10 enticement produces.

**[CHAR-11]** E — CHAR-12 (Sin as enslaving power) most closely resembles CHAR-11 — both address sin as a structural condition rather than a specific act, and both draw heavily from the Romans 5-8 evidence base. The precise distinction: CHAR-11 is the *universal condition* under which all persons stand — the structural state of being-under-sin and falling-short-of-glory (Rom 3:9/23 — "all are under sin... all have sinned"); CHAR-12 focuses specifically on the *enslaving power-dimension* of sin — sin as the master/tyrant that holds the person captive. CHAR-11 is the broader category (universal scope, all registers — VCG-01/02/03); CHAR-12 is the enslaving-power register specifically.

**[CHAR-12]** E — CHAR-11 (Sin as universal condition) most closely resembles CHAR-12 — both address sin as a structural force rather than a specific act, and both draw from overlapping evidence in the M10 corpus. The precise distinction: CHAR-11 is the *universal structural condition* all persons stand in — the bedrock state of being-under-sin affecting every person regardless of individual sinning patterns (Rom 3:9/23 — "all under sin... all have sinned"); CHAR-12 is the *active enslaving power* that specifically governs the will of those who practice sin — the power-mechanism within the condition. CHAR-11 is the broader ontological category; CHAR-12 names sin's specific governing function over the will.

**[CHAR-13]** E — CHAR-17 (Guilt as inner-being state) most closely resembles CHAR-13 — both address the person's standing in relation to sin's weight. The precise distinction: CHAR-13 is the *objective record* — the moral account existing before God regardless of the person's awareness or feeling (definition: "whether they feel it or not"); CHAR-17 is the *subjective inner experience* — the felt sense of guilt as the conscience's response to the record. The record (CHAR-13) exists before God independently; guilt (CHAR-17) is the inner-being experience that the record may or may not produce depending on conscience-engagement. CHAR-13 is the objective; CHAR-17 is the subjective experience of the same underlying reality.

**[CHAR-14]** E — CHAR-3 (Confession) most closely resembles CHAR-14's seeking dimension — both involve the person's verbal/volitional movement toward God in acknowledgment of sin. The precise distinction: CHAR-3 is the specific speech-act of acknowledging and naming the sin (the verbal confession); CHAR-14 is the broader characteristic that encompasses not just the verbal acknowledgment but the full seeking-and-receiving transaction — the bringing of the offering (Lev 4:14/5:6), the priestly mediation (Lev 10:17), the divine declaration (Luk 7:48), and the consequent transformation (Col 2:13; Act 2:38). CHAR-3 is one component that may accompany CHAR-14; CHAR-14 encompasses more.

**[CHAR-15]** E — CHAR-11 (Sin as universal condition) most closely resembles CHAR-15 — both address sin as a condition rather than a discrete act, and both apply to all persons. The precise distinction: CHAR-11 is the *ontological structural condition* all persons share (Rom 3:23 — "all have sinned and fall short" — individually constituted); CHAR-15 is the *lineage-transmitted moral liability* that enters through ancestral and communal belonging. CHAR-11 is universal without requiring ancestry; CHAR-15 is specifically transmitted through lineage and community belonging. Isa 43:27 — "your first father sinned" — names the lineage-mechanism that is absent from CHAR-11's structural condition.

**[CHAR-16]** E — CHAR-11 (Sin as universal condition) most closely resembles CHAR-16 — both address the person's standing under sin. The precise distinction: CHAR-11 is the ontological condition all persons share (structural, universal, undifferentiated); CHAR-16 is the characterological identity of a recognisable moral type (individual/communal, forming into a person-type, differentiated by degree and recognition). CHAR-11 names what all persons are structurally; CHAR-16 names what some persons have become characterologically through formation, imputation, or social recognition — "the sinner" as a recognisable moral category.

**[CHAR-17]** E — CHAR-13 (Sin as divine record) most closely resembles CHAR-17 — both address the person's standing in relation to sin's moral weight. The precise distinction: CHAR-13 is the *objective* moral account before God — the record exists whether the person feels it or not (CHAR-13's definition: "the person carries this record whether they feel it or not"); CHAR-17 is the *subjective* inner experience of moral liability — the conscience's felt recognition. **[CHAR-18]** E — CHAR-13 (Sin as divine record) most closely resembles CHAR-18 — both concern the accumulated moral account before God. The precise distinction: CHAR-13 is the *divine record*-characteristic — the account held in God's memory encompassing all sin-categories; CHAR-18 is one *content-type* within that record — specifically the crime-dimension of accumulated moral wrongdoing (a.von H5771G). **[CHAR-21]** E — CHAR-18 (Iniquity as accumulated moral crime) most closely resembles CHAR-21 — both address the inner moral-distortion reality. **[CHAR-22]** E — CHAR-21 (Perversion as inner inversion) most closely resembles CHAR-22 — both address the inner moral faculty's departure from the right moral standard.
