Char 1 (settled person-identity — ra.sha) and Char 5 (active inner scheming — a.ven/po.al a.ven) share the evildoer-class (Char 5 VCG-03 / Char 1's person-type). Distinction: Char 1 names who the person is (settled dispositional identity); Char 5 names what the person's inner life does (active generative process). The distinction is one of kind: identity vs. activity. (b) Char 3 / Char 4 — the most closely adjacent pair sharing the same vocabulary. Both use to.e.vah and both invoke divine revulsion. Distinction: the object triggering the revulsion differs — moral-character corruption (Char 3) vs. idolatrous devotion (Char 4). The distinction is one of content/kind, not degree or level. (c) Char 1 / Char 2 — sharing the evil person-type. Distinction: Char 1 (settled directional orientation of the will — the wicked person's chosen way) vs. Char 2 (structural constitution of the inner nature — the evil person's default generative output). The distinction is one of analytical level: orientation (Char 1) vs. constitution (Char 2).
findings.notes: outcome=E

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-1]** E — Characteristic 2 (Moral-inner defilement-state, M10c-C sub-group) most closely resembles Characteristic 1. Both are defilement-state conditions bearing on the person's inner integrity and sacred standing. The precise distinction: Characteristic 1's condition is acquired through bodily mechanism (contact, emission, disease-verdict) — the defilement is external in origin, entering through the body. Characteristic 2's condition originates in the inner person itself — the conscience, will, and heart are corrupted by desire, habitual sin, and idolatrous attachment (Rom 6:19: "prior master directing bodily members"; 2Cor 7:1: "defilement of body and spirit"). Characteristic 1 is managed through prescribed ritual remedies (washing, waiting, examination, water of impurity); Characteristic 2 requires the moral and volitional transformation of the inner person.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Characteristic 1 (Ritual defilement-state) most closely resembles Characteristic 2 (Moral-inner defilement-state). Both are defilement-states bearing on the person's sacral standing and inner integrity. The precise distinction: Characteristic 1's condition is acquired through bodily contact with a defiling agent (external, mechanical origin) or authoritative verdict; Characteristic 2's condition originates within the inner person itself — through desire, sin, and habitual moral failure (internal, volitional origin). Characteristic 1 is managed through prescribed ritual remedies (washing, waiting, examination); Characteristic 2 requires the transformation of the inner person's orientation — repentance, cleansing of body and spirit (2Cor 7:1), re-presentation of the will toward righteousness (Rom 6:19).

**[CHAR-3]** E — Characteristic 2 (Moral-inner defilement-state) most closely resembles Characteristic 3. Both involve moral defilement arising from volitional defection and idolatrous attachment. The precise distinction: Characteristic 2's locus is the individual inner person — conscience, will, and heart corrupted from within. Characteristic 3's locus is the corporate-covenantal domain — the defilement extends from the community's inner will outward to land, sanctuary, and divine name. The distinguishing feature is extension: Characteristic 3 requires the outward extension to sacred environmental objects (land, sanctuary, name) to be operative; Characteristic 2 operates entirely within the individual inner person without requiring external sacred-space extension.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Characteristic 1 (Ritual defilement-state) most closely resembles Characteristic 4 in that both produce a defilement-state not primarily the result of the person's own moral defection — the defilement arrives through an external mechanism. The precise distinction: Characteristic 1's mechanism is bodily contact with a material defiling agent or authoritative verdict — a physical-ritual mechanism governed by the Levitical system. Characteristic 4's mechanism is inhabitation by an external spiritual being — a personal, purposeful, adversarial agent who invades and dominates at the spirit level.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's nearest-neighbour pairings reveal its internal architecture. Characteristic 1 and Characteristic 2 are the nearest pair within the cluster — both are defilement-state conditions of the person with a primary vocabulary shared (ta.me, akathartos). The distinction: Char 1 originates externally (bodily contact with a material defiling agent or authoritative verdict); Char 2 originates internally (the person's own volitional/dispositional moral corruption). Characteristic 2 and Characteristic 3 are the second nearest pair — both involve moral defilement arising from volitional defection and idolatrous attachment. The distinction: Char 2's locus is the individual inner person; Char 3's locus is the corporate-covenantal domain extending outward to land, sanctuary, and divine name (individual vs corporate-extending). Characteristic 1 and Characteristic 4 are the outer-origin nearest pair — both produce a defilement-state not primarily from the person's own moral defection. The distinction: Char 1's external cause is impersonal and material (governed by the Levitical system); Char 4's external cause is personal, purposeful, and adversarial (a spiritual being). The cluster's internal nearest-neighbour structure: Chars 1-2 (bodily vs inner-moral; external vs internal), Chars 2-3 (individual vs corporate/extending), Chars 1-4 (external-material vs external-spiritual).
findings.notes: outcome=E

questions.section: T6 — Structural Relationships with Other Characteristics
questions.question_text: Where the evidence shows apparent overlap, what is the precise boundary?

findings.session_b_note:
The data identifies the apparent overlap but does not draw the precise boundary:

**Overlap zone (mercy and forgiveness):** Both mercy and forgiveness appear in Psa 86:5 as co-equal divine attributes; both share 16 verses (co-occurrence); the anchor Lev 4:20 is shared. In the shared verses, mercy and forgiveness appear to be operating simultaneously — it is not possible from the verse evidence alone to say where mercy ends and forgiveness begins.

**Partial boundary indicator:** The salach-root exclusivity (forgiveness = divine-exclusive act) and the hesed-breadth (mercy = broader covenant-loyalty) suggest that forgiveness may be the **specific judicial instance** of mercy directed at moral debt, while mercy covers the wider relational disposition. But this boundary is inferred from vocabulary structure, not from explicit verse statement.

**The resolution required:** A direct comparison of the mercy and forgiveness verse corpora — examining which verses carry both characteristics and which carry only one — would establish the boundary empirically. This has not been done in the existing analysis and is a Session D task.

findings.session_b_note:
Three apparent overlaps are identified in the data, with their current boundary status:

**Compassion / mercy (R111):** The boundary is unresolved. Partial evidence suggests a sequential model (compassion generates mercy) but Rom 9:15 parallel usage challenges this. Deferred to Session D (SD-009).

**Compassion / love (R103):** The boundary is the programme's most structurally significant open question. The 196-verse co-occurrence and the RACHAM root-sharing make the boundary between compassion and love the most urgent distinction work in C17. SD-001, SD-005, and SD-017 all approach this question from different angles without closing it. The distinction, if it holds, may be: love is the constitutive relational disposition toward the other; compassion is the specific form love takes when the other is suffering. But this is inference from the data, not a finding.

**Compassion / grace (R68):** The CHIN/CHEN root collision (SD-006) raises the boundary between channum (gracious character) and chen (grace as relational gift). The inner-being boundary: is graciousness (channum) a character quality that produces grace (chen), or are they two names for the same inner reality in different registers? Deferred to Session D.

**What is missing (P):** All three critical boundaries are Session D targets. None is established in the current data. These are the most significant structural gaps in T6.5.

findings.session_b_note: For goodness vs love (R103): the data suggests that goodness is the quality standard (what is genuinely beneficial and right) while love is the relational movement (orientation toward the other). At Mic 6:8, loving kindness is one component of what is good — love is positioned within the definition of goodness, not as identical to it. Goodness is the broader normative category; love is a specific directional expression within it. For goodness vs kindness (R99): the programme assigns G5544 to both R67 and R99. In R67 it is an OWNER term; in R99 it is apparently also held. This structural dual-ownership requires resolution — the precise boundary between goodness and kindness as inner-being characteristics sharing a vocabulary term is not drawn in the current data. This is a genuine gap requiring Session D examination. For goodness vs generosity (R65): the disposition/act boundary is the clearest — but H2896A in the Hebrew does not maintain this boundary, as it names both the quality and the action. (OBS-067-OBS-018, OBS-067-OBS-090, SP-067-001)

findings.session_b_note: The racham/chesed overlap at Lam 3:22 ('his chesed never ceases, his rachamim never come to an end') is the programme's clearest example of the boundary difficulty — the two terms are paired in parallel without distinction. At the definitional level the boundary is: chesed = covenantal-faithful love (disposition of the covenant partner); rachamim = compassion-love (response to suffering). But at the verse level they co-occur so consistently that their experiential separation is unclear. Gap: the boundary is analytically drawn but evidentially porous. Session D is the appropriate resolution context.

findings.session_b_note: Mercy-compassion overlap: the same verse can use both terms in parallel (Jam 5:11, Psa 78:38 — "being compassionate [rachum], he atoned [kipper]"). In Psa 78:38 the compassion (*rachum*) is the motivating inner state; the atoning act (*kipper*) is the expression. This suggests compassion is the inner state, mercy the expressed act — but this is interpretive, not definitively stated. The precise boundary between mercy and grace (*chen/chanan*) is similarly elusive — grace connotes unmerited favour more broadly; mercy specifically addresses need or guilt. OBS-111-038.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-006: T6 reveals compassion as the structural centre of the C17 cluster rather than a peripheral member. The love co-occurrence (196/351 = 55.8% of all OWNER verses) is uniquely dominant — compassion and lo…
findings.finding_value: T6 reveals compassion as the structural centre of the C17 cluster rather than a peripheral member. The love co-occurrence (196/351 = 55.8% of all OWNER verses) is uniquely dominant — compassion and love co-occur in more than half of all active verses, raising the programme-level question whether they are truly separable at the data level. Three structural observations from the co-occurrence landscape: (1) compassion sits at C17's centre of gravity (love, mercy, kindness as top three co-occurrences — all within-cluster); (2) compassion generates a human-response cluster (peace, faith, will, surrender, seeking co-occurring at significant levels — the pattern of divine compassion generating human inner-being responses); (3) compassion is constitutively responsive to human distress (despair, guilt, distress, evil all present in the co-occurrence table — compassion operates most characteristically in the presence of need). The CHASAD root crossing compassion (C17) and shame (C06) is the programme's most structurally unexpected finding — a root family that bridges two clusters. Exod 34:6 as the programme's most multiply-anchored verse (6 registries) must be treated as a cluster-level synthesis anchor. The compassion/mercy boundary (SD-009) is the most critical unresolved distinction. T6.7 (dimensional sharing) is programme-stage limited — formally deferred.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-012: T1's primary dimension (Relational Disposition) and T6's co-occurrence landscape are mutually confirming. The love co-occurrence dominance (196 verses) is the co-occurrence expression of T1's relation…
findings.finding_value: T1's primary dimension (Relational Disposition) and T6's co-occurrence landscape are mutually confirming. The love co-occurrence dominance (196 verses) is the co-occurrence expression of T1's relational-disposition classification: love and compassion co-occur at this extraordinary rate because they share the relational-disposition register. T1's finding that compassion is constitutively outward-facing explains why the co-occurrence landscape shows the C17 cluster (love, mercy, kindness) as the primary co-occurrence family. T6's unresolved compassion/mercy distinction (SD-009) is the most critical consequence of T1's definitional incompleteness — the boundary between compassion and mercy as adjacent Relational Disposition characteristics is the definitional question T1 cannot answer without T6 data.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-024: T4's scope-by-need finding (compassion crosses covenantal boundaries) and T6's co-occurrence landscape (the human-response cluster — peace, faith, will, surrender — co-occurring with compassion) revea…
findings.finding_value: T4's scope-by-need finding (compassion crosses covenantal boundaries) and T6's co-occurrence landscape (the human-response cluster — peace, faith, will, surrender — co-occurring with compassion) reveal a structural pattern: divine compassion reaching across boundaries generates a characteristic cluster of human inner-being responses regardless of the covenantal position of the recipient. The Nineveh response (repentance and turning) and the pattern of peace/faith/will/surrender co-occurring with compassion both confirm this: compassion-received generates a recognisable inner-being response cluster that is structurally consistent across relational positions. T6's mapping of the human-response cluster is the co-occurrence evidence for T4's structural finding about scope and response.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-006: T6 produces the most structurally significant finding in the review set for any single tier: grace is not produced by any other inner-being characteristic. It is the originating point of a causal chai…
findings.finding_value: T6 produces the most structurally significant finding in the review set for any single tier: grace is not produced by any other inner-being characteristic. It is the originating point of a causal chain, not its product. This categorically distinguishes grace from every other characteristic reviewed — all others can be produced by at least one other characteristic; grace cannot. This structural uniqueness is confirmed by T2.9's origin analysis (grace originates with God — it does not originate in the human constitutional system) and is analytically consistent across T6.2 (seeking is the posture before grace arrives, not its producer), T6.3 (S-rating on "is grace produced by another characteristic"), and T6.4 (the vocabulary's structural completeness without a generative human-side term). The co-occurrence pattern reveals grace at the intersection of divine initiative and creaturely need: seeking (R140 — 40 verses, dominant) as the creature's pre-grace posture; moral failure cluster (evil, guilt, sin, transgression) as the creaturely context; power cluster (strength, might) confirming the 2Cor 12:9 connection. The love co-occurrence (R103 — 14 verses) is the primary within-cluster signal raising the grace-love boundary question (SD013). All major boundary distinctions (grace-love, grace-mercy, grace-justice, grace-chesed) remain open at T6.5 — the most unresolved boundary cluster in the review set. T6.7 (dimensional sharing) is programme-stage limited.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-024: T4's relational architecture and T6's co-occurrence network express the same structural reality from relational and cross-registry perspectives. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (T6 — R140, 40 vers…
findings.finding_value: T4's relational architecture and T6's co-occurrence network express the same structural reality from relational and cross-registry perspectives. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (T6 — R140, 40 verses) is the co-occurrence expression of T4.2 (the human-to-God supplication direction): seeking is the relational posture, and R140 is the registry that names it. The sequential relationship confirmed in T6.2 (grace precedes and enables faith, repentance, supplication, mourning — SD003, SD006, SD026, SD038) is the causal expression of T4's architectural finding: grace is the enabling condition for every positive human-to-God relational posture. The boundary questions in T6.5 (grace-love, grace-mercy, grace-chesed) correspond to T4.5's scope analysis: the characteristics that share grace's scope (particularly love and mercy) are the same characteristics whose relational scope overlaps with grace's at T4.5.

findings.session_b_note: The hesed-covenant overlap is the most significant boundary question. From the available data: the overlap occurs in passages like Deu 7:9 where "keeping covenant and keeping steadfast love" (shomer haberit vehahesed) names them as parallel but distinct divine attributes. The distinction holds as: covenant = the structural bond (berit); hesed = the motivating quality (love/loyalty) that sustains the bond. The overlap occurs because hesed is what genuine covenantal commitment feels like from the inside — the willing, affective dimension of covenantal faithfulness. But covenant is not reducible to hesed (it includes the formal structure, oath, sign, and sanctions that hesed alone does not carry). Precise boundary: covenant is the form-with-content-and-structure; hesed is the inner relational quality. The boundary is kind-level (not degree-level) — they are different things that always co-occur in healthy covenantal life. Gap: whether this distinction holds uniformly across all 37 shared verses requires Session D cross-registry analysis (SP-034-003).

Gap: boundaries implied by co-occurrence and context but not explicitly theorised. Session D needed for full boundary analysis.

findings.session_b_note: The most precisely delineable boundary is peace vs. trust (R163): trust is the inner act of reliance; peace is the condition trust produces (Isa 26:3 — trust → peace; Psa 4:8 — trust posture → peace condition). They are causally ordered: trust precedes and produces peace; peace confirms and deepens trust. The boundary: trust is volitional (an act), peace is resultant (a state). They are not interchangeable. The peace-joy boundary: peace is the ground-condition; joy is the response-condition. Joy arises from peace but is the felt affective expression, not the existential ground. The peace-rest boundary remains partially unclear — these two may be dimensions of a single complex rather than distinct characteristics. Deferred to Session D.

findings.session_b_note: The overlap between R060 (na.tan — enacted giving) and R099 (hesed — kindness/covenant love) is apparent throughout the compassionate giving texts (872-002). Hos 11:8 — compassion (rahamim) prevents giving-over — shows hesed-like inner-being quality as the source of the giving decision. The boundary within the data: na.tan is the verb that enacts; hesed/rahamim is the quality that determines the direction of the verb. Na.tan can move in the direction of blessing (covenantal giving) or in the direction of judgement (giving-over) depending on the inner-being quality that determines it. Hesed/rahamim always moves toward the other in positive relational orientation. The boundary is: na.tan is the mechanism; hesed is the disposition. But the data does not produce this boundary with full clarity — the verses where both are present (Hos 11:8, the Nehemiah corpus) do not explicitly draw the distinction. Gap confirmed as Session D territory.

findings.finding_value:
The clearest distinctions are established by the anchor verse analysis:

- M15-A vs M15-B: Pro 16:23 (wisdom guiding expression) vs 1Ki 3:9 (asking for a hearing heart) — character expressed vs faculty requested.
- M15-B vs M15-C: 1Ki 3:9 (faculty for governance) vs Hos 6:3 (pressing on to know the LORD) — grasping faculty vs relational pursuit.
- M15-C vs M15-D: Hos 6:3 (knowing as relational pursuit) vs Gen 15:6 (evaluative crediting) — relational content vs evaluative judgment.
- M15-D vs M15-E: Gen 15:6 (divine crediting) vs Isa 14:24 (irresistible counsel) — evaluative act vs purposive declaration.
- M15-E vs M15-F: Pro 16:9 (heart planning) vs Psa 119:97 (meditation all the day) — prospective action vs receptive dwelling.
- M15-F vs M15-G: Psa 119:97 (sustained activity) vs 2Cor 4:4 (content held and targeted) — activity vs content.
- M15-G vs M15-H: 2Cor 4:4 (inner content blinded) vs Col 3:16 (word dwelling and moving) — static holding vs dynamic communication.

findings.finding_value: The boundary between anxiety and fear: anxiety is about the future (anticipated threat); fear is about the present (experienced threat). Mat 14:30 illustrates: Peter sees the wind (present threat → fear → phobos) and this produces distazō (doubt). Fear and doubt are distinguishable at the boundary; anxiety (merimnaō) is the sustained version of the forward-looking element.

findings.finding_value: Grace/mercy overlap in the Exo 34:6 formula (chan.nun and rachum appear together) — at this boundary, the most precise distinction the verse evidence supports is: chan.nun (gracious) names the character of the giver's disposition; rachum (merciful/compassionate) names the giver's inner movement in response to the receiver's condition. Grace is characterological; mercy is responsive. Both are present in the divine character simultaneously but they describe different aspects of how that character operates.

The precise boundary: the anger is M02 (the thermal inner state); the sustained hostile orientation toward the servant of God as a person is M06.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The boundary is most visible in Hab 3:18 ("yet I will rejoice in the Lord") and Psa 13:5 ("my heart shall rejoice in your salvation"). These are exultation — deliberate, surging, directed acts — in the face of adversity. Gladness (M04-O, M04-L) does not operate this way: it is the warm inner response to circumstances assessed as good. Exultation can survive the removal of all good circumstances (Hab 3:18); Gladness is characteristically responsive to present-good circumstances. This is the sharpest boundary.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The "joy and gladness" formulaic pairing (Est 8:16; Isa 35:10; 51:11; Jer 7:34; 33:11; Zep 3:17) is where the boundary is most porous. The pairing suggests co-occurrence rather than identity — both states arise together, confirming they are distinct but adjacent. The boundary is clearest at the extremes: Hab 3:18's volitional Joy under total material loss is not Gladness (Gladness would not characteristically persist under such conditions); conversely, Lam 3:26's "it is good that one should wait quietly for the salvation of the Lord" is Gladness (settled warm inner brightness under adversity) rather than active Joy.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The boundary is the role of suffering: where agalliao appears in contexts of blessing, faith-reception, or divine encounter without adversity as the constitutive occasion (Joh 8:56 — Abraham's anticipatory joy; Act 16:34 — coming-to-faith joy), it belongs to Characteristic 2 or sits in the boundary zone. Where agalliao appears with suffering as the constitutive context and occasion (1Pe 1:6 — grieved by trials yet rejoicing; 1Pe 4:13 — insofar as sharing Christ's sufferings; Mat 5:12 — persecuted yet commanded to rejoice; M04-F's ba.lag — attempted cheer under extreme adversity), it belongs to Characteristic 7. The 1Pe 1:6–8 passage is the most complex boundary case — it holds both the eschatological-Joy dimension and the suffering-paradox dimension simultaneously.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The formulaic "joy and gladness" pairing is the boundary zone. The boundary is clearest at the extremes: (1) Hab 3:18 — volitional joy despite total material loss — this is Joy, not Gladness (Gladness's circumstantial face would not persist under such conditions); (2) Lam 3:26 — "it is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the Lord" — this is Gladness (the evaluative recognition that quiet waiting is the appropriate and genuinely beneficial inner posture) rather than Joy (which would be the active exulting in what is coming). (3) The ki-tov praise declarations (M04-L-VCG-01) — these are primarily Gladness (cognitive recognition of divine goodness producing praise) rather than Joy (though they produce Joy as a co-occurrence).

**[CHAR-4]** E — The tov-comparative verses (Psa 73:28 — "it is good to be near God"; Psa 118:8–9 — "better to take refuge in the Lord") are the boundary zone. The boundary: these verses are assigned to M04-G-VCG-02 (Delight sub-group) rather than M04-L/O (Gladness sub-groups) because their inner-being content is specifically the experiential orientation of the soul toward God as refuge and nearness — object-focused Delight — rather than the evaluative recognition that God's character is good (Gladness). Psa 73:28's "it is good to be near God" is the soul's resting orientation toward God (Delight) rather than the cognitive appraisal that divine nearness is morally superior (Gladness), though both elements are present. The boundary is thin but real.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The a.nog overlap is the boundary zone: (1) a.nog in M04-G (Psa 37:4 — "delight yourself in the Lord") is Delight because it is specifically directed toward God as the treasured object with the reflexive hitpael; (2) a.nog in M04-K-VCG-02 (Deu 28:54, 56 — the pampered person's comfort) is Pleasure because it names a general quality of physical ease rather than directed orientation toward a specific object; (3) ta.a.nug appears in M04-N-VCG-01 (Mic 1:16 — parental Delight in children) as directed attachment and in M04-K-VCG-02 (Pro 19:10; Ecc 2:8; Mic 2:9) as ambient sensory luxury — the same term serving both directed-Delight and ambient-Pleasure contexts.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The Song of the Sea (Exo 15) is the boundary zone: Exo 15:11 ("who is like you… doing wonders?") appears in M04-I-VCG-01 (Wonder) — the question form and the pe.le term mark it as Wonder-language; but Exo 15's larger context is exultation-language (the whole poem is a song of triumph). The boundary: Exo 15:11 is Wonder because it specifically names God's incomparability through the wonder-vocabulary and the rhetorical question of non-comparability; the surrounding song is Exultation. The wonder-verse is the perceptive-cognitive hinge within the larger exultation-song.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The most analytically significant boundary evidence: (1) **Joy/Gladness**: the "joy and gladness" formula marks the co-arising but the extremes mark the distinction — Hab 3:18's volitional exultation in total loss is Joy but not Gladness; Lam 3:26's settled evaluative waiting is Gladness but not Joy; (2) **Joy/Suffering-Joy**: 1Pe 1:6–8 is the most complex boundary verse — it holds both Joy (the Spirit's gift) and Suffering-Joy (the suffering-context) simultaneously; the determining factor is the constitutive role of suffering as the occasion; (3) **Delight/Gladness**: Psa 73:28's "it is good to be near God" marks the boundary — assigned to Delight (M04-G-VCG-02) because the inner content is the soul's resting orientation toward God as refuge (Delight) rather than the cognitive appraisal of divine nearness as morally superior (Gladness); (4) **Delight/Pleasure**: Psa 37:4's a.nog (Delight — directed toward God with reflexive hitpael) vs. Deu 28:54's a.nog (Pleasure — ambient pampered ease) marks the boundary — direction determines the classification.

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-1]** E — The boundary is inner vs. outer. When ka.lam means "the inner confounded feeling" it is CHAR-1 territory; when it means "the social-bodily demotion" it is CHAR-2 territory. Many verses show both simultaneously (the servants covering their heads — Jer 14:3 — evidence the inner shame-response as well as the bodily expression of being brought low). The Phase 5/7 separation into sub-groups handled this: M07-A/B/C carry the inner-experience dimension; M07-D carries the enforced-outer-abasement dimension. The boundary is analytically clean even when the verse evidence naturally shows both at once.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The nearest neighbour distinction with CHAR-1: CHAR-2 is the outer-mechanism; CHAR-1 is the inner-experience. The distinction is of kind (mechanism vs. experience). CHAR-2 is also distinct from CHAR-5 (contempt producing shame): CHAR-5's mechanism is specifically contempt/dismissal; CHAR-2's mechanism is enforced downward movement (which can be produced by contempt but also by military defeat, divine judgment, natural loss).

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 is most closely related to CHAR-5 (shame produced by contempt): both involve the treatment of persons as of diminished worth. The distinction: CHAR-3 names the relational verdict (worth-denial as the act and its structural effect); CHAR-5 names the specific mechanism (contempt/dismissal as the producing agent and its received shame as the specific outcome in the recipient). CHAR-3 is broader — worth-denial can be produced by contempt (CHAR-5), by structural assignment (VCG-02), or by hypocrisy and favoritism (VCG-01) without being contempt in the strict sense.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 is most closely related to CHAR-1 in its moral-consequence register (M07-B — shame as the consequence of moral failure). The distinction: CHAR-1-M07-B is about shame as the experience that follows moral failure; CHAR-4 is about the conscience's recognition of what is shameful as a quality of conduct or desire. CHAR-4 is the evaluative faculty; CHAR-1-M07-B is the experiential consequence. They frequently occur together: the same act that CHAR-4 identifies as shameful produces CHAR-1's shame-experience in the person who commits it.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — CHAR-5 is most closely related to CHAR-3 (dishonour as relational worth-denial) and to M06 (contempt as the producing mechanism). The distinction between CHAR-5 and CHAR-3: CHAR-5 names the specific mechanism (contempt as the producing force) and the received shame as the specific outcome; CHAR-3 names the relational verdict of worth-denial more broadly (which can arise from causes other than contempt). The distinction between CHAR-5 and M06: M06 holds the contempt-projection (the contempt-er's inner act); CHAR-5 holds the contempt-received shame (the recipient's inner experience). CHAR-5 and M06 are relational complements — they are the two faces of the same contempt-shame dynamic.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-6 is most closely related to M12 (purity/holiness) through shared vocabulary, but the analytical distinction is clear: M12 holds the purity/holiness register of niq.qa.von and qe.ha.von as the primary meaning of these terms; CHAR-6 holds the innocence-as-counter-to-shame function of the same terms in every verse of the 8-verse corpus. The distinction is one of purpose and register: M12 = moral and ritual purity as the characteristic; CHAR-6 = innocence as specifically the protection against and structural counter to shame.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — The most important cluster-level distinctions: (1) Experience vs mechanism (Chars 1 vs 2) — the felt shame vs the enforced abasement are analytically distinct even when co-occurring. (2) Specific contempt vs broad dishonour (Chars 5 vs 3) — contempt as zero-worth-assignment is a subset of relational worth-denial. (3) Evaluative quality vs experienced state (Chars 4 vs 1) — what the conscience names as shameful vs what the person experiences as shame. (4) Protective positive condition vs the shame-states it counters (Char 6 vs Chars 1-5) — the one positive characteristic in the cluster vs the five naming shame's forms. These distinctions are the programme's analytical achievement in M07: a field experienced by the ordinary reader as a single phenomenon (shame) has been analytically differentiated into six genuinely distinct characteristics. The distinctness is not imposed but demonstrated by verse-evidence: different verses name different dimensions with different vocabulary in different relational contexts.

---

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-1]** E — The precise boundary is between inner posture (CHAR-1's domain) and specific transgressive act against a named limit (CHAR-2's domain). Num 15:30 (vc=65731, M08-A4-VCG-05) illustrates the boundary: "acting with a high hand" is treated as CHAR-1 because the evidence focuses on the inner posture of raised self-assertion ("an inner posture of defiant self-exaltation against God, where the will deliberately overrides divine command") — the high-hand idiom names the orientation, not the specific act of transgressing a named divine prohibition. The M08-B za.don/zed corpus names the specific wilful transgression of an established divine boundary (the presumptuous sin as a specific category of deliberate violation). The boundary is therefore: if the evidence emphasises the elevated inner posture as the primary datum → CHAR-1; if the evidence emphasises the specific wilful transgression of a named divine limit as the primary datum → CHAR-2. The same person may exhibit both simultaneously, but they remain analytically distinct characteristics.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Verses like Neh 9:16 (vc=34120, M08-B-VCG-01) — "they acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck and did not obey your commandments" — sit at the boundary: the stiff neck is dispositional (CHAR-1 territory); the specific act of disobeying commandments is CHAR-2. The verse is in CHAR-2's corpus because the primary datum is the act of disobedience (the zid boiling-over against a specific commandment), not a general self-elevation. The boundary is the presence of a specific named divine limit against which the will is asserting — when that is present, CHAR-2 is named; when it is absent (the general posture of self-elevation), CHAR-1 is named.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The boundary is between inner cognitive self-assessment (CHAR-4) and public verbal/social assertion of that assessment (CHAR-3). Rom 12:16 context (M08-D): "never be wise in your own sight" — an inner cognitive overclaim that remains in the evaluative register. Jam 4:16 (vc=33886): "you boast" — the same overclaim made public through speech. CHAR-3 is CHAR-4 that has been externalised into speech and social display; CHAR-4 is the inner cognitive stage from which CHAR-3 emerges when it is verbalised.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The boundary is between inner cognitive state (CHAR-4) and outer verbal/social expression (CHAR-3). 1Cor 8:1 (vc=33935, M08-D-VCG-01): knowledge inflating (fusioō) — the inner cognitive state is CHAR-4; when that inflation is then expressed through claims about one's knowledge to others (self-display of cognitive superiority), it crosses into CHAR-3. The cognitive self-inflation can exist before any verbal expression — that pre-verbal state is purely CHAR-4. When it becomes speech, the speech is CHAR-3.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The boundary is the presence of structural goods as the generating occasion and inner anchor. Eze 28:5 (vc=34046, M08-E-VCG-02): "wealth gained through wisdom caused the heart to become proud" — the wealth is the generating occasion for the heart-pride; without the wealth, this specific form of heart-pride (CHAR-5) would not have been generated. A person with CHAR-1 but no structural power has the dispositional elevation without the structural medium. A person with structural power who develops CHAR-5 has CHAR-1's dispositional pattern instantiated through the specific structural medium. CHAR-5 is CHAR-1 plus structural medium.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster comparison confirms the boundary criteria for each pair. CHAR-1/CHAR-2: the presence of a specific named divine limit against which the will is asserting determines CHAR-2; the absence of a specific named limit (general dispositional self-elevation) determines CHAR-1. CHAR-3/CHAR-4: verbalisation into public speech or social display determines CHAR-3; remaining in the cognitive self-assessment register determines CHAR-4. CHAR-1/CHAR-5: the presence of received structural goods as the generating occasion and inner anchor determines CHAR-5; general dispositional elevation without structural-goods requirement determines CHAR-1. The cluster-synthesis: M08's internal boundaries are consistently determined by the specificity of the medium (act vs disposition; verbal vs cognitive; structural-goods-grounded vs general).

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-2]** E — The most significant overlap is at Phili2:8 (Christ "humbled himself by becoming obedient") and Luk17:10 (the servant's self-assessment of unworthiness as the inner fruit of having submitted). The boundary: humility at Phili2:8 is the inner disposition (self-emptying, downward movement of the self); the obedience at Phili2:8 is the specific form that humbling takes in relation to the Father's authority. Luk17:10 shows submission producing humility (the servant's inner non-merit assessment flows from having done all that was commanded) — submission occasions the humble self-assessment rather than being identical to it. The boundary is: submission is the directional yielding to authority; humility is the general self-regarding posture that the submission both expresses and reinforces.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The precise boundary is: the lowly spirit of Isa57:15 (CHAR-1 register) can be present without the contrite spirit (CHAR-3 register) — a person can be genuinely humble without currently being in the acute state of contrition. But the contrite spirit (CHAR-3) is always also lowly (CHAR-1) — contrition implies and includes lowliness. Contrition is thus a subset of the humility register: specifically the acute, grief-laden, crisis-precipitated form that humility takes at the moment of genuine moral confrontation. The boundary is: not all humility is contrition, but genuine contrition always includes lowliness.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The precise boundary is evidenced at Heb5:2: the shared-weakness self-awareness that grounds metriopatheō is also the self-knowledge that characterises genuine humility (CHAR-1). The overlap is at this enabling self-awareness — both characteristics require genuine self-knowledge of one's creaturely limitation. The boundary: humility is what that self-knowledge produces as an inner posture (self-lowering before God and others); meekness/gentleness is what that self-knowledge produces as a relational quality in engagement with the erring and needy. One can have the inner posture (humility) without currently being in the act of engagement with the erring; one exercises meekness/gentleness specifically in the act of engagement.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The overlap between CHAR-1 and CHAR-5 is in the shared non-self-assertive register. The boundary: humility involves the person actively choosing to take the lower place (Phili2:3 — count others more significant; Jam4:10 — humble yourselves); dignity involves the person inhabiting their place and roles with settled gravity without needing to promote or defend their standing (1Ti2:2; 1Ti3:4; Tit2:7 — no active lowering but settled non-promotional inhabiting). The boundary is: humility is the active downward movement; dignity is the stable settled position that does not need to assert upward.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The overlap is at 1Ch28:21 — "every willing man… wholly at your command" — willing-heartedness and submission to command coexist in the same verse: the willing craftsmen are also submissively available ("at your command"). The boundary: the willing-heartedness is what motivates the prior to any command (the inner movement toward service); the submission is the responsive availability when direction is given. Willing-heartedness provides the motivational ground; submission provides the responsive structure. The two are complementary in the service context without being identical.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The overlap is clearest in Isa57:15 (CHAR-3 evidence) which pairs contrition with lowliness: "with him who is contrite and lowly in spirit." This verse sits at the boundary — the contrite person is also lowly, and the humble person who has genuinely failed will also experience contrition. The boundary is: humility is the *stable posture* that does not require the acute triggering of moral failure; contrition is the *acute response* to the specific recognition of failure. A person may be genuinely humble without being in a state of acute contrition; a person in contrition is in the most acute and specific form of the humility register. Contrition implies humility but humility does not always imply contrition.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Five intra-cluster boundary pairs require precise distinctions. CHAR-1/CHAR-3: Isa57:15 holds both — the contrite person is always also lowly, but the reverse does not hold; humility is the stable disposition; contrition is the acute intensity-form occasioned by specific moral crisis. The boundary: all contrition implies humility, but not all humility involves current contrition. CHAR-1/CHAR-2: Phili2:8 holds both — the boundary is relational structure; humility is the general self-lowering posture with no necessary specific authority-target; submission is the specifically authority-directed yielding of the will. One can be genuinely humble without being in an act of specific authority-submission; genuine submission requires some form of humility as its inner ground. CHAR-1/CHAR-4: Mat11:29 holds both — the boundary is register and occasion; humility is the inner posture of self-lowering; meekness/gentleness is the quality of relational engagement that the same self-awareness enables. CHAR-2/CHAR-6: 1Ch28:21 holds both ("willing and wholly at your command") — the boundary is source; willing-heartedness is inner-generated free movement toward service; submission is responsive availability when direction is given. The willing-heartedness precedes any command; the submission is the response to it. CHAR-1/CHAR-5: the boundary is kind and stance — humility is the active downward movement; dignity is the stable settled position that does not assert upward; both non-self-assertive but different in whether they move or rest.

The training is CHAR-10; the trained state is CHAR-6. The same verse (2Pe 2:14) evidences both the process (training) and its outcome (insatiable for sin — the formed CHAR-6-like condition).

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-1]** E — The precise boundary is the origin of the defilement. Characteristic 1: origin is external bodily contact or authoritative verdict — the body encounters a defiling agent or is assessed by a priest. Characteristic 2: origin is the inner person's own volitional and dispositional state — the heart's allegiance disorder, the will's habitual submission to unchecked desire. The VCG-04 sub-register within Characteristic 1 (Lev 11:43-44, M10c-A-VCG-04 — volitional self-defilement) sits at the boundary: the defiling contact is a bodily act, but the willful choice to make it is foregrounded. This sub-register is the closest point of Characteristic 1 to Characteristic 2, but it remains in Characteristic 1 because the mechanism is still bodily contact (the swarming creature), even though the will is explicitly named.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The boundary is the origin and locus of the defilement. Both characteristics use the same Hebrew vocabulary (H2931 ta.me adj) for their primary terms, creating apparent overlap. The boundary: the H2931 verses in Characteristic 2 (VCG-01: Job 14:4, Isa 6:5, Isa 64:6, Hag 2:14; VCG-03: Isa 52:11; VCG-05: Isa 35:8) operate in the Hebrew metaphorical-inner register — they name constitutional moral uncleanness before God, not a ritually defined bodily condition. The H2931 verses in Characteristic 1 (Lev 11-15, Num 5, 9, 19, etc.) name the ritual-status condition from bodily contact or verdict. The boundary is determined by the locus: when H2931 names a constitutional/moral/inner condition = Characteristic 2; when it names a ritual-status condition from bodily mechanism = Characteristic 1.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The boundary is the direction and object of the defilement. When the same ta.me vocabulary names the inner condition of the individual person's conscience, will, and heart = Characteristic 2. When the same vocabulary names the defilement of land, sanctuary, name, or the covenantal relational order as extensions of the community's inner defection = Characteristic 3. Some verses span both: Eze 36:17 (VCG-04) — "they defiled it [the land] by their ways and their deeds" — the "it" (the land) is Characteristic 3's object; the "their ways and their deeds" are the inner disposition of Characteristic 2 producing the extension into Characteristic 3's domain. Characteristic 3 presupposes Characteristic 2 as its generating inner condition.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The apparent overlap is in the shared feature of external causation without volitional cooperation. The precise boundary: Characteristic 1's external cause is impersonal (a material object, a biological state, a verdict) and produces a ritual-status condition managed by prescribed Levitical remedies. Characteristic 4's external cause is personal, purposeful, and adversarial (a spiritual being with its own will and agency) producing a condition of personal domination requiring divine command for resolution. The boundary is determined by the nature of the external cause: impersonal/material vs personal/spiritual-adversarial.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's boundary-points are determined by locus and mechanism in each case. Chars 1-2 boundary: when H2931 ta.me names a ritual-bodily condition from mechanism/verdict = Char 1; when H2931 names a constitutional/moral/inner condition before God = Char 2. The VCG-04 sub-register (Lev 11:43-44 — volitional self-defilement through deliberate contact) is the closest boundary-point: bodily mechanism (Char 1 side) but foregrounded will (Char 2 territory). Chars 2-3 boundary: when ta.me vocabulary names the individual inner person's condition = Char 2; when the same vocabulary names the defilement extended to land, sanctuary, name = Char 3. Eze 36:17 — "they defiled it by their ways and their deeds" — sits at the boundary: the "it" (the land) is Char 3's object; the "their ways and their deeds" are Char 2's generating inner-moral condition producing Char 3's outward extension. Chars 1-4 boundary: the nature of the external cause determines the boundary — impersonal/material = Char 1; personal/purposeful/adversarial spiritual agent = Char 4. The boundaries are all locus/mechanism determined, not vocabulary determined.

questions.section: T6 — Structural Relationships with Other Characteristics
questions.question_text: Is the distinction from the nearest neighbour one of degree, kind, direction, or constitutional level?

findings.session_b_note:
From the available evidence, the distinction between forgiveness and mercy appears to be **primarily one of specificity (kind) rather than degree, direction, or constitutional level**:

- Both operate from God toward the human person (same direction)
- Both appear at the divine-attribute level (same constitutional level — divine character)
- Both are positive relational characteristics (same valence)

The difference is in **what they specifically address**: mercy covers the broad relational generosity of God toward creaturely need and vulnerability; forgiveness specifically addresses the moral debt condition (guilt, trespass, sin). The kind of need each addresses differs — mercy responds to need and vulnerability generally; forgiveness responds to the specific need created by moral failure and its resulting guilt-charge.

This is a distinction of **kind and scope** — mercy is the broader category; forgiveness is the specific instance within it directed at moral debt. If this is correct, forgiveness is a subset of mercy rather than a distinct parallel characteristic. This hypothesis is supported by DIM-064-SD016 but not confirmed — it requires Session D synthesis.

findings.session_b_note:
From the partial evidence available:

**Compassion vs mercy — potentially constitutional level:** If the SD-016 three-stage model holds, the distinction is one of constitutional level (somatic event vs soul-level disposition) rather than of kind or degree. This would make compassion and mercy two stages in a single constitutional movement rather than two alternative expressions of the same inner quality. This is the most analytically productive hypothesis from the data but is not confirmed.

**Compassion vs love — potentially directional:** The data implies that love is the wider relational disposition and compassion is love directed specifically toward suffering. If so, the distinction is directional: the same inner quality oriented differently. But the RACHAM root-sharing makes this uncertain — the same vocabulary roots carry both concepts.

**Compassion vs grace — potentially directional:** Channum (gracious character) moves toward those who need favour; chen (grace) is the favour extended. The distinction may be directional (the inner character vs the relational act), similar to the compassion/mercy question.

**What is missing (P):** The precise nature of the distinction — degree, kind, direction, or constitutional level — cannot be determined from the current data for any of the three critical boundary pairs. All three require Session D synthesis across the full vocabulary of the adjacent registries. These are not new gaps — they are all captured in existing SD pointers.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-006: T6 reveals compassion as the structural centre of the C17 cluster rather than a peripheral member. The love co-occurrence (196/351 = 55.8% of all OWNER verses) is uniquely dominant — compassion and lo…
findings.finding_value: T6 reveals compassion as the structural centre of the C17 cluster rather than a peripheral member. The love co-occurrence (196/351 = 55.8% of all OWNER verses) is uniquely dominant — compassion and love co-occur in more than half of all active verses, raising the programme-level question whether they are truly separable at the data level. Three structural observations from the co-occurrence landscape: (1) compassion sits at C17's centre of gravity (love, mercy, kindness as top three co-occurrences — all within-cluster); (2) compassion generates a human-response cluster (peace, faith, will, surrender, seeking co-occurring at significant levels — the pattern of divine compassion generating human inner-being responses); (3) compassion is constitutively responsive to human distress (despair, guilt, distress, evil all present in the co-occurrence table — compassion operates most characteristically in the presence of need). The CHASAD root crossing compassion (C17) and shame (C06) is the programme's most structurally unexpected finding — a root family that bridges two clusters. Exod 34:6 as the programme's most multiply-anchored verse (6 registries) must be treated as a cluster-level synthesis anchor. The compassion/mercy boundary (SD-009) is the most critical unresolved distinction. T6.7 (dimensional sharing) is programme-stage limited — formally deferred.

findings.finding_value: T1's primary dimension (Relational Disposition) and T6's co-occurrence landscape are mutually confirming. The love co-occurrence dominance (196 verses) is the co-occurrence expression of T1's relational-disposition classification: love and compassion co-occur at this extraordinary rate because they share the relational-disposition register. T1's finding that compassion is constitutively outward-facing explains why the co-occurrence landscape shows the C17 cluster (love, mercy, kindness) as the primary co-occurrence family. T6's unresolved compassion/mercy distinction (SD-009) is the most critical consequence of T1's definitional incompleteness — the boundary between compassion and mercy as adjacent Relational Disposition characteristics is the definitional question T1 cannot answer without T6 data.

findings.finding_value: T4's scope-by-need finding (compassion crosses covenantal boundaries) and T6's co-occurrence landscape (the human-response cluster — peace, faith, will, surrender — co-occurring with compassion) reveal a structural pattern: divine compassion reaching across boundaries generates a characteristic cluster of human inner-being responses regardless of the covenantal position of the recipient. The Nineveh response (repentance and turning) and the pattern of peace/faith/will/surrender co-occurring with compassion both confirm this: compassion-received generates a recognisable inner-being response cluster that is structurally consistent across relational positions. T6's mapping of the human-response cluster is the co-occurrence evidence for T4's structural finding about scope and response.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-006: T6 produces the most structurally significant finding in the review set for any single tier: grace is not produced by any other inner-being characteristic. It is the originating point of a causal chai…
findings.finding_value: T6 produces the most structurally significant finding in the review set for any single tier: grace is not produced by any other inner-being characteristic. It is the originating point of a causal chain, not its product. This categorically distinguishes grace from every other characteristic reviewed — all others can be produced by at least one other characteristic; grace cannot. This structural uniqueness is confirmed by T2.9's origin analysis (grace originates with God — it does not originate in the human constitutional system) and is analytically consistent across T6.2 (seeking is the posture before grace arrives, not its producer), T6.3 (S-rating on "is grace produced by another characteristic"), and T6.4 (the vocabulary's structural completeness without a generative human-side term). The co-occurrence pattern reveals grace at the intersection of divine initiative and creaturely need: seeking (R140 — 40 verses, dominant) as the creature's pre-grace posture; moral failure cluster (evil, guilt, sin, transgression) as the creaturely context; power cluster (strength, might) confirming the 2Cor 12:9 connection. The love co-occurrence (R103 — 14 verses) is the primary within-cluster signal raising the grace-love boundary question (SD013). All major boundary distinctions (grace-love, grace-mercy, grace-justice, grace-chesed) remain open at T6.5 — the most unresolved boundary cluster in the review set. T6.7 (dimensional sharing) is programme-stage limited.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-024: T4's relational architecture and T6's co-occurrence network express the same structural reality from relational and cross-registry perspectives. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (T6 — R140, 40 vers…
findings.finding_value: T4's relational architecture and T6's co-occurrence network express the same structural reality from relational and cross-registry perspectives. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (T6 — R140, 40 verses) is the co-occurrence expression of T4.2 (the human-to-God supplication direction): seeking is the relational posture, and R140 is the registry that names it. The sequential relationship confirmed in T6.2 (grace precedes and enables faith, repentance, supplication, mourning — SD003, SD006, SD026, SD038) is the causal expression of T4's architectural finding: grace is the enabling condition for every positive human-to-God relational posture. The boundary questions in T6.5 (grace-love, grace-mercy, grace-chesed) correspond to T4.5's scope analysis: the characteristics that share grace's scope (particularly love and mercy) are the same characteristics whose relational scope overlaps with grace's at T4.5.

The distinctions confirm that covenant is genuinely a distinct inner-being reality, not reducible to adjacent characteristics.

findings.session_b_note: The distinction between R060 (na.tan) and its nearest neighbours (R099 hesed, R103 love) is one of kind rather than degree or direction. They are not more or less of the same thing — they are analytically distinct types of inner-being reality: (1) Hesed/love are dispositional — they name a stable inner orientation of the person toward the other; (2) Na.tan is actional — it names the specific act in which the disposition becomes external and real. The distinction is between inner quality and outer enactment, not between stronger or weaker versions of the same quality. The distinction from R059 (faith/trust) is of direction: trust is the inner-being movement toward God in reliance; giving is the inner-being movement toward the other in commitment. Different direction, not different degree. These are distinctions of kind (dispositional vs. actional) and direction — not of constitutional level (both operate across the full spirit-soul-body range) and not of degree.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-005: The disposition-in-action structure (T1) and the connecting-hub position (T6) are directly related. The characteristic's actional nature (it is a verb, not a noun) means it produces other characterist…
findings.finding_value: The disposition-in-action structure (T1) and the connecting-hub position (T6) are directly related. The characteristic's actional nature (it is a verb, not a noun) means it produces other characteristics as its outputs (worship, hope, wisdom) and is produced by others as its inputs (love, compassion, trust). This producing/produced-by structure is precisely what makes it a hub: it sits at the intersection of multiple causal chains. The distinction of kind from nearest neighbours (T6.5, Q&A-162 — dispositional vs. actional) confirms that its structural position in the landscape is as the enacted form of what dispositional characteristics name. What this pair reveals: the definition of faithfulness-as-giving (actional) is the structural reason for its hub position. Because it is an act that can express any of the adjacent dispositions, it sits at the centre of the dispositional cluster. It is the verbal form of a field of nouns.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-021: The structural landscape analysis (T6 — hub position, aman root architecture entangling R059/R044/R060, distinction of kind from nearest neighbours) and the vocabulary/methodological analysis (T7 — fu…
findings.finding_value: The structural landscape analysis (T6 — hub position, aman root architecture entangling R059/R044/R060, distinction of kind from nearest neighbours) and the vocabulary/methodological analysis (T7 — full vocabulary arc, grammatically actional, primary anchor Hos 11:8) produce the final convergent finding. The aman root architecture (T6.4.2, Q&A-157) and the vocabulary arc (T7.1.10, Q&A-179) are describing the same reality: the programme's separation of registries by word is an analytical convenience that cuts across a root-level unity. The vocabulary arc — enacted pole (na.tan/verb) + constituted pole (emunah/hesed/pistis/nouns) — names the same reality that the root architecture identifies: the aman root generates both the dispositional terms and the contextual terms, while na.tan provides the enacted verbal expression. The grammatically actional character of na.tan (T7.1.2, Q&A-171) is the structural reason for its distinction-of-kind from the nominal faithfulness vocabulary (T6.5.3, Q&A-162). What this pair reveals as the final synthesis: the vocabulary evidence and the structural landscape evidence independently converge on the same conclusion — this characteristic is the enacted form of what the faithfulness vocabulary names dispositionally, and this distinction is fundamental to understanding both the characteristic itself and its position in the inner-being landscape.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Primarily **degree and direction**. The constitutional level (soul and heart) is shared. The direction for both is primarily Godward. The difference is in degree (intensity: exultation is the more surging, triumphant state; gladness is warmer and more diffuse) and in the relationship to circumstances (exultation can transcend adverse circumstances; gladness is more responsive to them).

**[CHAR-2]** E — Primarily **kind and degree**, with some difference in constitutional level. Kind: Joy is active/participatory; Gladness is warm/diffuse — these are different kinds of inner-being state, not merely different intensities of the same state. Degree: Joy is consistently more intense than Gladness in the evidence (the feast-joy is exuberant; Gladness can be quiet). Constitutional level: both are primarily heart-located; Joy additionally appears at spirit level (Luk 1:47; Gal 5:22) more consistently than Gladness.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Primarily **kind and context**: (1) Kind — the paradoxical structure (joy through/in suffering rather than joy in what is good) marks a different type of inner-being state; (2) Context — the constitutive role of suffering is the defining contextual marker; (3) Constitutional level — Suffering-Joy has a stronger spirit-level evidence (Luk 1:47; Luk 10:21) than Joy's general corpus, though Joy also has spirit-level registers (1Th 1:6). The direction is similar (both Godward); the degree is similar in the agalliao register (both intense).

**[CHAR-3]** E — Primarily **kind** (different types of inner-being state: cognitive-evaluative warmth vs. active participatory engagement) with secondary **degree** differences (Joy is typically more intense) and minor **constitutional level** differences (Joy has stronger spirit-level evidence through the NT; Gladness has stronger cognitive-faculty evidence). The direction is similar (both primarily Godward in their healthy forms). Kind is the primary distinction.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Primarily **kind** — they are different types of inner-being state: object-focused resting-satisfaction (Delight) vs. diffuse cognitive warmth (Gladness). Secondary **constitutional level** difference: Delight's primary constitutional home is the soul and the inner being (Mat 12:18; Rom 7:22); Gladness's is the cognitive-evaluative faculty and heart. The direction is similar (both have God as their proper primary object); the degree varies (Delight can be more intense in the sha.a.shu.im register, Gladness more stable in the ki-tov register).

**[CHAR-5]** E — Primarily **direction and kind**: (1) Direction — Delight is directed toward a specific treasured object; Pleasure is received from what is genuinely agreeable; (2) Kind — Delight is fundamentally volitional-affective (the will and affect oriented toward the object); Pleasure is fundamentally receptive-experiential (the inner being receiving pleasantness); (3) Constitutional level — secondary difference: Delight's primary constitutional evidence is the soul and inner being; Pleasure's is more explicitly bodily and sensory.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Primarily **kind**: they are different types of inner response to God's extraordinary acts — one arrested-cognitive (Wonder) and one active-emotive-upward (Exultation). Secondary **direction**: Wonder is directed perceptively toward the wondrous object; Exultation is directed actively upward in response. Not merely a difference of degree (stronger Joy) but a qualitatively different inner state.

Secondary distinctions of **direction** (Delight is always toward a specific object; Pleasure is ambient) and **constitutional level** (Suffering-Joy has the strongest spirit-level evidence; Pleasure has the strongest body-level evidence) complete the picture. The cluster's phenomenological differentiation is genuine, not merely lexical.

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-1]** E — The distinction between CHAR-1 and CHAR-2 is primarily one of *kind* (inner experience vs. outer mechanism) with a directional component (inward vs. outward focus). It is not a difference of constitutional level (both operate at the soul-body interface) or degree (CHAR-1 is not simply a lesser form of CHAR-2). They are analytically distinct characteristics that frequently co-occur and share vocabulary but evidence different inner-being content.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The nearest neighbour distinction with CHAR-1: CHAR-2 is the outer-mechanism; CHAR-1 is the inner-experience. The distinction is of kind (mechanism vs. experience). CHAR-2 is also distinct from CHAR-5 (contempt producing shame): CHAR-5's mechanism is specifically contempt/dismissal; CHAR-2's mechanism is enforced downward movement (which can be produced by contempt but also by military defeat, divine judgment, natural loss).

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 is most closely related to CHAR-5 (shame produced by contempt): both involve the treatment of persons as of diminished worth. The distinction: CHAR-3 names the relational verdict (worth-denial as the act and its structural effect); CHAR-5 names the specific mechanism (contempt/dismissal as the producing agent and its received shame as the specific outcome in the recipient). CHAR-3 is broader — worth-denial can be produced by contempt (CHAR-5), by structural assignment (VCG-02), or by hypocrisy and favoritism (VCG-01) without being contempt in the strict sense.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 is most closely related to CHAR-1 in its moral-consequence register (M07-B — shame as the consequence of moral failure). The distinction: CHAR-1-M07-B is about shame as the experience that follows moral failure; CHAR-4 is about the conscience's recognition of what is shameful as a quality of conduct or desire. CHAR-4 is the evaluative faculty; CHAR-1-M07-B is the experiential consequence. They frequently occur together: the same act that CHAR-4 identifies as shameful produces CHAR-1's shame-experience in the person who commits it.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — CHAR-5 is most closely related to CHAR-3 (dishonour as relational worth-denial) and to M06 (contempt as the producing mechanism). The distinction between CHAR-5 and CHAR-3: CHAR-5 names the specific mechanism (contempt as the producing force) and the received shame as the specific outcome; CHAR-3 names the relational verdict of worth-denial more broadly (which can arise from causes other than contempt). The distinction between CHAR-5 and M06: M06 holds the contempt-projection (the contempt-er's inner act); CHAR-5 holds the contempt-received shame (the recipient's inner experience). CHAR-5 and M06 are relational complements — they are the two faces of the same contempt-shame dynamic.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-6 is most closely related to M12 (purity/holiness) through shared vocabulary, but the analytical distinction is clear: M12 holds the purity/holiness register of niq.qa.von and qe.ha.von as the primary meaning of these terms; CHAR-6 holds the innocence-as-counter-to-shame function of the same terms in every verse of the 8-verse corpus. The distinction is one of purpose and register: M12 = moral and ritual purity as the characteristic; CHAR-6 = innocence as specifically the protection against and structural counter to shame.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — The most important cluster-level distinctions: (1) Experience vs mechanism (Chars 1 vs 2) — the felt shame vs the enforced abasement are analytically distinct even when co-occurring. (2) Specific contempt vs broad dishonour (Chars 5 vs 3) — contempt as zero-worth-assignment is a subset of relational worth-denial. (3) Evaluative quality vs experienced state (Chars 4 vs 1) — what the conscience names as shameful vs what the person experiences as shame. (4) Protective positive condition vs the shame-states it counters (Char 6 vs Chars 1-5) — the one positive characteristic in the cluster vs the five naming shame's forms. These distinctions are the programme's analytical achievement in M07: a field experienced by the ordinary reader as a single phenomenon (shame) has been analytically differentiated into six genuinely distinct characteristics. The distinctness is not imposed but demonstrated by verse-evidence: different verses name different dimensions with different vocabulary in different relational contexts.

---

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-1]** E — The distinction is primarily one of kind (disposition vs. specific transgressive act) and secondarily of direction (CHAR-1's elevation is inward/upward — the self lifted; CHAR-2's defiance is outward/against — the will asserting itself against an external authority). It is not a distinction of degree (more or less of the same thing) nor of constitutional level (both CHAR-1 and CHAR-2 are located in the heart and will at the same constitutional depth — Dan 5:20, vc=34129, shows the heart and spirit engaged simultaneously in CHAR-1, while the M08-B corpus similarly locates CHAR-2 in the will). The distinction of kind means CHAR-1 can exist without any specific act of transgression (the proud dispositional walk of Dan 4:37, vc=34094, is CHAR-1 without a named specific divine limit being violated) while CHAR-2 requires a specific transgression-event. CHAR-1 is the inner climate; CHAR-2 is the storm.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Primarily kind (disposition vs. specific transgressive act) and, secondarily, specificity of the opposing authority (CHAR-1's elevation is general — above all; CHAR-2's defiance is specific — against this law, this judge, this divine word). The distinction is not of degree (one is not more intense than the other) or of constitutional level (both are located in the heart and will). The kind distinction (settled being vs. activated doing) is the primary analytical marker.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Primarily kind (inner cognitive vs outer verbal/social) and constitutional level (inner-evaluative level for CHAR-4; expressive/communicative level for CHAR-3). Not primarily degree (both can be equally intense at their respective levels). The direction is the same (both are self-directed); the constitutional level and expression mode differ.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Primarily constitutional level (inner cognitive vs outer verbal/social) and kind (epistemic vs communicative). Not degree (both can be equally intense at their level). The direction is the same (both self-directed). Constitutional level distinction: CHAR-4 operates at the mind level; CHAR-3 at the speech/social level. CHAR-4 is the inner cognitive stage from which CHAR-3 emerges when the self-assessment becomes verbalised.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Primarily kind (general dispositional elevation vs structural-medium-specific dispositional elevation) and structural medium (CHAR-5 requires structural goods; CHAR-1 does not). The direction is the same (both self-directed, both upward-elevation). The constitutional level is the same (both heart-dispositional). The distinction is in the specificity of the generating occasion and the structural anchoring: CHAR-5 is CHAR-1 with a structural-power medium; CHAR-1 is the universal dispositional form of which CHAR-5 is the structural-power sub-form.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster comparison reveals that M08's internal distinctions are consistently of kind and constitutional level rather than of degree. CHAR-1 vs CHAR-2: kind (disposition vs act) — not degree. CHAR-3 vs CHAR-4: constitutional level (communicative vs cognitive) — not degree. CHAR-1 vs CHAR-5: kind (general vs structural-medium-specific) — not degree. CHAR-1 vs CHAR-4: constitutional level (dispositional-heart vs cognitive-mind). The cluster-synthesis: M08's characteristics are qualitatively distinct — they are five different kinds of the same root disorder, not five intensities of a single kind.

findings.finding_value: **[CHAR-2]** E — The distinction is primarily one of *direction and relational structure*. Humility has no necessary specific authority-target (one can be humble in one's own inner posture without being in an active submission-relationship); submission is constitutively directed toward a specific authority. The distinction is not primarily of constitutional level (both operate at heart/will level) nor of degree (both can be deep or shallow). It is structural: humility is the inner posture relative to self; submission is the inner posture relative to a specific other-in-authority.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The distinction is primarily one of *intensity and temporal form* — which is close to *degree* combined with *occasion*. Both characteristics operate at the same constitutional levels (spirit and heart); both are Godward in direction; both are in the same semantic domain of inner lowering before God. What differs is the intensity (contrition is acute; humility is stable) and the specific occasion (contrition requires a moral-failure trigger or holiness-encounter; humility is the stable ongoing posture). The distinction is not of kind (both are inner postures before God) or of constitutional level, but of intensity-form and occasion.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The distinction is primarily one of *register and occasion*. Both operate at the same constitutional level (will, self-knowledge, heart), both are enabled by the same inner self-awareness, and both are Godward and other-directed. The difference is: humility is the inner posture that the self-awareness produces as a stable orientation; meekness/gentleness is the specific quality of outward relational engagement that the same self-awareness enables. The distinction is contextual-relational rather than of constitutional level or kind.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The distinction is primarily one of *kind and stance*. Both operate at the character-level and both are non-self-assertive. But humility is dynamic (the act of self-lowering) while dignity is settled (the stable character quality of grounded non-assertion). The distinction in kind: humility is a movement; dignity is a resting-place. The distinction in direction: humility points downward (active self-lowering); dignity does not primarily move in any direction but rests in settled gravity.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The distinction is primarily one of *source and occasion*. Both characteristics operate at the same constitutional level (will/heart) and both are Godward in their ultimate direction. The distinction: submission is occasioned by a command from a specific authority (responsive); willing-heartedness is generated from within the person's own freely-moving heart (spontaneous). The distinction in source (external occasion vs internal generation) is the primary characterising difference — not degree, kind, or constitutional level.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The distinction between Humility and Contrition is primarily one of *temporal form and affective intensity* — which is close to *degree* combined with *constitutional level*. Both operate at the heart and spirit level; both are relational toward God; both involve the person's posture before God's authority and rightness. The distinction is in the *intensity and occasion* (acute crisis-response versus stable disposition) and in the *affective loading* (contrition carries grief, crushed-spirit affect as primary; humility may or may not be accompanied by weeping at any given moment). It is not a distinction of *kind* (both are inner postures before God) or primarily of *direction* (both are Godward in their primary orientation).

**[CLUSTER]** E — The five boundary pairs involve different kinds of distinction. CHAR-1/CHAR-3: primarily degree and temporal form (same semantic domain; different intensity and occasion — not of kind or constitutional level). CHAR-1/CHAR-2: primarily direction and relational structure (both at heart/will level; different relational targets — general vs authority-specific). CHAR-1/CHAR-4: primarily register and occasion (same constitutional level; different contexts of expression). CHAR-2/CHAR-6: primarily source and occasion (same constitutional level — will/heart; different trigger — command-responsive vs spontaneously self-generating). CHAR-1/CHAR-5: primarily kind and stance (same non-self-assertive family; different character — movement vs settled resting position). Cluster-level: the distinctions within M09 are primarily of degree, direction, register, and source rather than of constitutional level. All six operate at similar constitutional depth; what differentiates them is the form, direction, occasion, and character of the inner operation.

---
